If I happen to wager on player futures props in any sport, I always look toward a guy with major contract motivations, and that's the spot the 24-year-old Gibbs is in. Because he was a first-round pick in 2023, Gibbs is now eligible for an extension on his rookie deal, and he might become the highest-paid running back in league history.
While the Lions disappointed last season, in large part due to injuries and having to replace both their offensive and defensive coordinators, Gibbs had another monster year. He had 1,223 yards rushing and 13 scores, along with 77 catches for 616 yards and five scores. His 18 total touchdowns were second in the NFL .
While Gibbs' rushing numbers were slightly down from 2024, all his receiving numbers were career highs. His 49 career touchdowns are an NFL record through a player's first three seasons in the league. He is the second player in NFL history to average at least 5.0 yards per carry in each of his past three seasons (minimum of 150 attempts in each).
Gibbs is tied for the second-best average yards per touch (5.9) of any running back in his first three seasons since the 1970 merger (minimum 750 touches). Finally, Gibbs is first in scrimmage touchdowns (38) and third in scrimmage yards (3,768) the past two seasons.  He is the only player in franchise history to have multiple seasons with 17 or more touchdowns.
Dude is going to get paid, but he and Atlanta tailback Bijan Robinson – taken four spots ahead of Gibbs in 2023 – are somewhat in a standoff, with neither wanting to set the market first. The Eagles ' Saquon Barkley reset the top of the tailback market in March 2025 by signing a two-year extension with Philadelphia at $20.6 million per year.
Late last week, DraftKings was kind enough to release updated trends for NFL Offensive Player of the Year. Gibbs is the +700 favorite and leads all players in both tickets and handle, although the book didn't give me those exact numbers – Robinson (+850) is second in both. Without question, OPOY is now a non-quarterback award, while MVP is pretty much for QBs.
Detroit's only two winners of Offensive Player of the Year were legendary tailback Barry Sanders in 1994 and '97. Gibbs has a lot more offensive talent around him than Robinson does, that's for sure, and he's now the clear featured back after Detroit traded David Montgomery to Houston in March. Gibbs and Montgomery had 15 games where they each scored a TD, the most by a duo in NFL history. The Lions were 15-0 in those.
Montgomery had 172 touches last year, and many of those will go straight to Gibbs, who took 67% of the offensive snaps in 2026 after getting 56% in 2024 and 57% as a rookie. Some Lions beat writers expect a number close to 75% this year.
"He's going to be our bell cow now," Dan Campbell said to the media. "He really became more of that last year, but we're going to hang our hat on him quite a bit. We're going to do a lot of things we feel like he does well."

title: Ranking top 10 NFL rookie wide receivers based on projected 2026 impact
summary: With five first-round receivers entering the league, we rank the first-year pass catchers poised to make the biggest immediate impacts
full_text:
Tight end usage is on the rise across the NFL , but only one stood among last season's top-20 in receiving yards. The game is still dominated by big-play wide receivers and several are entering the league in 2026.
There were five wide receivers taken in the first round and 17 picked in the top-100 overall of the 2026 NFL Draft . Nine rookie wide receivers have eclipsed 1,000 receiving yards over the past five years. With the exception of Puka Nacua , all were first-round draft picks. The average size of those players is just shy of 6-foot-1, 199 pounds. Using that information, which rookie receivers will be most impactful this season?
Over the last five years, there have been 25 wide receivers drafted in the first round. Excluding Jameson Williams, who played fewer than 10 games, those players averaged 62.08 receptions on 100.5 targets for 799 yards and 5 touchdowns.
Here are the top-10 rookie wide receivers, in terms of production, entering the 2026 season:
Douglas claims the final spot because someone has to catch passes in the Miami offense. Chris Bell was a preferred prospect, but injuries may complicate his rookie season. Of the 17 rookie wide receivers drafted top-100 overall, 10 made this list, but Malachi Fields ( Giants ), Zachariah Branch ( Falcons ), Ja'Kobi Lane ( Ravens ), Chris Brazzell ( Panthers ), Ted Hurst ( Buccaneers ), Zavion Thomas ( Bears ) and the aforementioned Bell were excluded.
Douglas is a bigger body, so his profile is a bit different than Malik Washington , Bell and some of Miami's other outlets. Among players with at least 25 pass attempts in 2025, Willis ranked first in air yards per attempt (10.1), according to TruMedia. A small sample size, but he is willing to push the ball downfield.
CBS Sports' fantasy football experts project 35 receptions for 432 yards and three touchdowns.
Bernard was a personal favorite during the pre-draft process because he is so reliable. He presents himself well against the soft spots in zone coverage, but is also willing to seal the edge in the run game or deliver a game-breaking open field block. His contributions may not always show up on the stat sheet, but accountability has always been important with Aaron Rodgers . Randall Cobb made a career understanding how to operate in space and hit his mark on time. DK Metcalf and Michael Pittman Jr. will almost certainly command high-volume shares in Pittsburgh's offense, but do not sleep on Bernard.
CBS Sports' fantasy football experts project 42 receptions for 508 yards and three touchdowns.
Stribling draft standing was a media point of contention. It led to surly responses from Kyle Shanahan and John Lynch in post-draft press conferences. Since the draft, sources suggested that Stribling was likely getting drafted soon had San Francisco not made the move first. The backlash may lead the team to force the player's involvement to validate the actions, despite the additions of Mike Evans and Christian Kirk .
Stribling is a dynamic performer who should be able to capitalize on Shanahan's ability to scheme players open. CBS Sports' fantasy football experts project 44 receptions for 574 yards and three touchdowns.
Williams was a steal for Washington. His capabilities surpass where he was taken in the draft. Aside from the potential addition of Brandon Aiyuk , which now looks less likely given recent social media posts, the Commanders ' depth chart is wide open for Williams to make an impact alongside Terry McLaurin . Dyami Brown , Luke McCaffrey , Jaylin Lane and Treylon Burks are others competing for a similar target share.
Williams is predominantly a slot receiver who can create yardage in the short to intermediate portions of the field. CBS Sports' fantasy football experts project 48 receptions for 678 yards and four touchdowns.
There are multiple young receivers in northeast Ohio, including second-round pick Denzel Boston , Concepcion and last year's coveted undrafted free agent pickup Isaiah Bond , in addition to Jerry Jeudy and Cedric Tillman . It would not be a surprise if Cleveland moved Jeudy and/or Tillman to create more opportunities for the youth.
Coming from Baltimore, where he had commanded the offense, Todd Monken was familiar with smaller body types and could manufacture touches for the likes of Zay Flowers . Concepcion is electric with the ball in his hands and may be used in the return game as well.
CBS Sports' fantasy football experts project 50 receptions for 644 yards and three touchdowns.
Concepcion was taken earlier and was rated higher, but Cooper has fewer roadblocks to productivity. Garrett Wilson is the breadwinner for the AFC franchise, but he missed 10 games this season after zero missed games in the first three years of his career. The team tacked AD Mitchell onto the Sauce Gardner trade last year, but there are hardly any proven commodities among the unit aside from Wilson.
Cooper's ceiling may not be as high as others in his draft class, but he is physical and accountable relative to his size. There is confidence producing modest production, at the very least, this season. CBS Sports' fantasy football experts project 53 receptions for 623 yards and four touchdowns.
Generally, little stock should be placed in pre-season buzz, but the Washington product is said to have hit the ground running and is poised to have a good rookie season. At 6-foot-4, 215, Boston is a physical ball-winner with a bit of nuance to his route-running. Tetairoa McMillan and Drake London are a few of the bigger receivers setting the course for those built like Boston.
CBS Sports' fantasy football experts project 46 receptions for 585 yards and three touchdowns.
Philadelphia said goodbye to A.J. Brown and hello to Lemon. Fans should not expect the first-round pick to be a 1-for-1 replacement of Brown, but the latter's team-leading 121 targets go back into the pile. The team acquired Dontayvion Wicks via trade, but there are plenty of opportunities within Sean Mannion's offense.
Lemon may be more diminutive in stature, but he plays bigger than his size and has a knack for creating yards after the catch.
CBS Sports' fantasy football experts project 53 receptions for 623 yards and four touchdowns.
Tate is in a similar situation to Lemon. Titans quarterback Cam Ward is willing to let the ball fly, and Tate has the size, speed, and tracking ability to allow for those downfield connections. Tate averaged 14.62 air yards per target last season with the Buckeyes, according to TruMedia. His ceiling may not be as high as Tyson's, but his floor is much higher. The ex-Buckeye has a physical play style to ensure he wins his share of contested catch opportunities.
Tennessee also has more mouths to feed within the offense between Calvin Ridley , Wan'Dale Robinson and emerging tight end Gunnar Helm .
CBS Sports' fantasy football experts project 56 receptions for 773 yards and four touchdowns for Tate in 2026.
Olave has not completed a season without missing a game, but, aside from the 2024 campaign, he also has not missed a lot of time. There are a few other rookies and underwhelming veterans on the depth chart, so Tyson should receive ample volume in the pass game if he is healthy. Injuries are another consideration with the Arizona State product, as he missed significant time throughout his collegiate career. Tyson is dynamic with the ball in his hands and capable of turning a missed tackle into a game-changing play.
CBS Sports' fantasy football experts project Tyson to be the top-performing rookie wide receiver: 61 receptions for 869 yards and four touchdowns. He was my personal WR1 during the pre-draft process as well.
author: Josh Edwards

title: Four NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year sleepers to consider, including 49ers' De'Zhaun Stribling
summary: Jeremiyah Love and Fernando Mendoza are the favorites to win OROY, but these four players offer value
full_text:
With training camps opening up around the NFL this week, one of the main storylines to watch is the rookies. Will quarterback Fernando Mendoza outperform Kirk Cousins on the practice field in Vegas? Could Carnell Tate skyrocket up fantasy big boards by showing he has an automatic connection with Cam Ward ?
Since several rookies are about to make headlines, this is a good time to revisit the odds for Offensive Rookie of the Year. You could probably guess the favorites. Over at DraftKings Sportsbook, No. 3 overall pick running back Jeremiyah Love of the Arizona Cardinals has the shortest odds at +400, followed by Mendoza at +425, Tate at +550, New Orleans Saints wideout Jordyn Tyson at +600 and Seattle Seahawks running back Jadarian Price rounding out the top five at +750. But what about some sleepers?
Below, we will break down four Offensive Rookie of the Year sleepers to consider. These players will have odds listed outside of the top five with a minimum of +1000.
The No. 20 overall pick of the Philadelphia Eagles is the reigning Biletnikoff Award winner, as he caught 79 passes for 1,156 yards and 11 touchdowns for USC last season. Makai Lemon had four games in which he recorded 150 yards receiving and a touchdown in 2025, which tied a Big Ten single-season record, and recorded the most yards after catch (502) in the conference. Lemon wasn't just a playmaker after the catch, but also a deep-ball weapon. His 16 receptions of 20+ air yards were tied for third-most in the FBS.
Lemon isn't A.J. Brown . He's a slot weapon, not a big-bodied perimeter threat. New offensive coordinator Sean Mannion, who played and learned under Sean McVay, could use a reliable playmaker like Lemon as a pillar in his new offense. I think it could be easy to scheme up quick touches for him.
As the Brandon Aiyuk saga continues to drag on, it seems very unlikely he will join his former college teammate Jayden Daniels in Washington. The Washington Commanders needed to add another wide receiver to help Terry McLaurin , who is coming off his worst season as a pro, and the most notable addition Adam Peters and Co. made this offseason was Antonio Williams in the third round.
Williams leaves Clemson with the fourth-most career receptions (208) in program history, and is tied for the fourth-most receiving touchdowns (21). He caught 15 touchdowns over the last two seasons, which ranks most in the ACC. This is a solid slot weapon that doesn't drop the ball and can create after the catch. He also possesses the vision necessary to create those game-changing splash plays. The only question I have with Williams is his ability to stay healthy, as he missed 12 games due to injury during his collegiate career. But he's someone that could play a big role in Washington's offense if Daniels can also remain healthy. He has a clearer path to picking up touches than another talent like Germie Bernard in Pittsburgh.
No one expected De'Zhaun Stribling to be the sixth wide receiver off the board, as he was CBS Sports' WR19 in this class. However, I trust John Lynch and Kyle Shanahan, and they clearly wanted this prospect.
Stribling is known for his blocking ability and physicality, but he also ran a 4.36 40-yard dash at the combine at 6-foot-2. He caught 55 passes for 811 yards last season for the Ole Miss Rebels and led the team with six receiving touchdowns. He also caught seven passes for 122 yards in the College Football Playoff Quarterfinal upset against Georgia. Surely he can find a role in this efficient San Francisco 49ers offensive attack -- and should have the opportunity, too.
The 49ers signed soon-to-be 33-year-old Mike Evans , who has missed 12 games over the last two seasons due to injury, and Christian Kirk while losing Jauan Jennings and Kendrick Bourne in free agency. Jennings was the most reliable wide receiver Shanahan had over the past couple of seasons, and Stribling has the potential to wear the hat he did in this scheme.
If the 49ers' weapons struggle again with injuries, Stribling may be the surprise player that was hiding in plain sight. This is a fast kid with good size joining a dangerous passing attack.
Well, we can't pick ALL wide receivers. And I'm not too interested in any of the rookie quarterbacks. So let's look at the running backs.
Kaelon Black is behind Christian McCaffrey in San Francisco, Mike Washington Jr . is an intriguing sleeper backing up Ashton Jeanty in Vegas, Emmett Johnson is behind Kenneth Walker III in Kansas City, and Nicholas Singleton is part of a deep room in Tennessee. So let's talk about Jonah Coleman .
Coleman is admittedly going to need some help if he's going to win Offensive Rookie of the Year, but there's a path for it to happen. J.K. Dobbins was effective for the Denver Broncos last season, averaging 77.2 rushing yards per game. However, he missed the last seven games due to a foot injury and still has never played a full NFL season. Rookie RJ Harvey stepped in and became the fifth rookie in NFL history to rush for five touchdowns and catch five touchdowns in a player's first season, but he cleared 55 rushing yards in just two of his seven starts.
Coleman was the fourth running back taken in this past draft. While he's just 5-foot-8, he's as shifty as he is productive. No player in the Big Ten scored more touchdowns than Coleman last season (17), and he's a legitimate receiver, too. Coleman may be buried on the depth chart right now, but how long will that be the case? This Broncos team has Super Bowl aspirations, and their rushing attack has to be better than it was in 2025.

full_text: DT Roy Lopez (Photo by Ronald Martinez/Getty Images) | Getty Images Training camp. What training? The annual event got its name from long ago. Players had offseason jobs and would show up to camp out of shape, so they had to go through the “training process” of getting back in football shape. The Arizona Cardinals are opening training camp for the 2026 version. RELATED: ROOKIE FOURTH-ROUND PICK HAS KNEE INJURY Let’s look at the defensive tackle room. This year’s group needs a lot of improvement and healthy bodies. New this year is the return of Roy Lopez III, signed during free agency after a one-year adventure with the Detroit Lions, along with Jonah Williams from the New Orleans Saints and Andrew Billings of the Chicago Bears. Rookies include Southeastern Louisiana’s Kaleb Proctor, who was chosen in Round 4 of April’s NFL draft, plus undrafted rookie Damonic Williams of Oklahoma. Cardinals’ DT depth chart Nose tackle: Roy Lopez,backup Andrew Billings, PJ Mustipher, Damonic Williams Defensive tackle: Walter Nolen, backup L.J. Collier, Zach Carter Injured: Kaleb Proctor Best expectations? The entire defensive tackle situation is relying on Nolen to become a dominant force. He never missed a game at any level until he hit the field in the desert. He was a First Team All-American and First Team All-SEC. Over his final two seasons, he had 22.5 sacks, including 14.0 in his final year. He also had 85 total tackles and 23.5 tackles for loss, which meant he was a good run stopper. Nolen needs to arrive in shape and healthy. He is currently healthy and preparing for the 2026 NFL season. Lopez replaces the departed Calais Campbell, who was a run-stopping force. Lopez needs to bring his “A” game each week and become a huge clog nestled next to Nolen. Arizona is certain that he is the answer due to his being signed to a two-year deal. Lopez isn’t a big sack guy, but his tackle numbers are very good. Billings has played for a handful of NFL teams, but he can stop the run if he isn’t huge coming into training camp. The defensive tackle position will become under a rotational basis. The Cardinals will keep just four from this group. The question that remains: Who will become DT4? Worst case? Not to jinx anyone, but Nolen has already had two injuries with the Cardinals. Although Lopez is a solid player, he is not an upgrade from Campbell. He will give the defense a good run defense, but there is a drop-off in pass rush. Billings is a big-bodied defensive tackle, but he often will show up to camp with way too many buffets around his waist. Already at 340 pounds, it has been a natural occurrence for him to have an extra 20 pounds and be slow off the snap. He is already on his fifth team, and in his eight seasons, he has only had 191 total tackles. 2026 version? This group had issues last year. Campbell was a bright spot, and why he wasn’t re-signed is a mystery. So, the team did what they had to do to bring in some capable bodies. Will it be enough? Has this position been solved? Last year, the Cardinals’ run defense ranked #25 and allowed an average of 126.9 yards per game. Also, 19 rushing touchdowns were scored. The entire defensive line will come under scrutiny this year. In the NFL draft, the third overall pick could have been one of three stud pass rushers, and instead, RB Jeremiyah Love was selected instead. So, here is the state of the defensive line, with an emphasis on the interior.

title: Cardinals roster: Training Camp WR Outlook
summary: The Arizona Cardinals are on the verge of opening up training camp. Most NFL clubs require the rookies to show up earlier, but the Cardinals’ rookies and veterans both show up on July 22. This training camp has a lot riding on during the preseason. A new head coach, Mike LaFleur, plus a new offensive […]
full_text: Jul 24, 2025; Glendale, AZ, USA; Arizona Cardinals wide receiver Michael Wilson (14) and Marvin Harrison Jr. (18) during training camp at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images The Arizona Cardinals are on the verge of opening up training camp. Most NFL clubs require the rookies to show up earlier, but the Cardinals’ rookies and veterans both show up on July 22. This training camp has a lot riding on during the preseason. A new head coach, Mike LaFleur, plus a new offensive scheme, is being installed. RELATED: THE RECEIVER NOBODY IS TALKING ABOUT Ahead of training camp opening, let’s look at the receiver room. This year’s group has a lot riding on it. There should be a lot of improvement with this group. New this year is Kendrick Bourne, signed during free agency from the San Francisco 49ers, Reggie Virgil, who was chosen in Round 5 of the NFL draft, along with undrafted rookie Harrison Wallace, III. Cardinals WR depth chart Right outside receiver: Michael Wilson, backup Fehoko, Jalen Brooks, Harrison Wallace, III Left outside receiver: Marv Harrison, Jr., backup Reggie Virgil, Xavier Weaver, Bryson Green Slot receiver: Kendrick Bourne, backup Devin Duvernay, Tejhaun Palmer, Ihmir Smith-Marsette Best expectations? Wilson had a coming-out year last season and has solidified the WR1 position. He is in line to get an extension, which should occur during training camp. He led all receivers last year in total yards with 1,006 yards and was the second most on the roster behind Trey McBride in targets with 126. With this new offense, expect a Pro Bowl year with Wilson. Harrison and Bourne, while neither broke the 1,000-yard hurdle last season, should be able to move the needle and display why their skills will need to increase their production this year. Harrison needs to prove why he was selected #4 overall, and Bourne should provide good hands with the slot position. Duvernay, Weaver, and Fehoko, plus the rookie Virgil, reward the Cardinals for showing patience and confidence in their abilities. This group can shine if the correct quarterback is found early enough. Worst case? Harrison’s sophomore slump becomes a sign of a complete unraveling, and Wilson shows his best effort was a one-off. Retreads of Duvernay and Bourne can’t get any production in the short game this new offense offers, and the rookie Virgil shows why he dropped to Round 5 before being selected. 2026 version? This group will love this new offense. It doesn’t throw deep much, but the talent is there with the few plays that do go long. It is geared for the short to intermediate game. Yards for stats won’t be generated in large chunks but in steady increments. The squad will rely heavily on both Wilson and Harrison, with Bourne getting looks for the short game. The only questions will be who will be the other three players that will gain roster spots, and how they will be used in the game plan. Like any year, there could be a complete surprise that wasn’t expected. The top three assist in order to slot the secondary guys into positions that are more suited to their skills. Which is how you want it to be, as opposed to relying on guys who try hard but are limited in what they can bring to the field. This entire group has the opportunity to become amazing and electric.

title: Baltimore Ravens Hidden Gems: 3 underrated players on the 2026 roster
summary: Through most of their history, the Baltimore Ravens have been a model of consistency. From 1996 to 2025, they had three head coaches — Ted Marchibroda, Brian Billick, and John Harbaugh. They’ve had two general managers — Ozzie Newsome and Eric DeCosta. They’ve had exactly nine losing seasons in 30 years, and three of those […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 4: Nate Wiggins #2 of the Baltimore Ravens looks on during an NFL football game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Through most of their history, the Baltimore Ravens have been a model of consistency. From 1996 to 2025, they had three head coaches — Ted Marchibroda, Brian Billick, and John Harbaugh. They’ve had two general managers — Ozzie Newsome and Eric DeCosta. They’ve had exactly nine losing seasons in 30 years, and three of those were in their first three campaigns. Then, 2025’s 8-9 season happened, and the Ravens changed a lot . Harbaugh was out, replaced by former Los Angeles Chargers defensive coordinator Jesse Minter. There’s a new offensive coordinator in former Chicago Bears OC Declan Doyle, and a new defensive coordinator in former Miami Dolphins DC (and ex-Ravens assistant head coach and defensive assistant) Anthony Weaver. Minter will call the defense, and given his history under Jim Harbaugh as Mike Macdonald’s DC replacement at Michigan in 2022 and 2023, one could be forgiven for thinking that the Ravens are attempting with Minter to replicate what Macdonald — also a former Ravens coach, of course — has accomplished in Seattle. “We spent two weeks; it was a sprint to the finish,” DeCosta said in February of the Harbaugh replacement process. “We talked to at least 20 candidates in different formats – Zoom, in person, on the phone. Really, really proud of the process, and it became apparent quickly that Jesse Minter was the right guy to be our next head football coach. Jesse’s smart, he’s a leader, he has great humility, he’s a problem solver, [and] a great tactician. We’ve enjoyed watching his defenses play. He started at the bottom [Minter was on the Ravens’ staff from 2017-2020 as a defensive assistant, assistant defensive backs coach, and finally as defensive backs coach], and now he’s here. I think that’s great. “I’m so happy to work with him as a partner over the coming months and coming years, and I think this is a great day for the Baltimore Ravens.” You don’t undergo this much offseason chair-shifting without questions to answer, and the 2026 Ravens obviously want to claw their way back to the contention status they’re used to. For that to happen, excellence will have to come from more than just the obvious names — as is the case for any NFL team, the whole roster will need to step up. To that end, I’ve identified three Hidden Gems for the 2026 Ravens — one underrated veteran, one underrated free agent, and one underrated draft pick. Underrated veteran: CB Nate Wiggins The 2025 Ravens ranked 17th in Defensive DVOA , down from sixth in 2024, and first in 2023. Which represents a rather precipitous decline. Injuries played a part, especially with Nnamdi Madubuike missing all but two games with a serious neck injury, but the secondary was also an issue overall. Baltimore’s pass defense allowed 399 completions in 625 attempts for 4,423 yards, 23 touchdowns, 11 interceptions, and an opponent passer rating of 89.7. Not epically bad, but certainly not on the same level as the 76.2 opponent passer rating allowed in 2023, the last year of the Mike Macdonald era. Minter is one of the game’s best defensive minds, so one can expect an uptick in performance in 2026, and third-year cornerback Nate Wiggins will be a key part of that. The 30th overall pick in the 2024 draft has played well in his first two NFL seasons — in 2025, he allowed 61 catches on 102 targets for 656 yards, 188 yards after the catch, two touchdowns, three interceptions, 14 pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 73.0. Wiggins was the only Ravens defensive back to allow an opponent passer rating lower than 80 last season, and given that he allowed a 74.8 passer rating in his rookie season, the consistency has been there. Wiggins has become especially conversant with press coverage — last season, he allowed just 20 catches on 43 press targets for 213 yards, one touchdown, two interceptions, and an opponent passer rating of 49.9. . @Ravens CB Nate Wiggins in press coverage last season. Even some of the NFL's best receivers found this a tough go. pic.twitter.com/yTn4N81YGz — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) July 18, 2026 Wiggins underwent offseason surgery to correct an undisclosed issue, and he’s excited about the future. “They’re going to see a big transition this year. How I move, all that,” he recently said. “I don’t think [anybody] has seen the full Nate. I’m just so happy going into this year… I know it’s going to be a big year for me, and I just can’t wait.” The new head coach is also eager to see what Year 3 will bring for his best cornerback. “I’ll keep [the surgery] between Nate, myself and the organization, but he’s a guy that I loved coming out from Clemson in the draft process,” Minter said of Wiggins at the 2026 scouting combine. “I am very excited to work with him, and I think there’s still a lot of room in his game. I know he knows that. I know he’s excited to work with us, and so I look forward to him having a big year.” Underrated free agent: DL Calais Campbell When the Arizona Cardinals selected Miami defensive lineman Calais Campbell in the second round of the NFL draft on April 26, 2008, the “Big Short” financial crisis was just coming into focus. Something called the iPhone was gaining traction. And the Democratic race for President saw Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton as its two primary battlers. So yeah… that was a long time ago. And here’s Calais Campbell about to play in his 19th NFL season, on a one-year, $5.5 million contract with $4.75 million guaranteed. Campbell previously played for the Ravens from 2020-2022, but this isn’t one of those “veteran depth” signings — the Ravens have reason to believe that the 39-year-old Campbell, who will turn 40 on September 1, can add some serious juice to Minter’s defense. Last season for the Cardinals, and with very little around him on that defense, he put up 6.5 sacks, 33 pressures, 26 solo tackles, 24 stops, and nine tackles for loss. Which put him in some fairly historic company. Sacks in a season, age 39, pro football history (from 1960): Bruce Smith (2002) 9.0 Doug Atkins (1969) 8.0 Calais Campbell (2025) 6.5 Andy Robustelli (1964) 6.5 Reggie White (2000) 5.5 Calais Campbell is ridiculous. pic.twitter.com/CAYt11iYzl — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) July 17, 2026 “Stoked,” Minter said in May of Campbell’s addition. ”We’ve agreed to terms with Calais. He’ll be here sometime this week to kind of finalize things, and [we’re] really excited about it. He’s still playing at such an unbelievable level. We all know what type of man and person and teammate and leader that he is, but this is because he’s such a really good player at this age and where he’s at. He’ll really help us. He’ll be great for the young guys, of course, because that’s who Calais is, but I’m looking forward to seeing what he brings on the field [and] in between the lines. And I really think he’ll help us both in the run and pass game.” Assuming that the level of play holds up, Campbell wouldn’t be a like-as-like fill-in for Madubuike at this point in his career, but he’s got enough on the ball as a multi-gap disruptor to help out. And hey — if the Ravens can get Campbell, Madubuike, 2025 Hidden Gem Travis Jones , and Trey Hendrickson on the line at the same time, wouldn’t that be a spicy meatball? Underrated draft pick: WR Elijah Sarratt The 2025 Ravens had a red zone problem with their receivers. Zay Flowers, Devontez Walker, DeAndre Hopkins, Rashod Bateman, and Tylan Wallace combined for just 13 touchdowns overall, and that’s not going to get the job done. To put that in perspective, the Los Angeles Rams led the NFL with 29 touchdown passes to their receivers last season, and that’s with all the 13 personnel stuff they used with three tight ends on the field. It was clear that…

full_text: Last year, the Buffalo Bills boasted the league’s best rushing attack, amassing 2,714 yards on the ground to go with 30 rushing touchdowns. Buffalo’s backfield was led by James Cook, who would go on to claim the league’s rushing title (rushing 309 times for 1,621 yards and 12 touchdowns in the regular season). What will Cook do for an encore in Joe Brady’s first season as head coach? Today’s edition of Buffalo Rumblinks leads off by examining the state of Buffalo’s running backs, including whether Brady will dial up more pass plays for Cook and Buffalo’s tailbacks this year. Check out the assessments and then be sure to leave your thoughts on the state of the Bills running backs heading into the season. Will the Bills dial up more passes to their backs? The Bills backfield consists of reigning NFL rushing champion James Cook, along with Ty Johnson, Ray Davis, Frank Gore Jr., and former United Football League champion Ian Wheeler. Last year, the Bills ran the ball on 49.84% of plays, the second-highest rate of all teams. And no team ran the ball more on first down than Buffalo, which, led by Cook, posted 38 carries of 10-plus yards on first down last season. But this year, it seems like changes are likely in Buffalo’s offensive game plan, which could mean a healthy dose of passes from Josh Allen to Cook and Johnson coming out of the backfield. We explore why Joe Brady should call more pass plays for Buffalo’s talented stable of running backs; speculate why the Bills would be wise to manage Cook’s workload to keep him fresh for the team’s potential run to a Super Bowl; hear why Cook is Buffalo’s second-most important player heading into this pivotal season; and figure out which backs will make the 53-man roster and which players are cut candidates. title: Ranking Buffalo Bills rookies by impact on 2026 season
summary: Believe it or not — Buffalo Bills rookies will report to training camp St. John Fisher University tomorrow. We aren’t quite back to football yet. But it’s getting close. Very close. With the rookies front-of-mind, I compiled a ranking of the first-year Bills based on how much I believe they will contribute in 2026. 10. […]
full_text: SALT LAKE CITY, UT - OCTOBER 19: Kaleb Elarms-Orr #3 of the TCU Horned Frogs celebrates after a sack in the first half against the Utah Utes at Rice Eccles Stadium on October 19, 2024 in Salt Lake City, Utah. (Photo by Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images | Getty Images Believe it or not — Buffalo Bills rookies will report to training camp St. John Fisher University tomorrow. We aren’t quite back to football yet. But it’s getting close. Very close. With the rookies front-of-mind, I compiled a ranking of the first-year Bills based on how much I believe they will contribute in 2026. 10. OT/OG Jude Bowry The Bills selected Bowry in Round 4, and that’s the round-grade I had on him . As a draft analyst, when that alignment occurs, it’s nirvana. However, these rankings aren’t strictly based on my pre-draft evaluations of each player. The Bills are apparently going to give Bowry a run at tackle to start his career, and there are three — if not four — players ahead of him on the roster, Dion Dawkins, Spencer Brown, Tylan Grable and 2025 draftee Chase Lundt. It would not surprise me if Bowry eventually passes Lundt on the depth chart to position himself as the backup swing tackle, but the former Boston College star does need to get noticeably stronger — a statement I can make for just about every rookie blocker each season. Because of that need to add power, I view Bowry as more of a player to be stored and developed for the 2027 season than an instant impact rookie, which is why he’s at No. 10 on this list. 9. OG Ar’Maj Reed-Adams I really liked Reed-Adams as a prospect. I had a third-round grade on him , therefore the Bills selecting him in Round 7 represented one of the larger steals in the entire draft based on my pre-draft evaluations compared to actual draft results. Why I elected to put Buffalo’s last 2026 draft pick at the second-to-last spot here instead of No. 10 — what Reed-Adams may lack in lateral quickness and pure explosion he compensates with close to NFL-caliber power, and some of that is due to his age. Reed-Adams will be 25 in November and spent the last two years blocking in the SEC after a stellar career at Kansas. At nearly 6’6” and 314 pounds with offensive-tackle length — 88th percentile arm length and 98th percentile wingspan — he’s a specimen, and on film at A&M he deployed his arms as real weapons at the point of attack. The Bills lost David Edwards in free agency, and even though the likes of Alec Anderson and Austin Corbett project as the two candidates for the vacant starting left guard job, I expect Reed-Adams to surprise in training camp and the preseason before serving as an emergency — but capable — backup on the interior of Buffalo’s offensive line. 8. DT Zane Durant We aren’t exactly sure what Jim Leonhard’s defense will look like — beyond drawing conclusions from his time at Wisconsin and in Denver — so everything regarding the players on said defense is drastically more of a guess that it was during the Sean McDermott era. I didn’t adore Durant on film as a prospect, yet his athletic and analytics profiles were outstanding, a combination that always leads to hesitancy regarding a prospect’s round grade. Ultimately, my pre-draft grading formula spit out a Round 5 grade on Durant , and the Bills picked him with the final selection in that round. With Durant, there are some physical and skill-set similarities to John Franklin-Myers, and being a draft pick of the new defensive regime will undoubtedly work in his favor during his rookie season. I don’t think Durant has the pass-rush move arsenal to regularly win one-on-ones in his first year as a professional. Explosiveness only takes interior defensive linemen so far in the NFL. How threatening his first step proves to be will determine if Durant plays like 10-20% of the snaps as a rotational piece throughout the season or if he’s a practice-squad mainstay in Year 1. 7. P Tommy Doman Jr. I don’t typically scout special teamers before the draft — simply because I have so many other prospects to get to — so I can’t provide anything pre-draft about Doman, so I’ll keep this short. I think Doman has his work cut out for him to beat Mitch Wishnowsky for the starting punter gig. Then again, teams typically don’t draft kickers/punters and cut them four months later. Also, if he does win the punter job, he’ll of course contribute in 2026 yet not as sizably as other rookies. 6. CB Davison Igbinosun IGB is quite polarizing — I had a third-round grade on him , and the Bills made him their second selection in the 2026 draft in the second round. Because of their reasonably high investment in him, Buffalo’s defensive staff will likely give Igbinosun every opportunity to win considerable playing time as a rookie. I, personally, don’t necessarily believe he can beat out Maxwell Hairston for the starting outside cornerback gig opposite Christian Benford. But we do know how Buffalo’s cornerback depth has been tested during the Josh Allen era (which doesn’t automatically mean it’ll happen again). And Igbinosun does have more size than Hairston, so there’s a chance he’s utilized in specific matchups throughout the season. Igbinosun’s an aggressive albeit unspectacular tackler, and I’m concerned he’ll get hit with the grabby label by referees early in his career. If he’s on the field, his play will be very important to Buffalo’s collective defensive effort. 5. CB Toriano Pride Jr. Going bold here — but not just for dramatic effect. The combination Pride Jr.’s specific athletic/skill profile, and the opportunity within the Bills defense make the seventh-round pick much higher in these rankings than his draft slot would indicate. I had a fourth-round grade on him . About equally as sized as Hairston — with close to the same measured athleticism — Pride Jr. is the exact type of late-round cornerback who can surprise as he develops in the NFL. He’s going to miss some open-field tackles like he did at Missouri, yet his ball production and suddenness should translate to the professional game. Pride Jr. is precisely built to handle high-caliber separators in today’s NFL, particularly from the slot. However, because he’s 5’10” and 185 pounds with experience on the boundary, there’s versatility to his game too. I expect a strong camp and preseason filled with impact plays. 4. DB Jalon Kilgore I thought highly of Kilgore as a prospect — he carried a third-round grade in my system — and his safety-slot defender-dime linebacker versatility is appealing. He could absolutely serve as Buffalo’s primary “big nickel” option when the much smaller Dee Alford is forced off the field by a big slot receiver or a tight-end heavy opponent. However, Kilgore will have to compete with the likes of the similarly sized/athletic Jordan Hancock and potentially the pure safety options on the roster like Geno Stone and Damar Hamlin, and even Wande Owens for that niche role. Then again, I can’t confidently write that any of those other options enter the season with a firm grasp on the full-time big nickel role. Kilgore is a highly explosive, former SEC Swiss Army knife, and if the Bills are now to prioritize dynamic athleticism and pure speed to the football, Kilgore will be a prime candidate to see the field more than most fifth-round rookies in the Bills new defense. I’m excited about him. 3. EDGE T.J. Parker No-brainer here — Buffalo’s first selection in the 2026 draft makes the Top 3 in these rankings. To summarize my thoughts on Parker — he’s an upgraded version of A.J. Epenesa with considerably more upside than Epenesa brought to the NFL in 2020. I had a second-round grade on him . And for as much as I felt the Bills needed what Brandon Beane often refers to as a “designated pass rusher,” I do understand why Buffalo decided to go with Parker, a clear high-floor option at the EDGE position. He’ll be able to generate positive plays against the run right away, and has enough of a burst + pass-rush move combo to threaten some…

summary: Training camp will be here before we know it — it starts next Wednesday! — and the Buffalo Bills will be back at St. John Fisher University. For me, the start of training camp always means that it’s time to start preparing for fantasy football drafts, and the expectations around the Bills. It should come […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - JUNE 9: Josh Allen #17 talks with DJ Moore #2 during the Buffalo Bills mandatory minicamp at Kaleida Health Performance Center on June 9, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images Training camp will be here before we know it — it starts next Wednesday! — and the Buffalo Bills will be back at St. John Fisher University. For me, the start of training camp always means that it’s time to start preparing for fantasy football drafts, and the expectations around the Bills. It should come as no surprise that ESPN experts have kept expectations in check for the Bills wide receivers. The group has received scrutiny in the past, and president of football operations/general manager Brandon Beane has added some new faces to the mix. Despite there being a bit of an overhaul, only two Bills have cracked ESPN’s top 60 . The first Bills receiver on the list is DJ Moore, who Beane acquired prior to the draft for the team’s second round pick. While that move immediately vaulted Moore into Buffalo’s top wide receiver slot, the expectations are in check heading into this season. With ESPN , Moore is currently ranked 27th on the list of 60, just behind his former Chicago Bears teammates Rome Odunze (25) and Luther Burden (26). Despite being a borderline WR2 in fantasy football, the statistical projections for Moore show quite a bump in Buffalo. ESPN has Moore projected going for 946 yards on 67 receptions (with 7 touchdowns). Personally, I would be pleased with that type of performance from Moore in 2026. The other Bills wide receiver to crack the list is Khalil Shakir, who comes in at the 47 spot. This makes Shakir a bit more of a FLEX play, or a bye week fill-in. Statistically speaking, the projections remain pretty consistent for Shakir. ESPN has Shakir finishing the 2026 season with 70 receptions and 765 yards (compared to 72 receptions for 719 yards in the 2025 season). While Shakir will offer consistency, with the occasional breakout week, you’re likely holding off until the late rounds to add him to your roster. Be sure to share your thoughts on the projections for Moore and Shakir in the comments section below, and if there are other wide receivers on the team that you would consider drafting.

summary: The Buffalo Bills have made changes and tweaks to their wide receiver group since last season. While they made some major moves, they’ve also done work on the fringes, adding and subtracting players who will battle for various roles without the glitz and glamor associated with household names. Some of those players Buffalo has added […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - JANUARY 04: Quentin Skinner #88 of the New York Jets catches a pass for a touchdown in the fourth quarter against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills have made changes and tweaks to their wide receiver group since last season. While they made some major moves, they’ve also done work on the fringes, adding and subtracting players who will battle for various roles without the glitz and glamor associated with household names. Some of those players Buffalo has added are already gone, too, their time with the team limited to pieces like the one you’re reading now. Just a few weeks ago, we were talking about whether Deven Thompkins had a chance to make the Bills’ roster as a return specialist. After his release on July 14, we know that isn’t going to happen unless the Bills bring him back again later in the summer. In today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss the man Buffalo acquired that led to Thompkins’ release. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Quentin Skinner Number: Not assigned; Skinner wore 88 with the New York Jets, but that number isn’t available with Buffalo Position: WR Height/Weight: 6’5” 195 lbs. Age: 24 (25 on 12/24/2026) Experience/Draft: 1; signed with Jets following the 2025 NFL Draft College: Kansas Acquired: Claimed off waivers on 7/14/2026 Financial situation (per Spotrac): Skinner enters the second year of the rookie free agent deal he signed last spring with the Jets. If he makes Buffalo’s 53-man roster, he carries a cap hit of $885,000 for the season. Buffalo would not have any dead cap charge if they were to release Skinner. 2025 Recap: Skinner finished up his college career with the Jayhawks by doing what he did best: making explosive plays in the passing game. He averaged 19.8 yards per catch across three seasons with Kansas, totaling 80 receptions for 1,584 yards and 11 touchdowns in 38 games where he actually appeared on offense. He did not receive an invite to the 2025 NFL Scouting Combine, but he participated in Kansas’ Pro Day. He ran the forty-yard dash in 4.51 seconds, completed the three-cone drill in 6.94 seconds, ran the twenty-yard shuttle in 4.34 seconds, and leapt 33” in the vertical jump and 10’2” in the broad jump. He went undrafted in the 2025 NFL Draft, signing with the New York Jets after the selection meeting concluded. He played in all three of Gang Green’s preseaosn games, catching eight passes for 114 yards and a score on ten targets. While he played well in the exhibition season, he did not make the final roster, as the Jets released him on August 26 as part of final roster cuts. They signed him to the practice squad the following day. Skinner made his NFL debut in the regular season finale against Buffalo, and while he officially caught one pass for ten yards, he also converted a two-point try in the fourth quarter after the Jets’ lone touchdown in a 35-8 loss. Therefore, Skinner can be the answer to a trivia question, as well, as he was officially the last player to score in Buffalo’s old home. Positional outlook: Skinner is one of fourteen receivers on the current roster. Khalil Shakir, Tyrell Shavers, DJ Moore, Keon Coleman, Joshua Palmer, Skyler Bell, Ja’Mori Maclin, Mecole Hardman Jr., Trent Sherfield, Jalen Virgil, Stephen Gosnell, Max Tomczak, and Mac Dalena are the others. 2026 Offseason: The Jets waived Skinner with an injury designation on June 8 to make room for wideout Jalen Walthall. 2026 Season outlook: Skinner is the tallest receiver on the roster, and like my good friend and coaching mentor once said of our basketball players, “You can’t teach tall.” That’s certainly a solid trait and a 6’5” player who excels in explosives can help any receiver room. Does Skinner have the juice to make an NFL roster? If he couldn’t see much time with a morbund team like the Jets last season, I’m tempted to think the answer is no, but the Jets, for all their shortcomings last season, did have a fairly solid receiver group, and they had plenty of players who fit Skinner’s prototype. Could a change of scenery and scheme help? It certainly can, and while Skinner is likely to see most of his reps with the third team, the possibility of working in with the Allens—both Kyle Allen and Josh Allen—should help him, as well, given that he wasn’t dealing with a great crop of quarterbacks in New Jersey last season. At best, Skinner shows himself to be a sound deep threat who can also handle playing the gunner role on special teams, which leads the Bills to keep him as a surprise sixth wideout once the preseason concludes. At worst, he is either injured or terrible and the Bills release him. The more realistic “best-case scenario” is likely somewhere in between. If Skinner can pick up the Bills’ offense and prove that he can handle special teams duty, maybe the team cuts him and keeps him on the practice squad while he better learns the team. Buffalo may not have a top-flight receiving corps, but they aren’t so desperate where a July addition with little experience is likely to make the 53-man roster. Skinner is likely fighting for a spot on the practice squad this summer.

summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - FEBRUARY 1: Receiver Ricky Proehl #81 of the Carolina Panthers catches a 12 yard touchdown pass in front of cornerback Asante Samuel #22 of the New England Patriots in the fourth quarter of Super Bowl XXXVIII at Reliant Stadium on February 1, 2004 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Ronald Martinez/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #54. Ricky Proehl Ricky Proehl was a semi-local product, having attended Wake Forest University just a couple hours outside of Charlotte. He had a very good junior season and followed that up with an even better senior campaign, leading him to be selected in the third round of the 1990 NFL Draft by the Phoenix (now Arizona) Cardinals. He immediately was a major factor in the Cardinals offense, getting 99 targets his rookie year despite only starting two games. The following four years saw his targets increase year over year, topping out at 110 in his final season in Arizona. His production matched the targets, averaging about 800 yards and four touchdowns per season. Following the 1994 season, the Cardinals traded Proehl to the Seattle Seahawks for a fourth round pick. Proehl’s Seattle tenure started horribly as he suffered a broken foot in their season opener in 1995. He did return, but ultimately only played eight games that year. The following season was a healthy one for Proehl but a disappointing one, so the Seahawks released him. He signed a one year deal with the Chicago Bears and had a pretty good year, leading to a career changing contract with the then St Louis Rams. Proehl’s first year with the Rams saw him reach a career high in targets opposite Isaac Bruce. The 1999 offseason saw the Rams add Torry Holt via the Draft and Marshall Faulk via trade with the Colts, leading to the legendary Greatest Show on Turf years. Proehl went from borderline top option to fourth option in one offseason but made the most of his now limited opportunities. He posted career highs in first down percentage (the percentage of receptions that resulted in a first down) and yards per target, while also boasting career highs in catch percentage as he truly became Kurt Warner’s reliable “got to have it” target. With a Super Bowl ring in tow and five memorable years in St Louis, Proehl signed on with a young up and coming team out of Charlotte. It was just the second year into John Fox’s tenure as head coach, and the team looked to be headed in the right direction despite being full of youth. The wide receiver room, in particular, had some promising but unseasoned players in Muhsin Muhammad and Steve Smith, and Proehl took on the grizzled veteran mentor role while maintaining his security blanket role for unheralded quarterback Jake Delhomme. Evidence of this limited but immensely important connection came in the very first game of Proehl’s Panthers tenure when Delhomme, the backup at the time who was inserted at half time, found Proehl with just 16 seconds left for a 12 yard game winning touchdown. That game launched the Panthers first Super Bowl run, and Proehl was at the center of many important moments. He had a couple major first down receptions late in the fourth quarter of Week 2 against the Bucs that led to an eventual overtime win. Proehl also hauled in one of the most iconic passes of the Panthers short history in Super Bowl XXXVIII. Trailing the Patriots with just over a minute to go in regulation, Delhomme again found his “ole reliable” receiver in the endzone from 12 yards out, tying the game at 29. While the Panthers would end up losing the game, Proehl’s performance would cement him in Panthers lore. He spent two more seasons with the Panthers before retiring after the 2005 season. Though his statistical impact pales in comparison to other short-tenured Panthers, his role on one of the most successful Panthers teams in franchise history is undeniable. He also returned to coach the wide receivers from 2011-2017, helping a ragtag group of busts and no-name receivers become a corps helped the team reach the Super Bowl in 2015. Hopeful future Hall of Famer Steve Smith credits Proehl for a large part of his own success due to Proehl’s mentorship helping Smith focus his infamous fiery play style. From his clutch plays on a Super Bowl bound team to his mentorship of younger receivers as a veteran player and as a coach, Proehl has no doubt earned his spot at No. 54 on our countdown of the Top 100 Panthers.

We can look at 74% of y’all having been around since the beginning (or near enough) a couple of different ways. For our part, Cat Scratch Reader is a purely written-word media outlet with little social media presence. We like it that way, even if our actual team here at CSR is more old-at-heart than actually-old. Still, only 6% of our readers coming from the Cam Newton Era doesn’t seem quite right. I’m going to go out on a limb and suggest that maybe only the truly long-in-the-tooth fans stick around for the deep offseason. We’ll test that hypothesis by running this survey again sometime during the season to see if the children have only seasonal literacy skills and attention spans. full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 01: Jeremy Chinn #21 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates breaking up a pass intended for T.J. Hockenson #87 of the Minnesota Vikings during the third quarter at Bank of America Stadium on October 01, 2023 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Grant Halverson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #55. Jeremy Chinn Panthers stats: 54 games, 50 starts, 324 tackles, 4.0 sacks, 2 interceptions Career stats: 86 games, 82 starts, 555 tackles, 7.0 sacks, 3 interceptions For many Panthers fans, Jeremy Chinn will always feel like the one that got away. Carolina selected the Southern Illinois product in the second round of the 2020 NFL Draft and from the outset it looked like they struck gold. As a rookie he started all 15 games in which he played and racked up 117 tackles. But it wasn’t just the quantity of tackles, it was the violence that accompanied them. Despite being a rookie from a small-time college program, Chinn punished opposing players who ventured into his realm. The most amazing moment from his rookie season was becoming the first player in NFL history to return two fumbles for touchdowns on back-to-back plays . As a result of his stellar play he finished No. 2 in Defensive Rookie of the Year voting behind Chase Young. It appeared back then the Panthers had found a long-term impact player. But what was also apparent was that Chinn was a “tweener” in that he wasn’t quite big enough to play linebacker full time, but he also didn’t quite have the coverage skills to play a true safety position. But the Panthers played to his strengths and he became a hard-hitting strong safety who often snuck up into the box as an excellent run stopper, but he also made Panthers fans nervous when he dropped into coverage. Chinn’s second season with the Panthers played out like his first. He had 107 tackles with a sack and five passes defended. In 2022, Chinn’s third season, he missed six games due to a hamstring injury but over 11 starts he put up 70 tackles, another sack, and seven passes defended. And it was in 2022 when the wheels started coming off for Jeremy Chinn in Carolina due to a host of absurd coaching changes and questionable defensive schemes. Matt Rhule was fired five games into the 2022 season and was replaced by interim head coach Steve Wilks. In 2023, Chinn’s fourth and final season in Carolina, the Panthers hired Frank Reich, fired him after 11 games, then appointed Chris Tabor as interim coach. In that tumultuous 2023 season, the final year of Chinn’s rookie contract, coach Reich and his staff deemed Chinn a “hybrid” player who didn’t fit their defensive scheme. He saw his playing time dramatically reduced. Chinn played over 90% of the team’s defensive snaps over his first three seasons, but in 2023 that number fell to just 39%. He also missed five games due to injury and by the end of the 2023 season, he was ready to bolt for more stability and opportunity. In 2024 Chinn was a free agent and signed with the Washington Commanders instead of re-signing with Carolina to try his luck with new head coach Dave Canales. In his one season in Washington he started all 17 games with 117 tackles, two sacks, and five passes defended. In 2025 he signed a two-year, $16.3 million deal with the Las Vegas Raiders and started off his tenure last year with 15 starts and 114 tackles. Coming out of his 2020 rookie season, Jeremy Chinn looked like a franchise cornerstone for the Panthers. As Panthers fans looked ahead back then, most of us were predicting he’d be a Pro Bowler by 2023 instead of an underutilized “tweener” mostly watching from the sidelines at the whims of a coaching staff that didn’t even last a year. As he continues to rack up 100-plus tackle seasons, many Carolina fans still wish he was doing it in a Panthers uniform.

title: Ben Johnson thinks D’Andre Swift has more in the tank for Chicago Bears
summary: It might be time to rethink our expectations for veteran Chicago Bears running back D’Andre Swift heading into a critical 2026 campaign. Some of us (pointing squarely at myself here) have been skeptical of Swift’s upside in the Bears offense long-term, even after he experienced a monster turnaround last season when Ben Johnson, his former […]
full_text: It might be time to rethink our expectations for veteran Chicago Bears running back D’Andre Swift heading into a critical 2026 campaign. Some of us (pointing squarely at myself here) have been skeptical of Swift’s upside in the Bears offense long-term, even after he experienced a monster turnaround last season when Ben Johnson, his former offensive coordinator in Detroit, took over as Chicago’s head coach. Both his absolute production (1,087 rushing yards and nine touchdowns) and his advanced metrics pointed to one of the most improved backs in the league from 2024 to 2025, with Johnson’s focus on the run game and overall offensive competence a big reason for the positive change. Turns out, Johnson thinks the 27-year-old back can still take things to another level this season—the final year of his current deal in Chicago. “He’s a dynamic player,” Johnson said, via the Bears’ website . “I’ve known that about him since he came into the league, firsthand up there in Detroit, and certainly last year I wasn’t surprised about the year he had. So, is he capable of more? Absolutely. He absolutely is. He’s a vital part of what we do here.” Swift hinted in an offseason presser that he agrees with his coach’s assessment, specifically noting that he feels he “ left some [plays] out there ” that could’ve helped him and the Bears offense have an even bigger year. He’s not wrong about that, as you could say for just about any player. But the important part is that Swift did far more good than bad for Chicago last year despite that being true. And the Bears, as currently constructed, no doubt have plans on using him a lot in 2026. Right now, even with Kyle Monangai returning and rookie Zavion Thomas potentially getting a carry or two here and there as a rookie, Swift is clearly the lead dog in that backfield and showed last year he can make the explosive plays Johnson loves out of this offense more consistently than anyone in the room. Unless we see a major trade for another vet, which feels unlikely given where the Bears are cap-wise, that’s not going to change. Swift will continue to carry the majority of the load both in the run and pass game, with Monangai serving as the change-of-pace thunder to his lightning. While the Bears’ championship aspirations depend significantly on the growth of Caleb Williams and the passing game in the star quarterback’s third year, Chicago’s run game will set the tone for this offense as long as Johnson remains head coach. And Swift, for the time being, is the head of the snake in that regard. Unlike last year, that actually feels like a strength heading into the season.
author: Khari Thompson

title: Training Camp Battle: WR3: Jahdae Walker vs Kalif Raymond
summary: We have a few more training camp battles to look at as the Bears are getting close to reporting to camp. This next battle, if I had to guess, will be the one that Chicago Bears fans will be most interested in throughout July and August. It’s the battle to see who emerges as the […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - NOVEMBER 02: Chicago Bears wide receiver Jahdae Walker (20) warms up before the game against the Chicago Bears and the Cincinnati Bengals on November 2, 2025, at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati, OH. (Photo by Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images We have a few more training camp battles to look at as the Bears are getting close to reporting to camp. This next battle, if I had to guess, will be the one that Chicago Bears fans will be most interested in throughout July and August. It’s the battle to see who emerges as the team’s WR3 between Jahdae Walker and Kalif Raymond. Walker emerged as a fan favorite after a stellar training camp and preseason. As a UDFA, he had a steep hill to climb to make the 53-man roster. But climb it he did. The Bears thought so highly of Walker that they didn’t want to risk putting him on the practice squad. They kept him on the 53 and for good reason. Walker was inactive for 7 of the first 12 Bears games, and when he played, he only saw six offensive snaps total. But as the season shifted into December, Walker earned opportunities on the offense, and he made it count. Walker had six catches, including 2 touchdowns (and a critical game-tying touchdown against the Green Bay Packers), while earning 78 snaps. Olamide Zaccheaus had 61 snaps over those last three games, and Walker started pushing OZ for snaps for the WR4 spot. Come playoff time, Ben Johnson went with the veteran, and Zaccheaus was active, and Walker was not. But Walker made it clear that he was going to be pushing for more playoff time in 2026. The Bears let OZ walk after the season and traded DJ Moore, which opened up the door for Walker to potentially be WR3, but the Bears went out and signed someone who has familiarity with Ben Johnson and his offense, former Detroit Lion Kalif Raymond. Raymond’s production has definitely dipped over the last two seasons in Detroit. Raymond had 500 yards receiving over the last two seasons after averaging over 500 yards per season from 2021 to 2023. Raymond, whether he’s WR3 or WR4, will have a role on this team because he will also contribute on special teams, but he and Walker are going to vie for that WR3 role. Now, to be fair, that role will not be as prominent in Chicago as it is on other teams. The Bears will feature a lot of 12 personnel with Cole Kmet and Colston Loveland, but not only that, you can expect 13 personnel with rookie Sam Roush as well. For some teams that sit in 11 personnel, that WR3 will be on the field for 75 or 80% of the snaps. For the Bears, the WR3 this season may only be on the field for 40% of the snaps, but that’s still going to be plenty of opportunities in this offense. You would have to think that the Bears would want Walker to take this job and run with it. Teams would always prefer their young players to earn jobs away from veterans, but they never want to hand the jobs to them; they want them to earn them. Walker definitely has places to improve. He needs to add muscle; he needs better blocking technique, but he’s already made significant progress in one year. Can he make more significant progress this year? I would expect that to happen. What do I think happens here? I think this situation plays out like Luther Burden and Zaccheaus did last year. In 2025, Rome Odunze and DJ Moore were the WR1 and WR2 on the team, OZ was the team’s WR3, and eventually Burden took over as he got more comfortable in the offense. This year, I expect Odunze and Burden to be the team’s top two WRs, and I expect Raymond to be the team’s WR3 out of the gate in September, but I think Walker will continue to improve and he will take over for Raymond at some point in the season and secure the WR3 status in Chicago. Fans might get frustrated when they don’t see Walker getting significant snaps in September, but be patient; Walker’s time certainly feels like it’s coming.

title: Chicago Bears 2026 Training Camp Position Breakdown: Defensive End
summary: I normally kick these Chicago Bears’ training camp positional preview articles off on offense, but the defense is where most of the questions are this year, so I wanted to begin there. The secondary and linebackers have some new faces to mix in, while the defensive line has been the chief concern from fans all […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MD - OCTOBER 26: Dayo Odeyingbo #55 and Shemar Turner #95 of the Chicago Bears warmup before the game against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium on October 26, 2025 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images I normally kick these Chicago Bears’ training camp positional preview articles off on offense, but the defense is where most of the questions are this year, so I wanted to begin there. The secondary and linebackers have some new faces to mix in, while the defensive line has been the chief concern from fans all offseason. So let’s start at defensive end. Roster Locks Some fans underrate Montez Sweat, but he’s an all-around good football player and also the most consistent pass rusher on the team. Austin Booker showed promise last year, and the Bears are banking on him to continue his ascent into a viable EDGE. He’s added some bulk, he’s worked on his get-off, and I feel by the end of the season he’ll have established himself as more than viable. He’ll be ready for a contract extension. Dayo Odeyingbo is ahead of schedule with his rehab from tearing his Achilles, and the Bears expect him to be the player they thought he’d be when they signed him last offseason to a 3-year contract worth $48 million, and $32 million in total guarantees. “We weren’t quite sure when we started the offseason program that we would get him for any length of time, but the fact that he’s on the field, he wants to be out there,” head coach Ben Johnson said last month via the BearsWire . “It’s just another step forward in terms of him gaining confidence again and how he’s moving. He’s done a great job of being attentive in meetings, and so I know he was really itching to get back out there with his teammates, and so it’s a step in the right direction for sure.” In eight games last year, Odeyingbo had 21 tackles, 2 tackles for loss, 1 sack, 4 QB hits, and a pass defended, which wasn’t enough. Earlier this month, Dayo attended the Sack Summit, which is a gathering of defensive linemen and pass rushers. It’s the defensive version of the OL Masterminds, where NFL players go to work on their craft. Considering he was a second-round pick a year ago, Shemar Turner isn’t going anywhere. He’s still coming back from a knee injury, and while the initial hope was he’d be back for the offseason program, now it looks like his availability for the start of camp is in question. He may need to start on the PUP list. A Good Bet To Make It Daniel Hardy provides some positional flexibility with his ability to get some emergency snaps at linebacker, but it’s his special teams skills that make him likely to stick around on the 53-man roster. Roster Bubble/Practice Squad Jonathan Garvin, Jamree Kromah, and Jeremiah Martin will again be fighting for a spot on the practice squad. All three ended last year there, and they could all make it again. Of the three, Garvin has the most experience, having appeared in 38 games from 2020 to 2022 with the Packers. The other two have yet to take a snap in the NFL. Do you see any surprise moves at defensive end for the Bears this year?

title: Can intriguing rookie Eric Gentry carve out a role in Cincinnati?
summary: Every year, one or two undrafted free agents emerge from relative obscurity to earn meaningful NFL roles. The Cincinnati Bengals are hoping linebacker Eric Gentry can become the next name on that list. After going undrafted out of USC, Gentry landed in Cincinnati as one of the more fascinating developmental prospects in this year’s rookie […]
full_text: Oct 28, 2023; Berkeley, California, USA; USC Trojans linebacker Eric Gentry (18) gestures during the third quarter against the California Golden Bears at California Memorial Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Darren Yamashita-Imagn Images Every year, one or two undrafted free agents emerge from relative obscurity to earn meaningful NFL roles. The Cincinnati Bengals are hoping linebacker Eric Gentry can become the next name on that list. After going undrafted out of USC, Gentry landed in Cincinnati as one of the more fascinating developmental prospects in this year’s rookie class. At 6-foot-7 with extraordinary length and athleticism, he looks unlike just about any linebacker currently in the NFL. Now, he’ll attempt to turn those rare physical traits into a roster spot under new defensive coordinator Al Golden. Eric Gentry Height: 6’7” Weight: 221 College: USC Age: 23 Years Pro: Entering Rookie Season Hometown: Philadelphia, PA Career at a glance Gentry’s college journey took a unique path. Originally beginning his career at Arizona State, the Philadelphia native flashed immediately as a true freshman before transferring to USC ahead of the 2022 season. Over four years with the Trojans, Gentry developed into one of the defense’s most recognizable playmakers. He totaled 271 career tackles, 27 tackles for loss, nine sacks, two interceptions, 13 passes defended and nine forced fumbles during his collegiate career. But what consistently stood out wasn’t just the production. It was his frame. Standing nearly 6-foot-7 with a wingspan more commonly associated with NBA forwards than NFL linebackers, Gentry became known for disrupting passing lanes, chasing down ball carriers from the backside and serving as a versatile chess piece capable of playing off-ball linebacker while occasionally rushing off the edge. Those traits intrigued NFL evaluators. Questions about his weight, play strength and positional fit ultimately kept him from hearing his name called during the draft. The Bengals wasted little time changing that. Why Cincinnati signed him It’s easy to understand why Al Golden wanted to get a closer look. Gentry simply possesses traits that can’t be coached. His length allows him to affect passing lanes in ways few linebackers can, while his athleticism gives him legitimate sideline-to-sideline range. He’s also shown flashes as a blitzer and has a knack for forcing turnovers, making him an intriguing developmental piece in a defense looking to become faster and more versatile. Of course, there are reasons he entered the league as an undrafted free agent. At roughly 220 pounds, Gentry remains undersized by NFL linebacker standards. He’ll need to add functional strength, improve his ability to shed blocks and become a more consistent tackler before he’s ready for significant defensive snaps. Fortunately for both player and team, Cincinnati doesn’t need him to contribute immediately. 2026 outlook The Bengals significantly reshaped their defense this offseason, but linebacker remains one of the more intriguing position battles entering training camp. Veterans and draft picks are expected to occupy the top spots on the depth chart, meaning Gentry’s clearest path to making the roster will likely come through special teams and showcasing his versatility throughout the preseason. His unique physical profile also opens the door for creative usage. Could Golden eventually mold him into a hybrid linebacker-edge defender? Could he become a designated passing-down defender who drops into coverage while creating disruption with his length? Those answers won’t come overnight. But they’re part of what makes Gentry one of the more fascinating long-term projects on Cincinnati’s roster. What to expect Making the initial 53-man roster won’t be easy for Gentry. The practice squad appears to be the most realistic outcome entering training camp, allowing Gentry to continue developing physically while learning Golden’s defensive system. That shouldn’t be viewed as a disappointment. Several productive Bengals contributors have begun their careers in similar fashion, and Gentry’s athletic ceiling may be higher than that of many players selected late in the draft. If he adds 15 to 20 pounds without sacrificing his movement skills, his long-term outlook becomes even more intriguing. His combination of length, speed and football instincts simply isn’t something teams encounter very often. Final outlook Eric Gentry is the definition of a developmental lottery ticket. His floor may be a practice squad linebacker who contributes on special teams. His ceiling, however, is considerably more interesting. The Bengals have spent the offseason searching for faster, longer and more versatile defenders capable of fitting Al Golden’s evolving scheme. Few players on the roster check those boxes quite like Gentry. He’ll need time, strength and refinement before becoming a meaningful contributor. But if everything clicks, Cincinnati may have quietly uncovered one of the biggest steals of its entire rookie class.
