title: Bengals Film Room: All-22 review of revamped defense
summary: The Bengals added a lot of proven veteran talent on the defensive side of the ball via free agency and the trade for Dexter Lawrence. Let’s take a deeper look at some of those additions. Kyle Dugger Dugger isn’t likely to unseat Jordan Battle for the starting safety spot opposite Bryan Cook. However, I do […]
full_text: Oct 7, 2024; Kansas City, Missouri, USA; Kansas City Chiefs safety Bryan Cook (6) intercepts a pass intended for New Orleans Saints wide receiver Rashid Shaheed (22) during the first half at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Jay Biggerstaff-Imagn Images | Jay Biggerstaff-Imagn Images The Bengals added a lot of proven veteran talent on the defensive side of the ball via free agency and the trade for Dexter Lawrence. Let’s take a deeper look at some of those additions. Kyle Dugger Dugger isn’t likely to unseat Jordan Battle for the starting safety spot opposite Bryan Cook. However, I do expect him to still be a valuable contributor who will see 15-20 snaps a game. The thing I find most impressive about Dugger is what he can do against the run when playing down in the box. For a team that still has questions about the young linebackers, Dugger could see a decent amount of snaps in a rotational role down in the box to help them out. Dugger is a former second-round draft selection, finishing the 2025 season with the Pittsburgh Steelers. He finished the year with 59 tackles, a sack, and two interceptions. Not the biggest addition to the defense this year, but I think he will still be a valuable addition. Kyle Dugger was another veteran addition to the Bengals defense. He should be a good rotational and depth piece with some versatility. pic.twitter.com/Q1idIZLf4w — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) July 16, 2026 Jonathan Allen Jonathan Allen is a former first round draft selection. He has two Pro Bowls during his career, initially starting out with Washington. He spent the 2025 season with the Minnesota Vikings. Allen put up 68 tackles and 3.5 sacks last year. He has 45.5 sacks during his career. While he may not be the dominant pass rusher he once was, he still has plenty of juice to be an effective player on the defensive line. The ability to rotate with BJ Hill, while having a monster like Dexter Lawrence drawing so much attention, should allow for all of those guys to benefit from playing together. The PFF grades for Allen were poor, but the tape I watched showed a player much better against the run than those grades would indicate. He does a great job working down the line, his awareness as a run defender, and overall football IQ stand out. He is a reliable tackler, and he can still get some quick wins as a pass rusher. After playing over 800 snaps in 2025, he should be able to get that number down this season, allowing for him to remain fresh throughout the year. The Bengals also added veteran Jonathan Allen at defensive tackle. Allen recorded 68 tackles and 3.5 sacks last season for the Vikings. https://t.co/mQmOnEaOpe pic.twitter.com/ZFbrZ11hyx — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) July 15, 2026 Boye Mafe Mafe was another addition to a revamped Bengals defensive line. He was part of a deep defensive line for the Super Bowl-winning Seattle Seahawks during the 2025 season. While he recorded just 2 sacks during the 2025 season, he was still getting pressure at a high rate when on the field. You don´t have to go very far back to see more sack production throughout his career. He recorded 6 sacks in 2024, after having 9 sacks during the 2023 season. He will play a lot more snaps with the Bengals this year, and I expect a big jump back up in his sack production. The expectations should be for him to get back to being an 8-10 sack player. He isn’t a liability against the run, as some would say Trey Hendrickson was during his time with the Bengals. Mafe is a high-effort player, has great athleticism, and knows how to effectively use his hands to discard blocks. The Bengals should have a decent rotation with Shemar Stewart, Cashius Howell, and Myles Murphy at defensive end, but Mafe will be expected to lead that charge as a pass rusher in 2026. Boye Mafe is another addition to the Bengals revamped defensive line. His ability to generate quick pressures will be critical for a team replacing Trey Hendrickson. pic.twitter.com/mE5o56VWIC — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) July 15, 2026 Bryan Cook It is hard to understate just how big of an upgrade Cook should be in comparison to Geno Stone. Cook is the complete opposite when it comes to physicality and reliability as a tackler at the safety position. He is a fantastic pre-snap communicator, which has been lacking the last couple of seasons on the defensive side of the ball. The Cincinnati native should help stabilize the back end of the defense. Cook had an 83.2 coverage grade, along with an 80.1 run defense grade. He had just a 5.6% missed tackle rate last season. In comparison to Stone, who had a 50.7 coverage grade, 53.9 run defense grade, and a brutal 18.7% missed tackle rate on the season. Bryan Cook is a HUGE upgrade at safety for the Bengals defense. Physical, rangy, dependable tackler, and a great pre-snap communicator. pic.twitter.com/tbj5EyH5fF — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) July 15, 2026 Dexter Lawrence The Bengals’ biggest defensive addition, both figuratively and literally, was Dexter Lawrence. Listed at 6’4” and 342 pounds, Lawrence is a massive man on the interior defensive line. While he didn’t record any sacks in 2025, he was consistently disruptive and pushed the pocket for the Giants. It is also no coincidence that Brian Burns had a career year as a pass rusher. Lawrence will open up the rest of the defensive line to make plays, along with the Bengals young linebackers. Lawrence is a stout run defender who commands a lot of attention. He has a powerful bull rush, better movement skills than a guy that size should have, and had just a 5.6% missed tackle rate during the 2025 season. Dexter Lawrence commands so much attention. He takes on doubles to free up teammates, and when he is not doubled, he is getting push directly into the lap of the quarterback. Tone setter on the defensive line that will make everyone around him better. pic.twitter.com/yp0PnuN6Zz — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) July 15, 2026 With training camp just around the corner, there is reason for a lot of optimism based on the additions the Bengals have made to a defense that sorely needed reinforcements. Nothing matters until the pads come on during the regular season, but it is encouraging that the front office went out and made some moves that they normally wouldn’t.

title: Can Howard Cross III become the Bengals’ next undrafted gem
summary: After starring at Notre Dame, Howard Cross III now has an opportunity to prove that his size isn’t nearly as important as his relentless motor. Howard Cross III Cap Status Cross is signed to a 1-year, $1,005,000 contract with the Bengals, which carries a cap hit of $1,005,000 in 2026. Background Howard Cross III should […]
full_text: After starring at Notre Dame, Howard Cross III now has an opportunity to prove that his size isn’t nearly as important as his relentless motor. Howard Cross III Height: 6-foot-1 Weight: 285 pounds Age: 24 College: Notre Dame Hometown: Paramus, New Jersey Experience: 1 year Cap Status Cross is signed to a 1-year, $1,005,000 contract with the Bengals, which carries a cap hit of $1,005,000 in 2026. Background Howard Cross III should have heard his name called during the 2025 NFL Draft. Instead, the former Notre Dame standout watched all seven rounds come and go before signing with Cincinnati as an undrafted free agent. Fortunately for the Bengals, draft position has never determined NFL success. Cross arrives with one advantage that few rookies possess. He spent three seasons playing under current Bengals defensive coordinator Al Golden at Notre Dame, giving him a thorough understanding of Golden’s defensive concepts. During six seasons with the Fighting Irish, Cross appeared in 65 games, recording 169 tackles, 19.5 tackles for loss, and 11 sacks. He earned Second-Team All-American honors in both 2023 and 2024 while helping lead Notre Dame to the College Football Playoff National Championship Game. His biggest obstacle has never been production. It has been perception. At 6-foot-1 and 285 pounds, many NFL teams questioned whether he had the size to consistently hold up against professional interior offensive linemen. What they couldn’t question was his effort, leverage, hand usage, and football intelligence, traits that made him one of college football’s most disruptive interior defenders. Cross spent much of his rookie season on Cincinnati’s practice squad before appearing in four games, finishing with four tackles and recovering his first NFL fumble in the season finale against Cleveland. Outlook on the 2026 Season and Beyond The Bengals have spent this past offseason rebuilding the defensive line, but there is still room for another contributor to emerge. Cross has all the tools to become that player. No one expects him to become an every-down starter overnight. But rotational defensive tackles who consistently create pressure and play with maximum effort are valuable pieces of any successful defense. If Cross can continue developing his strength while maintaining the explosiveness that made him so successful at Notre Dame, the Bengals may have found another overlooked talent who outplays his draft status.

That gives us a few more days to focus on what the offseason looked like and what the future might hold for the Browns, including any last-minute free agent additions . Betting lines continue to have little faith in Cleveland’s 2026 season. With a new head coach , a fully revamped offensive line , questions at quarterback , and a reliance on a lot of young players , the Browns have a lot to prove this season. The future, on the other hand, is bright. ESPN’s ranking of players at each position saw DE Jared Verse , LB Carson Schwesinger , RB Quinshon Judkins , and TE Harold Fannin Jr. given a lot of positive regard for young players entering just their second or third seasons. Veteran CB Denzel Ward remained near the top of his position as well. All in all, especially for a team given low expectations externally, Cleveland’s roster had a lot of players listed by executives, coaches, and scouts in ESPN’s rankings: The Browns had two players (Ward, Schwesinger) voted in the top-10 of their positions. Five players (Judkins, Fannin, Verse, Elgton Jenkins, Delpit) were listed in honorable mention. Tyson Campbell also received votes. https://t.co/8hSbgkEkQA — Daniel Oyefusi (@DanielOyefusi) July 16, 2026 Obviously there are teams with more players ranked and more players ranked at a higher level, but for a Cleveland roster seeing a ton of changeover, Browns fans should be more and more excited about the young talent that is setting the foundation.

title: Browns offseason look back: 5 moves I loved
summary: The Cleveland Browns made a ton of moves this offseason, with a big turnover on the coaching staff and the offensive side of the football. The biggest move was trading DE Myles Garrett, but the impact of that decision will take a couple of years to play out, even if some of it is felt […]
full_text: GM Andrew Berry of the Cleveland Browns | Getty Images The Cleveland Browns made a ton of moves this offseason, with a big turnover on the coaching staff and the offensive side of the football. The biggest move was trading DE Myles Garrett , but the impact of that decision will take a couple of years to play out , even if some of it is felt in 2026 . With training camp opening next week and rookies reporting in a few days, now is a good time to look back at the offseason decisions and see where things stand. Not everything was perfect this offseason (more on that in a different piece), but there are some positive decisions that still look good months later: Retaining GM Andrew Berry To be honest, I think Berry has done an okay to good job in his role given some of the constraints around him. While I know some of you will stop reading this list after seeing Berry’s name here, just know I’m not someone who just assumes everything he does is good. On the other hand, I have the privilege of talking to NFL types from all over the league every year at the NFL Combine, and their respect for Berry is pretty universal. The reason I have Berry on this list, however, is continuity. It is one of the few things that the Cleveland organization hasn’t had since “The Return.” Berry’s vision continues after a very good 2025 NFL draft class, which led to this year’s being pretty exciting, and keeps the Browns roster from seeing complete turnover just because “they aren’t my guys.” Hiring an offensive-minded coach Whether Todd Monken was the right hire or not is still up in the air, but Cleveland needed someone to help right the ship on that side of the ball. The NFL has now added “offensive play caller” to the list of “must-haves” (along with an owner who will spend, a good head coach, and a good quarterback). Finding a good play caller to work under a defensive-minded head coach is far more difficult, so hiring an offensive-minded head coach just made sense. Drafting Spencer Fano The Browns obviously needed a left tackle, and Fano provided the most certainty at the position. At the Combine, the consensus was that Fano would be at least a five- to 10-year Pro Bowl player. Does he have the same upside as some others? Maybe not, but he creates a lot of certainty for Cleveland’s offensive line. I also like that Berry still had his pick of offensive linemen when he took Fano (no second-guessing), while adding draft picks in the initial trade down. Letting veterans walk While the Browns may have tried to get Joel Bitonio to return, letting David Njoku, Wyatt Teller, Devin Bush, and others walk away allows for the team’s future to create the identity of the locker room. Bitonio’s return may have been nice, but now Cleveland’s younger players must take control of the team and its future instead of being appropriately respectful of the long-standing veterans. Back-to-back WRs Saving the best for last, I can’t be more excited about the combination of KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston. The Browns have often waited to add receivers and, often, been forced to take big swings in free agency or trades to fill those positions. Not in 2026. Concepcion is a big play waiting to happen with the ball in his hands, while Boston provides a contested catch, big-bodied option along the sidelines, in the middle of the field, and as a redzone threat. Receivers are very dependent on quarterback play, so their stats may not be high in 2026, but Cleveland fans will be excited to watch the duo make plays that predict a strong future for the Browns offense. Focusing on the positives, what offseason moves do you look back on as positive? Do you disagree with any of the five I’ve listed above? full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - SEPTEMBER 29: Fullback Jim Brown #32 (R) and right tackle John Brown #70 of the Cleveland Browns look on from the sideline during a game against the Los Angeles Rams at Cleveland Municipal Stadium on September 29, 1963 in Cleveland, Ohio.. (Photo by James Drake/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cleveland Browns captured the 1964 NFL Championship by defeating the #1-ranked Baltimore Colts 27-0. The game was standing room only at Cleveland Municipal Stadium, which has 78,000 seats. The attendance was announced at 79,544. Fans were standing along the end zone lines and in every crevice of the venue. The Colts came into the game as 17-point favorites. The score at halftime was 0-0, which means the Browns erupted in the second half for all of the game’s points. WR Gary Collins hauled in three touchdown passes and was voted the game’s MVP. RELATED: 1964 BROWNS OT ROGER SHOALS INTERVIEW John Brown was a right tackle for the Browns in the 1964 NFL Championship Game. The Browns have eight pro football championships , tied for the third most with the New York Football Giants. The Green Bay Packers have 13 titles while the Chicago Bears have won nine. The 1964 club was the last championship team in Cleveland. In that 1964 season, Cleveland had gone 10-3-1 in the Eastern Conference, one game ahead of the St. Louis Cardinals, who finished 9-3-2. Meanwhile, the Colts crushed everyone en route to a 12-2-0 record in the Western Conference. Back then, the league was devoid of a playoff system, so the winners of each division, labeled “conferences,” were placed in the NFL Championship Game, with the winner named “World Champions.” Offensive tackle John Brown came to the Browns as a fourth-round draft pick after a good career at Syracuse University. He played with Ernie Davis, with whom he became great friends and was later roommates. At the time, the Washington Redskins were the only NFL club to have zero black players on their roster. The United States government came down on them and was about to ban them from using the brand-new 56,000-seat state-of-the-art D.C. Stadium (later renamed JFK Stadium), which was paid for by taxpayer money. The Redskins’ owner, George Preston Marshall, had a fresh 30-year lease and was given an ultimatum by U.S. Interior Secretary Stewart Udall to hire black players beginning the 1962 season, or forfeit the lease. This would mean the Redskins would have to go back to antiquated Griffin Stadium, which held 27,000 and was built in 1937. It featured wooden bleachers and was built for baseball. Fitting a football field was problematic from Day 1. Marshall was a well-known racist and never denied this. Of course, this was the time period when black Americans, although no longer enslaved, had a boatload of restrictions and minimal actual rights. Few restaurants accepted black patrons. In grocery stores, the white clientele was served first. Black folk had to sit in the balcony in theaters. They weren’t allowed in most stores at all. The only black doctors were employed in black medical facilities. No black judges, police, lawyers, or few teachers and athletes in college and the professional ranks. Marshall refused to draft a black college athlete , so instead, he handed over the draft to his GM/head coach, Bill McPeak, who selected Davis with the first overall pick in the 1962 NFL draft. Davis had just won the Heisman Trophy, the first black player to do so. Brown and Davis were really good friends while playing for Syracuse. And rightly so, not only did an offensive lineman with a running back make a lot of sense, but there were only four black players on the roster. Back then, coaches did not match black players with white players with housing. It just wasn’t done, so most schools recruited black players in pairs. Davis refused to go to Washington after the draft. Paul Brown then made a trade with Marshall that sent Davis to Cleveland for RB Bobby Mitchell (a very good player on his own and a favorite teammate of Jim Brown) and the Browns first round draft pick that year, Leroy Watson. Coach Brown envisioned Jim Brown with Ernie Davis as a monster backfield. Think: Barry Sanders and Emmitt Smith suddenly in the same backfield. John Brown was in negotiations with the AFL Chargers and the NFL Browns. When he heard that Davis was now with Cleveland, Brown signed with the Browns, and suddenly, he and Davis were once again teammates. Davis never played a down with Cleveland after being diagnosed with leukemia. His story was well-chronicled in the movie, “The Express.” Brown’s character in the movie was called “JB” throughout the film. In the summer of 1962, Brown shared an apartment with Davis while he went through treatment in the hospital, and then Davis passed away in May of 1963 at the age of 23-years old. Brown grew up in Camden, New Jersey, and played high school football at Camden High School . He lettered three years at Syracuse and played 10 seasons in the NFL: five with the Browns and the final five with the Pittsburgh Steelers after he was traded in 1967. Back then, the Browns-Steelers rivalry wasn’t a thing. Pittsburgh was annually one of the worst teams until it hired Chuck Noll in 1969. Although the two teams were in the same division, Cleveland’s main rivalry during this time frame was the Giants. Dawgs by Nature staff writer Barry Shuck interviewed John Brown, one of the surviving members of that 1964 NFL Cleveland Browns title team, the franchise’s last championship team. A lot of Shuck’s questions center on racial unfairness, because back in the 1950s and into the early 1960s, it was a tradition in every American city to shove black people to the bottom and keep them there. Including athletes. There are also a fair number of questions centered around Davis, because you can’t tell the story of Ernie Davis without discussing John Brown. And vice versa. Get this: Brown blocked for Ernie Davis and Jim Brown at different levels. Both running backs passed away exactly 60 years apart , and Brown moved defenders out of the way for both. Brown’s journey is full of oppression, and so some of these questions have to address what happened. For goodness’ sake, Brown was banned from using the elevators in a hotel in Dallas just because he was black. Race was part of Brown’s trek to and in the NFL. To know what America was like in the 1950s-1960s gives the reader an idea of just how remarkable Brown’s trail towards becoming an NFL player actually is. Brown, now age 87, became a bank executive after his NFL career concluded. He has remained in the Pittsburgh area after that retirement. He was baptized in 1947. His wife passed away years ago, but he has three sons, four granddaughters, and one great-granddaughter. Shuck: Besides football, what other sports did you play at Camden High School ? Brown: I ran track. I ran the 100 and 200. Then I put on weight, and I stopped running and did the shot put, discus, and the high jump. Back then, my best time in the 100 was 11.5. But the guy who won was like 10.1. We had a guy who was fast at my high school who later played for Rutgers. Shuck: Back in those days, black athletes did not have the opportunities they have today. How did you end up at Syracuse? And did you get any offers from predominantly black colleges? Brown: We did not have those opportunities. We had a referee who refereed some of our high school games. He gave my name to (Syracuse head coach) Coach Schwartzwalder. I was on my way to a college that I loved, called Colby College in Waterville, Maine. They had only one or two black students at the time, but I liked the college. They had a lake in the middle of the campus. I then went to Rutgers for a visit, and all they talked about was Paul Roberson. I was an admirer of his, but they put me off because I thought they could talk to me instead of just about Paul Roberson. Talk to me about me. I came to understand, as I got older, why they just talked about Paul Robeson.…

title: Cowboys news: Jaishawn Barham is an intriguing player as a rookie
summary: Jaishawn Barham: A Dark Horse 26′ Defensive Rookie of the Year Candidate – Cody Warren, Inside The Star The Cowboys will need a pass rush by committee approach this season, and rookie Jaishawn Barham could fit into that very well. Christian Parker has a defender, much like Downs, who he can move around the defensive […]
full_text: Jaishawn Barham: A Dark Horse 26′ Defensive Rookie of the Year Candidate – Cody Warren, Inside The Star The Cowboys will need a pass rush by committee approach this season, and rookie Jaishawn Barham could fit into that very well. Christian Parker has a defender, much like Downs, who he can move around the defensive front seven. Barham can play just about every position from linebacker to the defensive line. We don’t have to watch Dallas force this guy into a job. If Christian Parker is as advertised , he will find a way to put this young man in a position to succeed. Or find the position that Barham can cause the most havoc and keep using him there. Jaishawn Barham Gives Dallas Options I would hate to see the Cowboys line Jaishawn Barham up at inside linebacker every snap and just call it good. He can do much more than that . At Michigan, Jaishawn Barham handled linebacker duties while also succeeding near the line. He has the size to fight through traffic and enough burst to make a quarterback nervous. I would keep him inside against a running team and let him get downhill. He could even spy a mobile quarterback, and on passing downs, walk him up to the line and make the offense decide if he’s coming or not. I want to see that kind of uncertainty from this defense. Cowboys 2026 roster rundown: DT LT Overton – Jess Haynie, Blogging The Boys LT Overton was a great pick to help the Cowboys continue adding size to the defensive line. Background Years in NFL: 0 Acquired by: 2026 4th-round pick Overton is no stranger to change. He spent 2022-2023 at Texas A&M before transferring to Alabama, where he’s started the last two years at edge. He posted career highs as a senior with 26 solo tackles, six tackles for loss, and four sacks. Overton just missed playing college ball with fellow Cowboys rookie Caleb Downs, who left the Crimson Tide for Ohio State in the same offseason that Overton left the Aggies. Despite the extra recognition from playing at Alabama, Overton only had middling appeal in the 2026 draft class. He was too big and not athletic enough for the modern NFL pass rusher, looking more like a run stopper. There was pre-draft talk that he might fare best by bulking up and moving inside, and that’s exactly what the Cowboys saw in Overton when they use a late fourth-round pick to select him. 2026 Projections Role: Backup DT Roster Chance: 95% That said, we expect Overton to at least get a season. The Cowboys took him with a clear plan to move him inside. While he may not be a traditional 3-4 defensive end, Overton does fit the modern build of athletic 3-tech tackles. He will likely see work in nickel and other formations where size isn’t as important up front, rotating with veteran Jonathan Bullard as similar players. The transition may keep Overton on the sideline most of the year, or at least the early portion. He will need to learn technique while also developing physically for the role. We’ll probably see more of Bullard and Otito Ogbonnia in the rotation with Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark. There are some excellent mentors for Overton in that group, hopefully helping him to develop quickly. If the Cowboys are going to carry him on the 53-man roster this year, he may end up having to play more once any of the veterans gets injured. Role Call: Jalen Thompson has the IQ, versatility to lead Cowboys – Patrik Walker, DallasCowboys.com Even before drafting Caleb Downs, the Cowboys made a splash on the backend of the defense by signing Jalen Thompson. How He Got Here: Jalen Thompson began his journey to the NFL in Compton, where he began to make a name for himself at La Serna High School before transferring to Downey High School, ultimately finding his way as a three-star recruit to Washington State. He went on to earn Second-team All-Pac 12 honors (2017), catching the eye of NFL scouts in the process, and ultimately got the call from the Arizona Cardinals in the fifth round of the 2019 NFL Draft — where he spent seven seasons before signing with the Cowboys in 2026, reuniting with secondary coach Ryan Smith in the process. Plenty — Thompson’s exceedingly high football IQ and versatility makes him a ready-made fit for what defensive coordinator Christian Parker wants in a defensive back. The 27-year-old was signed to multi-year deal in free agency for a reason, and that’s because he’s part of a bigger long-term solution in the Cowboys’ defensive backfield. Expect to see him move around between free safety, strong safety and nickel corner, with a rep or two at off-ball linebacker mixed in as well, at times. Thompson is a field general of the highest order (which is why he’s a green dot candidate) and is expected to combine with rookie first-round pick Caleb Downs to help turn Dallas’ secondary into something … different. Did You Know : Caleb Downs enters as the headline defensive acquisition by the Cowboys this offseason, but Thompson is one of the most important additions in free agency ahead of the NFL Draft that sent Downs to Dallas. Thompson provides a veteran presence but at the age of 27, an exceptional mix of youth and experience. NFL coach hits the nail on the head with Cowboys’ George Pickens conundrum – Levi Dombro, The Landry Hat The Cowboys want to see a repeat performance from George Pickens alongside CeeDee Lamb in 2026. NFL coach perfectly encapsulates George Pickens issue Dallas Cowboys are grappling with Hidden in the top 10 NFL wide receiver rankings that ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler compiled by polling executives, coaches and scouts around the league was a quote from an anonymous NFL offensive coach about Pickens, who came in at No. 7 on this list, just one spot behind CeeDee Lamb: “One of the best I’ve ever seen at the contested catch,” a veteran NFL offensive coach said. “There’s such untapped ability there. It’s just a consistency issue and where his head’s at week to week.” That is the perfect encapsulation of the Cowboys’ Pickens conundrum. On the one hand, Pickens does things on a football field that even some of the best NFL wide receivers can’t dream of. When Pickens is on, he’s on , and there is no stopping him. Scarier for other teams is the fact that he may not have even reached the peak of his powers yet in his young career. And yet consistency is an issue for Pickens, who had almost as many games with fewer than 40 receiving yards (4) as games with over 130 (5). That is a wide range of outcomes for a team to expect from a player in a game, especially one who may be getting paid in the ballpark of $40 million annually. Dak Prescott’s Super Bowl comments spark the wrong question about the Dallas Cowboys’ 2026 season – Mauricio Rodriguez, A to Z Sports The Cowboys are looking for their first playoff berth in three seasons, and first under Brian Schottenheimer. “Each year you think that, but when you have the last year that we did, the offense that we did, you’ve been making changes and you’ve got a great defensive coordinator and you’ve got young guys, old guys, a great mix of veterans with talent, and us understanding what needs to be done,” Prescott said. He added that if a teammate doesn’t share that mentality, “honestly, I don’t want you on my team.” That’s what you want to hear from your quarterback. You never want to hear Prescott say the team would settle for a playoff appearance. And he’s not alone. Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer recently said in an interview that his plan is to be playing in the Super Bowl on Feb. 14. Whether it comes off as wildly optimistic, realistic, or straight out of a fantasy is not for us to say. But clearly, the organization is leaning into the conversation rather than dodging it. But are they that good? Here’s the thing about that label, though. It typically applies to teams so loaded that anything short of a championship feels like a failure. Take the Los Angeles Rams. They traded for Myles Garrett, acquired cornerbacks Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson, retained Matthew Stafford,…

title: How much Cowboys failure belongs to Dak Prescott
summary: The Dallas Cowboys have perfected the art of the January heartbreak. Over time, we have watched them play extremely well during the regular season, only to watch the entire operation come apart in the playoffs. What starts out as hope and a chance to break the long-lasting Divisional Round curse inevitably turns into another letdown […]
full_text: The Dallas Cowboys have perfected the art of the January heartbreak. Over time, we have watched them play extremely well during the regular season, only to watch the entire operation come apart in the playoffs. What starts out as hope and a chance to break the long-lasting Divisional Round curse inevitably turns into another letdown and another year added to this dreadful streak. It is exhausting. There are plenty of people deserving of blame. The front office gets a lot of it, often accused of not stocking enough groceries in the cabinet to supply the team with what they need come playoff time. Others point fingers at the coaching staff, who have been out-schemed by their counterparts when things matter most. And finally, there are the players who sometimes just fail to make enough plays. It is a team game, and there is plenty of blame to go around. While you can scrutinize these playoff performances and come up with a laundry list of offenders, one of the most notable culprits has been quarterback Dak Prescott. Fans come at him routinely, and recently, Emmanuel Acho claimed that it is Prescott, and not Jerry Jones, who has held this team back when the postseason rolls around. "Dak Prescott didn't become a punch line because of Jerry Jones… Dak Prescott became a punchline because he pissed down his leg against the 49ers" – @EmmanuelAcho SOUNDS OFF on Dak Prescott being widely labeled as "under appreciated" WE ARE LIVE: https://t.co/4gYorvL6DT pic.twitter.com/Q11VjsAviF — Speakeasy (@speakeasytlkshw) July 17, 2026 The hard truth is that Acho does have a leg to stand on with this argument. This is not to suggest that everything is Prescott’s fault, but there is a mountain of evidence showing that when it is time to be great, Dak has fallen a bit short. We owe it to ourselves to be transparent about those shortcomings. So, what exactly can we say about Prescott’s performance that supports his critics? It’s important to clarify that this isn’t suggesting that Prescott has been terrible in the postseason. He has played decently and, at times, pretty darn well. The real issue, however, is that more often than not, he just does not elevate his game to the level needed to help his team come out on top. Where exactly is he falling short? Paralysis by Analysis Prescott is as good as anyone when he can see what is going on and make quick decisions. When he is sharp, in a good rhythm, and getting the ball out on time, he can be super fun to watch. Unfortunately, the kitchen gets a little hot come playoff time, and smart coaching will challenge his medulla oblongata. When things are not as he expects post-snap, it can get a little dicey. He will hold the ball too long and miss out on key hot routes designed to get him out of trouble. The result is costly sacks or wasteful throwaways on third down that kill much-needed drives. In the playoffs, when possessions are precious, there is simply no room for stalled drives. Off-Balance Misfires When elite defenses are coming right at you, it is hard to stay composed and deliver perfect throws. The mental element is just one part of the equation. There have been many instances where you can see Prescott get a little rattled and succumb to internal pressure. Sometimes he can be a little too amped up and be off target. Whether it is panicked footwork or just poor mechanics reacting out of haste, it has led to some wildly errant throws in the playoffs. There have been several instances where Dak has sailed the ball over the head of his intended receiver or thrown behind them. These things happen, but when they happen on crucial third downs when continuing the drive is paramount to keeping his team in the game, it stings. But those moments pale in comparison to this next one. Blatant Misreads Interceptions happen, but when they happen in the playoffs, they can be detrimental to the season. Sadly, the picks Dak has thrown over the team’s last three playoff exits have had a catastrophic effect on the outcome of the games. He has thrown five interceptions across those three matchups. Four of those picks were thrown deep in Dallas territory, turning into immediate points for the opposition. The one interception that wasn’t in their own territory happened when the offense was on the verge of scoring in a nail-biter of a game where points were scarce. It is not just that these throws hurt their chances. It is the manner in which they happened that is tough to stomach. All five of these picks were balls that never should have been thrown. We are not talking about tipped passes or bad-luck deflections off a receiver’s hands. These were moments where the defense had him completely figured out, watched his eyes, and smothered his intended target. Throwing into heavy coverage will crush your team’s chances, and unfortunately, Dak has just done this too many times in recent playoff games. Look at the evidence over his last three playoff appearances: First pick: Threw into coverage, setting up an immediate Deebo Samuel touchdown Second pick: Threw right into the arms of a defender in his own territory, gifting the 49ers a field goal Third pick: Threw into heavy coverage in the red zone, wiping away guaranteed Dallas points Fourth pick: Threw into coverage deep in his own territory, giving the Packers an easy touchdown Fifth pick: Entirely missed the defender who jumped the route, resulting in a 64-yard Packers pick-six The Warm-Up Effect Mistakes on offense can have severe consequences, especially when the defense cannot keep its opponents out of the end zone. That happened in both playoff games Prescott played against the Packers, but it is not always just a defensive collapse. Sometimes an inefficient offense does plenty of damage on its own, which is exactly what happened in both of Dak’s playoff games against the 49ers. In either scenario, the offense played a major part in digging a massive hole early in the game. And it always seems to happen: 2016: Trailed by 18 points, scoring only three points until late in the second quarter 2018: Trailed by 16 points, scoring only seven points until late in the third quarter 2021: Trailed by 13 points, failing to score until late in the second quarter 2022: Failed to score a single point until midway through the second quarter 2023: Trailed by a staggering 27 points, failing to score until the clock hit zero in the second quarter Even in Prescott’s first-ever playoff win against Seattle in 2018, the Cowboys only had three points with less than 30 seconds to go in the second quarter. They just never get rolling early. Ever. Whether it is falling short on third down or making errant throws that give the opponent free points, this tendency to repeatedly dig a massive ditch in playoff games has completely ruined their chances in recent years. Prescott deserves a lot of credit for continuing to fight, and there have been moments where he has gotten the team right back into the thick of things. The problem is that when they continuously fly too close to the sun, they’re just asking to get burned. Discussing Prescott and playoffs is difficult because he plays well, mostly. The thing is, if the Cowboys are ever to have a deep playoff run or sniff another championship, something has to be elevated. Maybe that something is a stellar defense or a brilliant coaching staff. Other teams with lesser quarterbacks have made that work with those exact things. And frankly, it has made some fans jealous to the point where they convince themselves that Prescott hasn’t gotten a fair shake. But he has. That’s because there is another option that remains, and that is for Prescott to be the thing that is elevated. That is not a crazy expectation. Dak is compensated heavily, and it is totally fair to expect a player who commands that type of team resources to make a bigger impact. He has to, at some point, be the guy who punishes aggressive defensive attacks instead of falling victim to them. When the clock is…

Mandatory Credit: Chris Jones-Imagn Images | Chris Jones-Imagn Images LT Overton isn’t just transitioning from college ball to the NFL in 2026, but he’ll also be moving to a new position. One of three fourth-round picks last April by the Cowboys, Overton is going from playing edge rusher at Alabama to an inside position in Dallas. Background Years in NFL: 0 Acquired by: 2026 4th-round pick Overton is no stranger to change. He spent 2022-2023 at Texas A&M before transferring to Alabama, where he’s started the last two years at edge. He posted career highs as a senior with 26 solo tackles, six tackles for loss, and four sacks. Overton just missed playing college ball with fellow Cowboys rookie Caleb Downs, who left the Crimson Tide for Ohio State in the same offseason that Overton left the Aggies. Despite the extra recognition from playing at Alabama, Overton only had middling appeal in the 2026 draft class. He was too big and not athletic enough for the modern NFL pass rusher, looking more like a run stopper. There was pre-draft talk that he might fare best by bulking up and moving inside, and that’s exactly what the Cowboys saw in Overton when they use a late fourth-round pick to select him. Contract Status Years Left: 4 2026 Cap Hit: $1.08 million Even in the first year, Day 3 picks don’t get much security. Overton’s contract would only trigger $789k in dead money if he’s released, so that won’t save him if Dallas doesn’t find a spot for him on the roster. 2026 Projections Role: Backup DT Roster Chance: 95% That said, we expect Overton to at least get a season. The Cowboys took him with a clear plan to move him inside. While he may not be a traditional 3-4 defensive end, Overton does fit the modern build of athletic 3-tech tackles. He will likely see work in nickel and other formations where size isn’t as important up front, rotating with veteran Jonathan Bullard as similar players. The transition may keep Overton on the sideline most of the year, or at least the early portion. He will need to learn technique while also developing physically for the role. We’ll probably see more of Bullard and Otito Ogbonnia in the rotation with Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark. There are some excellent mentors for Overton in that group, hopefully helping him to develop quickly. If the Cowboys are going to carry him on the 53-man roster this year, he may end up having to play more once any of the veterans gets injured. title: Cowboys countdown to kickoff: Top 100 iconic games – Day 55
summary: It is Day 55 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like […]
full_text: Sep 28, 2008; Irving, TX, USA; Dallas Cowboys says goodbye to Texas Stadium with a 'Farewell Season' before kick-off against the Washington Redskins. Mandatory Credit: Matthew Emmons-Imagn Images It is Day 55 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like how big the game was for the organization, how memorable the game was, games that had unusual events take place, games that are a part of NFL lore, Cowboys firsts, and games where the Cowboys just plain dominated. Variety is the spice of life and we have all different kind of Cowboys games to review. At the bottom, we’ll link each day of the countdown so you can go back and check out any you missed. Get ready for an emotional entry for Day 55 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff, when we revisit one of the most soul touching nights in Cowboys history. This was the final game ever played at Texas Stadium, the building with the hole in the roof and decades of Cowboys memories attached to it. Dallas had a playoff push, a national stage, and a postgame ceremony ready to honor the old stadium. Saturday, December 20, 2008 — 8:15 p.m. ET Texas Stadium, Irving, Texas Final Score: Baltimore Ravens 33, Dallas Cowboys 24 The Cowboys actually started the night the right way. DeMarcus Ware forced a Joe Flacco fumble on Baltimore’s opening possession, and Dallas quickly turned the short field into a two-yard Tashard Choice touchdown. For a moment, it looked like the stadium might get the storybook ending everyone wanted. But Baltimore slowly took control. Matt Stover kept stacking field goals, hitting four on the night, and the Ravens led 9-7 at halftime despite not scoring an offensive touchdown. In the third quarter, Flacco found Derrick Mason for a 13-yard touchdown, pushing Baltimore ahead 16-7 and putting Dallas in chase mode. The fourth quarter is what made the game unforgettable, and painful. Nick Folk cut the deficit to 16-10, then Stover answered to make it 19-10. Tony Romo finally gave Dallas life with a seven-yard touchdown pass to Terrell Owens, trimming Baltimore’s lead to 19-17 with 3:50 left. The Cowboys needed one defensive stop to give Texas Stadium one last chance at a miracle. Instead, the Ravens delivered one of the cruelest closing stretches Dallas has ever allowed. Willis McGahee broke free for a 77-yard touchdown run to make it 26-17. Romo answered again, finding Jason Witten for a 21-yard touchdown that cut the score to 26-24 with 1:36 left. Then, on Baltimore’s very next offensive snap, Le’Ron McClain ripped off an 82-yard touchdown run, sealing the game and silencing the old stadium for good. Romo threw for 252 yards, two touchdowns and two interceptions, while Choice gave Dallas a tough 90 rushing yards and the opening score. But the Cowboys could not overcome the late defensive collapse. Baltimore ran for 265 yards as a team, with McClain and McGahee both going over 100 yards, and the two backbreaking fourth-quarter runs became the lasting football memory of Texas Stadium’s final night. This game belongs on the countdown because it was the end of an era. Texas Stadium opened in 1971, hosted championship teams, Hall of Famers, playoff classics, Thanksgiving memories, and some of the most iconic moments in franchise history. The Cowboys did not get the farewell they wanted, but the night still matters because it closed the book on the most famous home the franchise has ever had. And that is always worth remembering, making the game a hugely iconic moment in franchise history. We will never forget you Texas Stadium. Who remembers Texas Stadium? Today there’s no single game highlight, no emotional victory or heartbreaking loss. It’s a moment to say thank you to a place that saw unforgettable moments, legends that walked the field, records broken…a place that was more than a stadium, a… pic.twitter.com/SsWKtpUOY9 — Mike Poland (@kenfigkowboy) July 19, 2026 Interesting Facts About the Game This was the last NFL game ever played at Texas Stadium. The Cowboys held a postgame ceremony afterward, with legends including Roger Staubach, Randy White, Mel Renfro and Emmitt Smith among those tied to the farewell coverage. full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 27: Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs scrambles away from Donovan Ezeiruaku #41 of the Dallas Cowboys during the fourth quarter in the game at AT&T Stadium on November 27, 2025 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images We continue our Dallas Cowboys camp prediction series. Today we’ll analyze a group that has had an influx of defensive talent this offseason – the defensive line. On to the prediction. Prediction: Donovan Ezeiruaku becomes a star in camp Dallas is looking to replace its sack leader from 2025. Jadeveon Clowney had 8.5 sacks for the Cowboys last year, and it’s not a stretch to think there’s still a void left after Micah Parsons was traded to Green Bay just before Week 1. Enter second-year pro Donovan Ezeiruaku. He’s not on the NFL’s Top 100 list, but after this year, players voting on that list might think differently. The Boston College product is entering his sophomore season, and expectations are high. Ezeiruaku secured two sacks and one forced fumble in his rookie campaign. Not necessarily impressive numbers, but Ezeiruaku added 26 QB pressures in 2025, meaning his impact was felt regularly by opposing QBs. Now he’s tasked with replacing lost sack production, and the rotational competition brought by Dallas adding guys like Rashan Gary and Malachi Lawrence on the edge should have Ezeiruaku playing 110% every snap in camp. With the new defensive identity brought by new DC Christian Parker, the second-year end should blossom, and with his ascension, the defensive line and the defense as a whole can become a unit that opposing teams fear. What is your prediction for the defensive line at training camp? Who are we overlooking that might break out? Hit the comments and let us know.

title: The biggest question training camp must answer for Cowboys
summary: At the moment most fans are rather pleased with the state of the Dallas Cowboys. The offseason was very successful. Improvements were made, plenty of them. Effort was given, truly, for the first time in a minute. At the very least there is a common goal and a will to reach it. Despite the narrative […]
full_text: May 1, 2026; Frisco, TX, USA; Dallas Cowboys cornerback Caleb Downs (18) speaks with defensive coordinator Christian Parker during practice at the Ford Center at the Star Training Facility in Frisco, Texas. Mandatory Credit: Chris Jones-Imagn Images | Chris Jones-Imagn Images At the moment most fans are rather pleased with the state of the Dallas Cowboys. The offseason was very successful. Improvements were made, plenty of them. Effort was given, truly, for the first time in a minute. At the very least there is a common goal and a will to reach it. Despite the narrative of Cowboys fans across the internet (“It’s our year!” and We Dem Boyz), we aren’t declaring anything at the moment. We are excited and hopeful, but the stove has burned our hands way too many times. We wear oven mitts. Right now we are looking at training camp set to begin and wondering which part of the stove we are going to need them for specifically, though. The Cowboys have to figure out their cornerback situation Who are the starting cornerbacks on the Cowboys right now in your opinion? It’s a legit question. My take: DaRon Bland, Shavon Revel, and Cobie Durant. Caleb Downs’ abilities in nickel matter here as well, but we are looking at answering with three corners for this conversation. Just because we can put names on a two-deep does not mean that things are good, though. To be clear they could be! Bland, Revel, and Durant could form a legitimate group and all of this worrying could wind up being for not. For all of the improvements and changes to the roster though, cornerback has been left alone (relatively speaking), and given that the Cowboys had one of the worst defense in NFL history last year, that’s worrisome. There is a particularly optimistic side of this. The Cowboys hired Christian Parker this offseason to run their defense and the secondary is his specialty. Perhaps he is simply going to be the cornerback amplifier. Think of it when you are playing a video game, hopefully this analogy lands, and pick up a weapon or suit that increases certain attributes. That’s what Christian Parker is. He’s the cornerback suit. On some level this is the only thing that really makes sense anyway. The Cowboys know as much as we do how poor their defense was last year, and they proved that by making so many changes to it over the last few months. It’s not like they simply ignored cornerback for fun. But this is far and away the biggest question that needs to be answered during training camp for this group. Right?

title: There are fewer “elite” QBs in the NFL than you’ve been told
summary: We’ve become surprisingly casual with the word “elite.” One of the most common shortcuts for “elite QBs” in the NFL is counting Super Bowl rings. That may have worked forty years ago. The problem is that rings have become a remarkably poor way of separating truly elite quarterbacks from everyone else. When nearly one-quarter of […]
full_text: We’ve become surprisingly casual with the word “elite.” One of the most common shortcuts for “elite QBs” in the NFL is counting Super Bowl rings. That may have worked forty years ago. The problem is that rings have become a remarkably poor way of separating truly elite quarterbacks from everyone else. When nearly one-quarter of the NFL’s starting quarterbacks own a Super Bowl ring, winning one can no longer be the benchmark for elite quarterback play. Think about it. Elite literally means rare. If almost one fourth of starting quarterbacks satisfy your definition… your definition is wrong. But that hasn’t always been the case. Somewhere during the early stages of the Super Bowl era (Super Bowl I was played after the 1966 season) the idea of the elite QB must have been born, and with it the notion that an elite QB had to have won a Super Bowl ring. And that notion held true throughout the 70s and 80s when only a select few QBs in the league were actual Super Bowl winners. Up until 1991, there were never more than four or five active QBs in the league with a Super Bowl ring to their name. From 1992 to 2006, the NFL averaged 5.3 active Super Bowl-winning QBs, with the total never exceeding six in any single season. In the 12 years from 2007-2018, the average climbed to 7.3, and six seasons had eight active Super Bowl-winning QBs playing at the same time. In 2019 the number of QBs with a ring peaked at nine, and the average through 2025 stayed high at seven. In 2026, there will be six QBs with a Super Bowl ring playing in the NFL. Whether the increase is driven by player longevity, free agency, the salary cap, or simple chance doesn’t really matter. What matters is that a Super Bowl ring no longer separates the truly exceptional from the merely accomplished. If we’re looking for “elite,” we need a better definition. One way of doing that is by quantifying how much better a given quarterback was versus his peers who were playing at the same time. ProFootballReference.com provides such a metric which they call Passer Rating Index (or Rate+) and which calculates a QB’s passer rating relative to his NFL peers playing at the same time . body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table { border: 1px solid #000 !important; border-collapse: collapse !important; } body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th { padding: 4px 6px !important; } Passer Rating Index (Rate+) For each NFL season, PFR.com compute two things: 1. The league average passer rating for the three-year period with the given year in the middle. 2. The standard deviation of the stat for all individuals who had 14 or more pass attempts per scheduled game during the three-year period. Next, they compute how many standard deviations away from the league average each player was in each of his seasons. Then they multiply that number by 15 and add it to 100, and that is the number you see. Reading the results : 100 is league average. 115 is one standard deviation better than the NFL average at the time, 85 is one standard deviation below the average. A typical league-leading season will be in the high 120s or the low-to-mid 130s. The best QBs of the Super Bowl era. Here’s a list of the 11 QBs that were at least one standard deviation better than their peers over the course of their entire career : body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table { border: 1px solid #000 !important; border-collapse: collapse !important; } body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th { padding: 0px 6px !important; } Top 11 Rate+ QBs of the Super Bowl era Player Games Started Rate+ Steve Young (HOF) 143 126 Joe Montana (HOF) 164 122 Len Dawson (HOF) 159 120 Roger Staubach (HOF) 114 119 Peyton Manning (HOF) 265 118 Aaron Rodgers 257 118 Drew Brees (HOF) 286 117 Lamar Jackson 107 117 Joe Burrow 77 116 Tom Brady 333 115 Tony Romo 127 115 The list contains multiple champions, multiple non-champions, Hall of Famers, and players who will never reach Canton. Notice what’s missing from this list. Super Bowl rings. Five Hall of Famers sit at the top of the list. Steve Young, Joe Montana, Len Dawson, Roger Staubach, and Peyton Manning top the list, and there’s little doubt in my mind that these guys were some of the best to play the game – in their time. Montana and Young played until they were 38, (Staubach played until he was 37 but only started at age 27 due to his Navy commitment), so QB longevity is nothing new to the NFL, but long careers often come with a downside: they tend to ebb away towards the end. Aaron Rodgers is a good example of this. No doubt he is a top 10 QB of all time, but a decade ago, with 103 starts under his belt (2008-2014), he was sitting at the top of this list with a Rate+ of 127. Since then he’s mixed standout years with average years and his career Rate+ has dropped to 118 accordingly. This is obviously a watchout for the two “young” QBs on this list, Lamar Jackson and Joe Burrow, and a reason I’ve set the minimum threshold for most of the tables in this post to 50 starts. Tony Romo recently said his only regret is not winning the Cowboys a Super Bowl . I might have phrased that differently; the Cowboys were unable to put together a team capable of leveraging the 12th best passer in league history to get to a Super Bowl. Rate+ of Super Bowl-winning QBs since 1996 Thanks in no small part to Tom Brady, who vacuumed up seven Super Bowls by himself, there are only 18 Super Bowl winning QBs over the last 30 years. Here they are, sorted by their Career Rate+: body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table { border: 1px solid #000 !important; border-collapse: collapse !important; } body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th { padding: 0px 6px !important; } Rate+ of Super Bowl-winning QBs since 1996 Player SB Season Games started Career Rate + Peyton Manning 06, 15 265 118 Aaron Rodgers 10 257 118 Drew Brees 09 286 117 Tom Brady 01, 03, 04, 14, 16, 18, 20 333 115 Kurt Warner 99 116 113 Russell Wilson 13 202 113 Patrick Mahomes 19, 22, 23 126 113 Brett Favre 96 298 109 Ben Roethlisberger 05, 08 247 109 Jalen Hurts 24 82 106 John Elway 97&98 231 105 Matthew Stafford 21 239 105 Brad Johnson 02 125 103 Eli Manning 07, 11 234 98 Joe Flacco 12 201 94 Nick Foles 17 58 93 Sam Darnold 25 90 92 Trent Dilfer 00 113 88 When one third of the Super Bowl winning quarterbacks (6/18) have a below average, or slightly above average (Brand Johnson, 103) Career Rate+, then using Super Bowls to define elite passers is no longer a relevant argument. There are 207 QBs, active between 1955 and 2025, with at least 50 starts to their name. Here’s where you could draw the line by Career Rate+: 115 or higher: 5% (11 players) 112 or higher: 11% (23 players) 110 or higher: 15% (31 players) 115 feels a bit restrictive for the elite tier, 112 feels about right (113 would be 9%), and 110 feels a bit generous, but is a nice round number. If we use the 110 as the cutoff for an elite QB, then only seven of the 18 Super Bowl winners above were truly elite, further rendering moot the argument that elite passers can be defined by their number of rings. Peerless Cowboys Passers At least once in his of her life, every single Cowboys fan out there has been involved in a debate about how the different quarterbacks the Cowboys have had over the last 60+ years compare to each other. The difficulty in these discussions is that you’re discussing different players, on different teams, in different eras. But now you can compare them with Rate+, which might actually change our understanding of Cowboys history. So below is a rundown of the Cowboys illustrious list of QBs along with each QBs Career Rate+ along with a Rate+ number for his time in Dallas. body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body…

title: Cowboys news: Dallas’ secondary success this season is a gamble
summary: Cowboys’ turnaround at key position hinges on a series of gambles – Jason Kandel, The Landry Hat The cornerback position is far from locked down. Dallas is lucky they brought in DB guru Christian Parker to be their new defensive coordinator and work with these guys, but red flags are still flying. Let’s start with Bland, because […]
full_text: Detroit Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown makes a catch against Dallas Cowboys safety Malik Hooker (28) and cornerback DaRon Bland (26) during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Thursday, Dec. 4, 2025. | Junfu Han / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images Cowboys’ turnaround at key position hinges on a series of gambles – Jason Kandel, The Landry Hat The cornerback position is far from locked down. Dallas is lucky they brought in DB guru Christian Parker to be their new defensive coordinator and work with these guys, but red flags are still flying. Let’s start with Bland, because his inability to stay healthy has plagued this defense across the last two seasons, and he will still play a key role. It wasn’t long ago that the 27-year-old led the NFL with nine interceptions (and five pick-sixes) in 2023, but he’s only played 19 games in the two years since. Recent history suggests that the $92 million man can’t stay healthy. And he did not participate in offseason activities. And then there’s Durant, who was one of the bigger free-agent signings the Cowboys made this offseason. While he was a solid starter in Los Angeles last season, he has some issues of his own, so the Rams were quick to cast him aside in favor of Jaylen Watson and Trent McDuffie. The fifth-year cornerback is far from a sure thing. According to Pro Football Focus, Durant’s 66.8 PFF grade ranked 39th out of 114 qualified CBs , while his 67.4 coverage grade ranked 37th. However, he allowed an 85.6 passer rating when targeted, and is also pretty below average as a run defender. Then there’s Revel, who’s facing similar question marks to both of them. The 2025 third-round pick out of East Carolina missed the first 10 games of last season while rehabbing from the ACL tear that ended his college career. And once he returned, it got worse for him, as he played at less than 100%. 6 under-the-radar Cowboys who could shock in 2026 training camp – K.D. Drummond, Cowboys Wire Keep an eye on these names you may have forgotten about. OT Ajani Cornelius There’s no secret that the Dallas Cowboys have a really strong offense. As long as QB Dak Prescott is healthy, the team routinely finds themselves in, or in close proximity to, top-5 ranking in many metrics for that side of the ball. The one roster weakness they have there, though, is at the tackle position. Neither Tyler Guyton nor Terence Steele inspire visions of Pro Bowl appearances or All-Pro accolades. Most conversations around who could challenge them are centered around Nate Thomas or this year’s fourth-round pick Drew Shelton.Expert NFL picks: Exclusive betting insights only at USA TODAY. But perhaps Cornelius, who is in the same position this season as Thomas was last year, could shockingly join the conversation. The No. 204 selection from 2025 out of Oregon, Cornelius was identified by this current staff as someone they hoped to develop. There are several people in his way, but the climb to the top isn’t nearly as steep as other positions. TE Michael Trigg There’s no question about it, the tight end in Dallas’ offense has been fed as a result of whatever else is happening on the field. Jake Ferguson is a good outlet, but he’s not a dominating force and gives nothing after the catch. His fumbling issues has made him even less of a compliment. His backups leave a lot to be desired as pass catchers, meaning that if there’s anyone with juice at the position, they have a chance to contribute. The question for Trigg isn’t about juice; he’s a plus-level pass catcher… like highlight reel worthy pass catchter. The question is whether or not he can do the rest of the job description for being a professional tight end, and whether he can do that in the matter of one offseason. He went undrafted for those reasons, can he turn things around and become the shock player of this year’s camp. Cowboys Dubbed Logical Landing Spot for All-Pro Who May Be Final Piece to the Puzzle – Mike Moraitis, Sports Illustrated There’s still time to add depth. Despite all of their moves, Bleacher Report’s Kristopher Knox is of the opinion the Cowboys should make one more addition to their linebackers room by signing Bobby Wagner . “At this stage in his career, Wagner would make the most sense for a team seeking both talent and experience on its defense and with enough overall talent to make a strong push for the postseason,” Knox wrote. “Logical Landing Spots: Dallas Cowboys, Jacksonville Jaguars,” Knox added. Cowboys’ current situation at linebacker The Cowboys had a dire situation at the position going into the offseason, but things have improved since then. Dallas traded for Dee Winters before opting to select Jaishawn Barham in the third round of the 2026 NFL Draft, and those two join a linebackers room that also includes both DeMarvion Overshown and Shemar James. While that should be an adequate group, there are questions about each player in it. Overshown has been plagued by injury during his career, Barham and James are unproven and Winters amounts to an OK but not great starting option. If there’s one position group that could use a final piece to put it over the top, it’s linebacker. Christian Parker’s Hire Follows a Cowboys Super Bowl Pattern – Cody Warren, Inside The Star Fans have to hope history repeats itself. Ernie Stautner, Dave Wannstedt, Butch Davis, and Dave Campo all led defenses during Super Bowl seasons . We know those names now because of what came later, but it doesn’t mean each one arrived as some famous NFL coordinator everybody wanted. Stautner built his reputation with the defensive line under Tom Landry. Wannstedt followed Jimmy Johnson from the University of Miami and got his first NFL coaching job in Dallas. Davis worked his way up through the defensive front. Campo climbed through the secondary. Dallas didn’t always chase the hottest name available, but instead trusted coaches who were still moving up and gave them a defense before the rest of the league knew who they were. I think that’s where I’m at on the Christian Parker hire. He’s getting his chance because the coaches and players who have been around him knew he was ready for more, not because he bounced around collecting coordinator titles. I think we can all get behind that aspect of it easier than another recycled hire everybody knows. Daily discussion question: What is the ceiling on this team in your opinion?

title: Horse Tracks: Three players who could make a big leap in Year 2
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country! Training Camp is just 10 days away, and all the excitement for the 2026 season will finally move from speculation on paper to speculation on the field. And while all eyes will be on how Bo Nix’s ankle is doing, how Jaylen Waddle is fitting into the offense, how the rookies […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - NOVEMBER 16: Jahdae Barron #23 of the Denver Broncos celebrates during an NFL football game against the Kansas City Chiefs at Empower Field at Mile High on November 16, 2025 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country! Training Camp is just 10 days away, and all the excitement for the 2026 season will finally move from speculation on paper to speculation on the field. And while all eyes will be on how Bo Nix’s ankle is doing, how Jaylen Waddle is fitting into the offense, how the rookies are adjusting and which stars look solid again, there are several second-year players who could go under-the-radar if you’re not paying attention but have the potential for strong sophomore campaigns. Here are four second-year players I’m most curious about as our July 31 start date inches closer. WR Pat Bryant Bryant quietly became a trusted target for Bo Nix during the second half of his rookie season. He isn’t the fastest receiver on the roster, but he was a reliable target. With strong hands and good route discipline, he could quietly become a secret weapon while defenses focus attention on Jaylen Waddle and Courtland Sutton. If he develops into a consistent red-zone threat, Bryant could easily double last year’s touchdown production. “He’s a quick study. He gets it real fast,” said head coach Sean Payton earlier this summer. “I think one of his great skill sets is his run after the catch because his feet stay on the ground when he catches it. He’s got strong hands in traffic. He’s having a good stretch here.” Payton added that there’s a maturity to Bryant already this season, which is exactly what you hope for with the second-year players. They know the ropes, the system and the playbook. “He’s healthy…he knows exactly what to do and, and there’s a confidence about him, a maturity,” Payton added. “You wouldn’t feel like he was a second-year player if you didn’t know it.” Bo Nix throws it up to Pat Bryant II for the TD! The first career TD for the rookie WR 🙌 DALvsDEN on CBS/Paramount+ https://t.co/HkKw7uXVnt pic.twitter.com/C3z7yWt6ft — NFL (@NFL) October 26, 2025 CB Jahdae Barron The Broncos first-round draft pick in 2025 was basically a non-entity for the Broncos’ defense last season, but the second-year cornerback seems ready to step up for a big Year Two. Payton noted that Barron’s early offseason work was looking good and Barron’s film room study was paying off. “You can tell that he is progressively getting better,” Payton said during OTAs. “His IQ and his fundamentals of the game, it seems like he is wise beyond his years going into his second year. I’m excited for him.” As a rookie Barron played just a little over 300 defensive snaps. He and his coach hope for a bigger impact from the former Texas cornerback this season. “I think he’s an instinctual player,” the coach said, “so I think for him it’s just getting the reps and the practice work.” Barron’s progress in the offseason was noted by All Pro cornerback Patrick Surtain, so that’s always a good sign. “He’s been studying in the film room. You can tell he’s progressively getting better,” Surtain said last month. “His I.Q. and his fundamentals of the game, it seems like he’s wise beyond his years going into his second year, so, I’m excited for him.” I think we all forget Jahdae Barron was robbed of a pick-six on Mahomes last season pic.twitter.com/W1Mxj9rBsT — 𝙀𝙙𝙜𝙚 💥 (@BroncosEdge_) May 25, 2026 RB RJ Harvey There’s been a lot of talk already about the running back room this season with the addition of an intriguing rookie in Jonah Coleman and the return of veteran JK Dobbins. How Harvey plays in year two could have a lot to do with how the Broncos’ rushing attack goes in 2026. From everything Payton has said, and everything we began to see the second half of his rookie season, suggests Harvey has the skill set to thrive in year two. Not only can he run, he can catch in the backfield, create explosive plays and pass protect. But perhaps the best indicator of Harvey’s second year potential is how he has spent his offseason — studying fellow running back stars like Christian McCaffrey, Jahmyr Gibbs and Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker. “Just watching more film, watching other guys around the league, watching their film … just trying to see things on film that they do, trying to help better my game,” Harvey said. “In Year Two in the system, I feel way more comfortable and it’s only going to get better from where I left off.” Even with Dobbins considered the starter, the Broncos will want to be careful with the veteran’s load, and the guy poised to take that on will be Harvey. With more consistency than his rookie year, Bryant could easily become Denver’s most dynamic offensive weapon out of the backfield. BO NIX TO RJ HARVEY FOR THE LEAD DENvsKC on Prime Video Also streaming on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/wePrfadcIq — NFL (@NFL) December 26, 2025

title: Denver Broncos roster review: Running back Jaleel McLaughlin
summary: The Denver Broncos have depth at running back. There are three guys you can insert into the depth chart in ink: J.K. Dobbins, RJ Harvey, and rookie Jonah Coleman. How it falls after we’ll find out over the course of the six weeks. Included in that is how many running backs Sean Payton and Davis […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - JANUARY 04: Jaleel McLaughlin #38 of the Denver Broncos runs the ball in the first quarter against the Los Angeles Chargers at Empower Field At Mile High on January 04, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Matthew Stockman/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos have depth at running back. There are three guys you can insert into the depth chart in ink: J.K. Dobbins, RJ Harvey, and rookie Jonah Coleman. How it falls after we’ll find out over the course of the six weeks. Included in that is how many running backs Sean Payton and Davis Webb decide to keep on the roster and who gets placed on the practice squad. One of the backs looking to keep his spot on the Broncos’ active roster is Jaleel McLaughlin. Player Profile Age: 25 | Experience: Fourth Year | College: Youngstown State | Height: 5’7” | Weight: 187 pounds McLaughlin is entering his fourth season in Denver, but coming off the lowest production of his career. If you base what could happen in 2026 off last season and his status on the roster, it’s iffy at best. However, McLaughlin adds a different element than the three guys above on the roster. Jaleel McLaughlin’s 2026 outlook with the Broncos McLaughlin is one of the running backs and players with a speed element who could break any play as a runner or receiver. Granted, it’s been inconsistent, and that’s because of the lack of touches he gets. And those were even more rare for McLaughlin in 2025 when he had just 37 carries and four receptions. In his first two seasons with the Broncos, he had 76 and 113 carries and 31 and 24 receptions in 2023 and ’24. The dropoff is easy to diagnose, and makes McLaughlin’s status up in the air: the addition of Harvey. Both are versatile threats out of the back field as runners and receivers. Both have that playmaking ability that makes them a threat when they touch the ball. The difference between the two is that Harvey is bigger and more physical. And Harvey proved how reliable he can be, even as a rookie, after Dobbins was lost to injury. Now, Harvey has a year of experience in Denver’s offense and the NFL under his belt. Dobbins is looking to break his injury luck with a full season. And you add Coleman to the mix. You get the picture. The likeliest route for McLauglin to make the roster is on special teams as a returner. But even then, you have one of the best in the NFL in Marvin Mims. Final thoughts McLaughlin is a fun player in the Broncos offense. In his first two years, he became a fan favorite. When he touches the ball, he can make things happen. But the depth and the type of running backs above him on the depth chart, coupled with his drop in production in 2025, mean McLaughlin is looking at a steep hill to climb over the next six weeks to keep his spot on the roster.
