title: Denver Broncos roster review: WR Jaylen Waddle
summary: The Denver Broncos entered free agency with some high expectations from their fans. The team made it to the AFC Championship Game; they were the number one seed, won the AFC West, and were likely a Bo Nix broken ankle away from advancing to the Super Bowl. So many fans and media anticipated the Broncos […]
full_text: CENTENNIAL , CO - JUNE 4: Jaylen Waddle (17) of the Denver Broncos speaks to members of the media during OTAs at the Broncos Park in Centennial, Colorado on Thursday, June 4, 2026. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images The Denver Broncos entered free agency with some high expectations from their fans. The team made it to the AFC Championship Game; they were the number one seed, won the AFC West, and were likely a Bo Nix broken ankle away from advancing to the Super Bowl. So many fans and media anticipated the Broncos to go big in free agency and take advantage of their current Super Bowl window. However, they instead decided to run it back and re-sign many of their own free agents and passed on making any outside additions. Then it happened. On an early morning in Mid-March, the news broke that the Denver Broncos were trading with the Miami Dolphins for explosive wide receiver Jaylen Waddle. The full trade details have the Broncos getting Waddle and a 2026 4th round pick, while the Dolphins get the Broncos 2026 1st round pick as well as their 3rd and 4th round picks in 2026 as well. Jaylen Waddle highlights 🐧 pic.twitter.com/ihVGq2lj7y — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) March 17, 2026 This blockbuster trade quieted the noise a bit and reignited the hype in Broncos Country as the Broncos add an explosive playmaking weapon to their offense. This is something the team has desperately been lacking, and with quarterback Bo Nix proving he is a top franchise quarterback, the team went out and got him a top playmaker to help this offense take that next step this offseason. Waddle joins a now-loaded Denver Broncos wide receiver room that includes longtime Broncos veteran wide receiver Courtland Sutton and a group of talented young wide receivers that includes Troy Franklin, Marvin Mims Jr. and Pat Bryant. This talented and deep group should prove to be a strength for the Broncos this upcoming season with Jaylen Waddle leading the way. Player Profile Jaylen Waddle | Wide Receiver | Denver Broncos Height: 5-10 Weight: 185 pounds Age: 27 years old Experience: 6th NFL season 2025 stats: 64 receptions for 910 yards and 6 touchdowns Jaylen Waddle’s 2026 outlook with the Denver Broncos He is expected to be the Broncos’ number one wide receiver, their top playmaker, and someone they feature in their offense each and every week. He will pair with veteran wide receiver Courtland Sutton to give the Broncos a talented top two wide receivers, while Pat Bryant, Marvin Mims, and Troy Franklin Head Coach Sean Payton told reporters earlier this offseason that they have a clear vision and plan for wide receiver Jaylen Waddle and that he will play inside and out for the Broncos this upcoming season. “Absolutely. You could start slot to outside, or go outside to slot, just pick. There’s a crystal-clear vision prior to the trade as to, ‘All right, this is what we see, this is where he plays and these are the things that we feel like he’s exceptional at.’ Then, ‘Let’s apply them into what we’re doing.’” He added that Waddle’s initial home will be outside, but that “there may be some packages where we have some flex” and that he’s doing too well outside to move him from there. Waddle’s impact will be felt throughout the offense. His presence will open things up for Courtland Sutton, who may not see a team’s top corner every snap and take attention off Mims, Franklin, and/or Bryant and open up things for them. Payton told reporters they have depth in their wide receiver room and it is their job to find the strengths of those players and take advantage of them. “There’s depth at that room. There are things that the guys do very well. Our job is to find those strengths and put them in those positions. He has been a great addition, and we’re just getting started.” What will stand out the most with Waddle is his speed and ability to separate and get open quickly. The Broncos haven’t had a player with that sort of speed AND route running ability in a longtime and I believe Waddle is going to explode for a huge season in 2026. We saw former Saints wide receiver Michael Thomas be heavily targeted in the passing game under Payton, and I could see a similar type of production from Waddle this season. If the Broncos want their offense to take that next step, they need Waddle to have a big breakout first season with the team, and I believe he can and will do that. Final Thoughts Man, I am excited. Waddle is the type of playmaker I wanted the Broncos to add for years now. His speed and playmaking ability are elite, and I believe he is going to thrive under Sean Payton/Davis Webb and quarterback Bo Nix. His impact on the team will be felt throughout the offense as he will open up things for everyone else. Sutton won’t see a team’s top corner or double coverage; Mims/Franklin/Bryant will see a team’s third or fourth best corner, and the tight ends should see more room in the middle of the field. Also, defenses will not be able to load the box to stop the Broncos’ run game due to Waddle’s speed, so that could open things up on the ground as well. Clearly, I have high hopes for Waddle this upcoming season and cannot wait to see him torch the Chiefs’ secondary in Week One and continue that throughout the 2026 season, postseason, and all the way to the Super Bowl.

title: Detroit Lions 2026 training camp preview: How quickly will Cade Mays adapt to scheme?
summary: In this installment of our Detroit Lions 2026 training camp preview series, we examine the Lions’ interior offensive line, speculate on current and future roles, and discuss how many players from this group could make the 53-man roster. Previous training camp previews: Roster construction Under the Brad Holmes and Dan Campbell regime, the Lions have consistently added offensive […]
full_text: From left, Detroit Lions offensive tackle Penei Sewell (58), guard Tate Ratledge (69), center Cade Mays (64) and offensive lineman Christian Mahogany (73) before OTAs at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Thursday, June 11, 2026. | Junfu Han / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images In this installment of our Detroit Lions 2026 training camp preview series, we examine the Lions’ interior offensive line, speculate on current and future roles, and discuss how many players from this group could make the 53-man roster. Previous training camp previews: Quarterback: Can Luke Altmyer force a QB3 role? Running back: How RB roles could shift in 2026 Wide receiver: WR depth roles up for grabs Tight end: How many TEs will make the roster? Offensive tackle: Can Blake Miller win the starting RT job? Roster construction Under the Brad Holmes and Dan Campbell regime, the Lions have consistently added offensive linemen as the season progresses. While they typically begin each season with eight to 10 offensive linemen, they’ve consistently finished with 10 or 11 on the active roster. Let’s take a look at what they’ve done on the interior offensive line in the previous five seasons: 2021 : Opened with five IOL (Frank Ragnow, Jonah Jackson, Halapoulivaati Vaitai, Evan Brown, and Logan Stenberg) but finished with seven (Parker Ehinger, Ryan McCollum). 2022 : Opened with six IOL (Ragnow, Jackson, Vaitai, Brown, Stenberg, and Tommy Kraemer), but finished with seven (Kayode Awosika and Ross Pierschbacher; Kraemer landed on IR). 2023 : Opened with five IOL (Ragnow, Jackson, Graham Glasgow, Vaitai, and Colby Sorsdal) but finished with six (Awosika). 2024 : Opened with five IOL (Ragnow, Kevin Zeitler, Glasgow, Awosika, and Michael Niese), but finished with six after rookie Christian Mahogany was removed from PUP. 2025 : Opened with five IOL (Tate Ratledge, Mahogany, Glasgow, Awosika, and Kingsley Eguakun) but finished with six (rookie Miles Frazier was added after a PUP stint, Niese was re-added, and Eguakun was demoted to the practice squad, then poached by the Browns ). Investment at center The Lions’ offensive line took a step back in 2025, with the majority of the blame falling on the play of the interior positions. Following the sudden retirement of Frank Ragnow, the Lions were forced to alter their approach: they moved Glasgow inside to center, which cleared the way for rookie Tate Ratledge to start at right guard and second-year guard Christian Mahogany to start on the left side. Unfortunately, they struggled from the jump. Their communication faltered; Glasgow looked his age, Ratledge looked like a rookie, and Mahogany failed to live up to the promise he showed in three games as a rookie, while also missing a portion of the season with a broken leg. The Lions’ top priority this free agency period was to find a new starting center who could anchor the middle of the offensive line. They targeted Cade Mays for the role, and on the opening day of free agency, they signed him to a three-year contract. Ratledge showed enough growth as a rookie that the Lions appear comfortable with his return to the starting right guard role; however, Mahogany will face competition for his starting left guard job. Both young guards started at their respective roles during OTAs and minicamp in the spring, but Mahogany is expected to be pushed by second-year OL Miles Frazier, newly acquired veteran Ben Bartch, and center/guard hybrid Juice Scruggs (who the Lions acquired in the David Montgomery trade) during training camp. For additional depth at center, the Lions brought back veteran center Michael Niese and signed center Seth McLaughlin to futures contracts, while guard/tackle hybrids Mason Miller and UDFA rookie Melvin Priestly were also added for more depth inside. The battleground How quickly will Cade Mays adapt to the Lions’ scheme? Mays was the top target in the Lions’ free agency period, and looks like a great stylistic match for new offensive coordinator Drew Petzing’s scheme, but he’ll need to get up to speed quickly with the scheme and his new teammates in order for the offensive line to have success early in the season. Mays primarily played right guard in college—though he saw snaps at all five OL positions—and was known for his power and ability to pull. He was drafted by the Carolina Panthers and repped at right and left guard his first two seasons before shifting him into center in 2024, where he turned a developmental corner. Over the last two seasons, Mays has started 21 games at center, and while he is still relatively young at the position, his upside is evident. From an athletic standpoint, Mays’ ability to lean into his power, as well as pull and block in space, should give the Lions a skill set they’ve been craving at center since Ragnow’s retirement. The main questions surrounding his impact will center on how quickly he can mentally process what’s asked of him. The talent’s there; now he just needs the reps in training camp and the preseason. Will Christian Mahogany hold onto his starting LG job? Mahogany’s power and pulling skill set should blend nicely with Petzing’s offense, and he is expected to enter training camp fully healthy and in the pole position at left guard. However, like most players who don’t reach their potential the year prior, Mahogany will face competition for his job. Here’s an excerpt from coach Dan Campbell discussing the left guard job in the spring: “Listen it is open, and look, Mahogany is very much in that. He played a couple of games for us in ’24, and then he started for us until he had the injury, came back, started again. So, we know he has got ability, he’s got potential, but there is a reason why we (added) Bartch, there is a reason why Frazier is here, […] We are going to let this thing go and see what happens. It will be good for all of them, when you have some nipping at your heels or constantly – you are having to compete with and push, and you guys are all competing for the same thing, it is good for everybody.” Bartch figures to be the biggest challenger for the left guard role, bringing eight years of NFL experience and a terrific athletic profile. However, Bartch has only started 24 games over his career, mainly due to injury. He hasn’t started more than three games in any season since 2022 (when he started five), and didn’t practice in the spring for “precautionary” reasons. Bartch certainly has NFL starting skills, but even if he wins the job out of training camp, how long can he realistically be expected to hold up? Frazier, like Mahogany, was a Day 3 draft pick who was expected to be taken on Day 2 because of their upside, and both were considered “steals” in their respective drafts. While Mahogany’s path to a starting role was quicker due to situational circumstances, Frazier has similar upside and will get a chance to prove his worth in training camp. Frazier is also being cross-trained at tackle for emergency depth, which further illustrates how the team values his skills and improves his chances of making the 53-man roster. Overall, this should be one of the more entertaining camp battles to watch in August, and will make for some interesting conversations surrounding roster construction. Is there room to keep two reserve guards on the active roster? Especially considering the fact that Scruggs looks like his role is safe as the primary backup center. Can Juice Scruggs be the new Graham Glasgow? When Scruggs was acquired by Detroit, most assumed he would simply operate as Mays’ backup at center, but his experience playing both left and right guard gives him tremendous positional value, similarly to what Glasgow provided the Lions with for multiple seasons. For reference, over the past three seasons in Houston, Scruggs has registered 13 starts (1,045 snaps) at left guard, eight starts (568 snaps) at center, and two starts (216 snaps) at right guard. That level of experience across three positions is incredibly…

title: 2026 Detroit Lions 53-man roster prediction: Pre-training camp
summary: We’re just over a week away from the Detroit Lions opening training camp for the 2026 season. With that in mind, I figured now was a good time to give my own perspective on the team’s 90-man roster and what it may look like after the dust of camp and the preseason has settled. Obviously, […]
full_text: First-round pick Aidan Hutchinson (97) huddles with teammates during Detroit Lions rookie minicamp Saturday, May 14, 2022 at the Allen Park practice facility. Lionsrr Rook We’re just over a week away from the Detroit Lions opening training camp for the 2026 season. With that in mind, I figured now was a good time to give my own perspective on the team’s 90-man roster and what it may look like after the dust of camp and the preseason has settled. Obviously, the outlook of this projection will change over the next month as the players jockey for spots. But here’s how I believe the roster stands before the players take the field. Quarterbacks (2) QB Jared Goff QB Teddy Bridgewater QB Luke Altmyer I am not counting out rookie UDFA Luke Altmyer winning a roster spot by the end of training camp, but the much more likely scenario is that he sticks around on the practice squad to continue his development. But if he balls out in the preseason, it could produce an interesting conversation. Running backs (4) RB Jahmyr Gibbs RB Isiah Pacheco RB Sione Vaki RB Jacob Saylors RB Kye Robichaux RB Jabari Small Gibbs through Vaki are essentially locks to me. The question is whether Detroit should carry a fourth running back. Generally, they do , and when the Lions chose Saylors over Craig Reynolds last season, I think it was a revelation of how much they value his special teams. Tight ends (3) TE Sam LaPorta TE Brock Wright TE Tyler Conklin TE Zach Horton TE Thomas Gordon TE Miles Kitselman The Lions have recently only kept three tight ends on their roster, but I do wonder if last year’s depleted depth will make them reconsider in 2026. It’s hard for me to pick between Horton, Gordon, and Kitselman with little observations on each. If Drew Petzing plans on running more 13 personnel in Detroit, the Lions would almost certainly keep a fourth. However, they also invested heavily in their wide receiver group, so I’m not convinced 13 personnel is coming to Detroit. Therefore, I’m keeping three tight ends for now. Wide receivers (6) WR Amon-Ra St. Brown WR Jameson Williams WR Isaac TeSlaa WR Greg Dortch WR Cedrick Wilson Jr. WR Dominic Lovett WR Jackson Meeks WR Tom Kennedy WR Tay Martin WR Lawrence Keys WR Lucky Jackson WR Tarik Black WR Malik Cunningham When I made my initial picks for the 53-man roster, I was only at 52 players with Dominic Lovett out. He’s thus far underwhelmed as both a receiver (too many drops) and special teams (just 50 snaps his rookie season). However, Detroit invested in him, and he could see a Year 2 jump. I very much considered Jackson Meeks here, especially considering I went light at tight end, but I still think he is a work in progress at both WR and TE. Offensive tackles (4) OT Blake Miller OT Penei Sewell OT Larry Borom OT Giovanni Manu OT Devin Cochran Giovanni Manu was also one of my last players in. Admittedly, he may spend most weeks as an inactive in this role, but I do think Detroit would be willing to give him one more year to develop. After all, Larry Borom is only on a one-year deal. I’m still giving Manu a shot to become the OT3 of the future, even if the door to a starting offensive tackle job is closed for him. Interior offensive linemen (6) iOL Christian Mahogany iOL Cade Mays iOL Tate Ratledge iOL Ben Bartch iOL Miles Frazier iOL Juice Scruggs i OL Seth McLaughlin iOL Melvin Priestly iOL Michael Niese iOL Mason Miller OL Colby Sorsdal I do like the depth here, and I think the Lions would be wise to keep as many of these players as they can. Bartch and Scruggs are two experienced players who provide solid depth. Frazier will not only compete for the starting left guard spot, but he brings tackle versatility and has plenty of potential entering his first training camp (after missing all of last year’s practices). I’m not sure anyone else on the depth chart can realistically challenge for a starting position, but I am admittedly intrigued by Seth McLaughlin. It’s just hard to see him winning the backup center job after Detroit traded for Scruggs. Edge defenders (3) EDGE Aidan Hutchinson EDGE DJ Wonnum EDGE Derrick Moore EDGE Ahmed Hassanein EDGE Payton Turner EDGE Anthony Lucas EDGE Eric O’Neill Three edge defenders sounds like a small amount, and I would have loved to find a place for Ahmed Hassanein or Payton Turner, but the truth is there is enough versatility among the defensive tackles to complement this group. Hutchinson, Wonnum, and Moore are all more “rush” ends, while Tyler Lacy and Levi Onwuzurike can play the “big” end roles in this defense. That said, Hassanein, Turner, or even Anthony Lucas could very much convince me to keep fourth over someone like Manu. Defensive tackles (6) DT Alim McNeill DT Tyleik Williams DT/EDGE Levi Onwuzurike DT/EDGE Tyler Lacy DT Skyler Gill-Howard DT Jay Tufele DT Chris Smith DT Myles Adams DT Aidan Keanaaina DT Mekhi Wingo DT Tyre West I like this group a lot. McNeill and Williams will both hold down the nose and three-tech spots. Onwuzurike and Lacy can play anywhere from the 3- to 5-tech. Gill-Howard should bring some much-needed interior pass rush, and Tufele takes the backup nose tackle roles lost by DJ Reader and Roy Lopez. I briefly considered rookie UDFA Aidan Keanaaina over Tufele, but it’s too early for me to bank on an undrafted rookie unseating a veteran. Linebackers (5) LB Malcolm Rodriguez LB Jack Campbell LB Derrick Barnes LB Jimmy Rolder LB Damone Clark LB Trevor Nowaske LB Erick Hunter LB Joe Bachie Five linebackers is not a lot for the Lions, but their push for more nickel sets gives me a little more comfort in leaving this position shorthanded. Nowaske was one of the final players out on my roster, and he could very well win a job over Clark given his special teams skills. But I think Clark brings a little more proven defensive help while not taking a significant step back on special teams. Cornerbacks (6) CB D.J. Reed CB Rock Ya-Sin CB Ennis Rakestraw CB Roger McCreary CB Keith Abney CB Khalil Dorsey CB Nick Whiteside CB De’Shawn Rucker DB Aamaris Brown Detroit is going to need some cornerback depth after moving on from Terrion Arnold, and this will certainly be a competitive room in training camp. I wanted to find room for Whiteside, but the truth of the matter is that even after his awesome “Legion of Whom” performance, he only played 11 defensive snaps and 53 special teams snaps the rest of the season. Khalil Dorsey, meanwhile, is one of the most valued special teamers on the roster. Safeties (5) S Kerby Joseph S Avonte Maddox S Chuck Clark S Christian Izien S Thomas Harper S Dan Jackson S Loren Strickland PUP list: S Brian Branch Branch to the PUP is a no-brainer after coach Dan Campbell sounded pretty pessimistic about his chances to heal by training camp. Joseph’s situation is much harder to predict, but I’m taking the optimistic route, because it certainly seems like the Lions safety has done everything he can to make it back on the field in 2026. As for the depth, I do have a feeling there could be only one roster spot up for grabs between veterans Avonte Maddox and Chuck Clark, but I am more comfortable keeping both on the roster given the uncertainty surrounding the room. Izien and Harper round out the room with both youth and special teams upside. Specialists (3) K Jake Bates P Jack Fox LS Hogan Hatten No competition. No surprises.

title: Discussion: How many Detroit Lions rookies will start by the end of 2026?
summary: Ever since the Detroit Lions have been ran by general manager Brad Holmes, they have valued getting rookie contributors. This has usually meant first-round starters, as expected, but the Lions have also turned later picks into instant impact players. Amon-Ra St. Brown (fourth round, 2021), Kerby Joseph (third round, 2022), Sam LaPorta and Brian Branch […]
full_text: Ever since the Detroit Lions have been ran by general manager Brad Holmes, they have valued getting rookie contributors. This has usually meant first-round starters, as expected, but the Lions have also turned later picks into instant impact players. Amon-Ra St. Brown (fourth round, 2021), Kerby Joseph (third round, 2022), Sam LaPorta and Brian Branch (second round, 2023), and Tate Ratledge (second round, 2025) are just some of the non-firsts that have made a mark as rookies. Some of the rookie listed above did not start from the onset, but by the time the season came to an end, they were entrenched as important parts of the team. Could we see a similar feat for the Lions’ 2026 draft class? Today’s Question of the Day is: How many Lions rookies will be starters by the end of 2026? My answer: Two, Blake Miller and Keith Abney. Miller is an obvious choice, as the first-round pick is the heavy favorite to start at right tackle as early as Week 1. That being said, Larry Borom is still in contention and if he outperforms Miller in training camp and preseason, he could win a starting role—a spot has to be earned, not given. My other choice of Abney is more about opportunity. He was the fourth Lion selected in the draft, but as a cornerback with potential to play inside and outside, there is ample opportunity for him to win a starting spot. With the release of Terrion Arnold, the depth chart ahead of Abney is D.J. Reed, Rock Ya-Sin, Ennis Rakestraw, and Roger McCreary. Reed will undoubtedly start if healthy, but none of Ya-Sin, Rakestraw, or McCreary are guaranteed starters. Ya-Sin was solid in relief for the Lions last season, but it is worth remembering that he has not been a full-time starter since 2022. Asking the veteran to play at a career-best level across an entire season might be an unrealistic expectation for the 30-year-old. Unlike Ya-Sin, Rakestraw has age on his side, but he has now battled two significant injuries over his first two seasons and has essentially zero experience on defense. As a former second-round pick, he has the talent to earn a starting role, but he has not earned our benefit of the doubt. As for McCreary, he seems like the sure-fire starter at nickel, but there is an important rule to remember: follow the money. The Lions signed McCreary to a one-year contract worth just $1.2 million. While this was perceived as a steal for the Lions, it also highlights that the team might not view him as a starter—in contrast, the Lions signed Borom to a one-year, $5 million deal as offensive tackle insurance. Abney has a lot of players to challenge for a starting role, but he has as good of a chance to impress as they do. Regarding the other draft selections, the late-round picks of Skyler Gill-Howard and Tyre West are fighting for a roster spot, let alone a starting spot. Of the two players selected ahead of Abney, I think Derrick Moore has the best chance to become a starter by season’s end, but I also think he may fall victim of the Lions lack of defined “starters” on defense. I expect this team to run a rotation along the defensive line, so while Moore might play a decent number of snaps, he might not start ahead of, say, DJ Wonnum. Jimmy Rolder, meanwhile, not only has to usurp Malcolm Rodriguez as the third linebacker, but he would need to justify being the third linebacker on the field in the first place . How many rookies will enter the starting lineup by the end of the season? Let us know in the comments below.
author: John Whiticar

title: Packers sign DT Devonte Wyatt to extension
summary: The Green Bay Packers have signed former first-round pick Devonte Wyatt to a three-year, $57 million contract that includes a $20 million signing bonus, according to NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport. Wyatt was one of the few starters remaining on the 2026 roster who were going into a contract year this year, as he was set […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 23: Devonte Wyatt #95 of the Green Bay Packers reacts to a penalty during the second quarter of the game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on November 23, 2023 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Mike Mulholland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers have signed former first-round pick Devonte Wyatt to a three-year, $57 million contract that includes a $20 million signing bonus, according to NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport . Wyatt was one of the few starters remaining on the 2026 roster who were going into a contract year this year, as he was set to play on a fifth-year option this season. For what it’s worth, the contract that has frequently been floated as a Wyatt comparison was the deal that John Franklin-Myers signed in free agency this year. Franklin-Myers, like Wyatt, is more of a contributor as a pass-rusher than as an overall defensive tackle. Franklin-Myers signed a three-year, $63 million deal with the Tennessee Titans. Wyatt’s deal comes $2 million per year under the Franklin-Myers number, but still in roughly the same ballpark. Franklin-Myers also only received a $12 million signing bonus, but had $42 million in total guarantees on his deal. Generally, the Packers only guarantee players money in the form of a signing bonus, with the major exceptions being quarterbacks and their deal with superstar Micah Parsons. On paper, this seems to be a little lower on the “average per year” front than we expected but significantly lower in terms of guaranteed money. Full details of the contract have yet to be announced, but there’s a good chance this three-year deal goes on top of Wyatt’s 2026 season, meaning that he’ll be under contract through the 2029 season. With Wyatt out of the way, the only full-time starters left going into the 2026 season who don’t have multi-year deals are cornerback Keisean Nixon and tight end Tucker Kraft. A Kraft extension is a no-brainer, while it seems pretty unlikely that the Packers will give Nixon, who turns 30 this week, any significant long-term contract.
author: Justis Mosqueda

title: Green Bay Packers Roster Preview: Running Backs
summary: We’re officially one week away from Packers rookies reporting to Green Bay for training camp, so it’s time to tie a bow on our roster preview series. The big question at this position is whether running back Josh Jacobs will or won’t face legal and/or league ramifications for an alleged domestic abuse incident, but at […]
full_text: ASHWAUBENON, WISCONSIN - JUNE 09: Josh Jacobs #8 of the Green Bay Packers participates in drills during the Green Bay Packers mandatory minicamp at Don Hutson Center on June 09, 2026 in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re officially one week away from Packers rookies reporting to Green Bay for training camp, so it’s time to tie a bow on our roster preview series. The big question at this position is whether running back Josh Jacobs will or won’t face legal and/or league ramifications for an alleged domestic abuse incident , but at this time the Brown County district attorney is still investigating the case and has not made a decision, one way or another, on the situation. We’ll touch on Jacobs’ potential on-field impact, along with the rest of the backs on the roster, in this article, but if you want to read any of our previous installments in this series, here are our breakdowns of Green Bay’s other position rooms: Quarterback Receiver Tight End Offensive Line Defensive Line Edge Rusher Linebacker Cornerback Safety Josh Jacobs If able, Josh Jacobs will be the Packers’ starting running back in 2026. If is the big question here. Green Bay has allowed Jacobs to return to practice for the Packers after he was released from jail, and the team has communicated little with the public about their stance on Jacobs. Generally, when members of the team have been questioned about Jacobs, they refer back to the team’s statement and add no further information. Remember, these situations can take some time. There’s no promise that Brown County has to make their decision before the start of the regular season. For perspective, the Ray Rice video dropped on TMZ 205 days after the incident actually occurred back in 2014. Until Brown County makes a decision, the possibility of a Jacobs suspension lingers. As a reminder, too, the league isn’t held to the legal system. They are free to suspend a player, essentially up to the discretion of the commissioner, whether or not the player is found guilty or not in a court of law. MarShawn Lloyd The next man up from a ball-carrier perspective is 2024 third-round pick MarShawn Lloyd, who has only played in one regular-season game in two years due to a string of injuries. The staff clearly likes Lloyd, as they’ve talked him up every offseason and are still giving him the opportunity to make the roster this year, but it’s hard for fans to trust a back who has only been healthy enough to play 10 offensive snaps over two years. Beyond Jacobs’ situation, the biggest X-factor in the Packers’ backfield in 2026 is whether or not Lloyd will be healthy or not. Hopefully, he can have his first healthy season in his NFL career. The team needs him now more than ever, as Emanuel Wilson, who was previously the number two ball-carrier in Green Bay, signed with the Seattle Seahawks this offseason. Chris Brooks While Chris Brooks has never had a large volume of carries, he did essentially average the same per carry as Wilson did last year. With that being said, Brooks is used more as almost a fullback, as he sees the field frequently in split-back looks as the team’s lead blocker and on obvious passing downs where he enters the game as an extra pass-protector who helps allow tight ends to instantly release into a route. On top of the blocking contributions on offense, Brooks plays some of the most special teams snaps of any running back in the NFL, usually in a blocking role. He is the only back who contributes in any meaningful way on special teams, and he’s one of the team’s core players in that unit. His roster spot shouldn’t be at risk, considering how his unique skillset frees up the Packers’ roster in other ways. Pierre Strong Jr. Pierre Strong Jr. signed with the Packers’ practice squad in early September last year and was actually activated for two regular season games in 2025, even though he never got on the field for those two games. The former fourth-round pick has posted 692 yards from scrimmage over four years in the league, with the majority of those yards (550) coming in a two-season stretch with the Cleveland Browns. As of right now, he’s probably the next man up if there’s an injury (or suspension) at the position, but if everyone can go, Strong will likely be a practice squad candidate going into the 2026 regular season. Keep an eye on the backfield this preseason. Damien Martinez Damien Martinez is another former draft pick, as he was selected in the seventh round by the Seattle Seahawks in 2025 after he was initially mocked as a potential top-100 selection going into draft week. Not only did Martinez slip in the draft, though, but he failed to make the Seahawks’ initial roster and was eventually released from the team’s practice squad. Clearly, there was some talent to Martinez’s game (he was twice an All-Pac-12 back before his transfer to Miami in 2024), but the 22-year-0ld was out of the NFL entirely from September 19th (when he was released from the Seahawks’ practice squad) to December 30th (when he signed with the Packers’ practice squad). Martinez could push Strong, and is five years younger than Strong, but that will be sorted out in the preseason. Jaden Nixon The only new face in the Packers’ backfield this year is former UCF running back Jaden Nixon, who also worked as a kick returner for the Knights in college. As an undrafted free agent, Nixon signed with Green Bay for just $15,000 in guaranteed money. For perspective, the Packers gave 11 times that (or more) to five other undrafted free agents this cycle. $15,000 guaranteed places Nixon 18th among undrafted running backs alone , and 12 running backs league-wide took home at least $90,000 guaranteed this undrafted free agent cycle. One of those high-guaranteed backs was Damon Bankston of New Mexico, who the Packers had in on a pre-draft visit before he ended up signing with the New York Giants. Personally, I don’t have super high hopes for Nixon, considering his low guarantees, and think that Green Bay might take another look at Bankston, who they seemed to want more than Nixon until they saw the price tag associated with him, if he becomes available at some point in 2026.

title: Decoding Jonathan Gannon’s Eagles Defense: What the Coverage Data Reveals
summary: When the Philadelphia Eagles finished the 2022 season ranked 2nd in defensive DVOA, much of the credit rightly went to a historic pass rush — 70 sacks, the third-most in NFL history through the regular season. But the coverage data tells an equally important story about how Jonathan Gannon built that defense, and it reveals […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - DECEMBER 04: Philadelphia Eagles defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon warms up during the game between the Tennessee Titans and the Philadelphia Eagles on December 4, 2022 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Andy Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images When the Philadelphia Eagles finished the 2022 season ranked 2nd in defensive DVOA, much of the credit rightly went to a historic pass rush — 70 sacks, the third-most in NFL history through the regular season. But the coverage data tells an equally important story about how Jonathan Gannon built that defense, and it reveals a coordinator whose scheme evolved meaningfully over the course of the year in ways that go beyond the box score. The most basic finding confirms what film study already suggested: this was a zone-based defense at its core. On early downs, the Eagles played zone coverage more than three times as often as man (42.48% to 12.26%), with Cover 3 alone accounting for roughly one in five snaps — comfortably their most-used single call all season. This wasn’t incidental. A Cover 3-heavy approach is the schematic signature of the Fangio-tree defenses Gannon came from, prioritizing depth and disguise over individual matchup wins. The selection of Cover 4 and Cover 1 as secondary options, rather than more aggressive looks like Cover 0, reinforces that this defense was built to prevent explosive plays first and create havoc second. What’s more revealing is what they avoided entirely. Cover 2 Man didn’t appear on a single early-down snap across 824 plays. That’s not a statistical quirk — a defense that runs six different coverage shells over an entire season doesn’t accidentally skip one of them 824 consecutive times. It points to a coordinator making a conscious philosophical choice, likely because Cover 2 Man asks corners to sustain difficult trail-technique man coverage while still respecting deep halves’ responsibility — a demanding teaching point that may not have suited Gannon’s personnel or his risk tolerance. Perhaps the most significant trend in the data is the clear directional shift from the first half of the season to the second. On early downs, man coverage cratered — falling 41%, from 15.5% in Weeks 1-9 down to just 9.2% in Weeks 10-18. Cover 0, the most aggressive man-coverage call in the playbook, nearly disappeared entirely, dropping from 2.5% to a mere 0.47%. Third down followed the same arc: blitz rate fell 22% from the first half to the second (21.05% to 16.41%), with two separate weeks — 9 and 13 — featuring zero third-down blitzes at all. This pattern is worth noting because it cuts against a common narrative about good defenses needing to “evolve and adjust” as the season progresses. Here, the evolution ran toward simplicity and restraint, not complexity. One interpretation is that Gannon found his players were more effective executing fewer, better-rehearsed calls than mixing in higher-variance, higher-risk concepts — a defense optimizing for consistency over surprise as familiarity within the system grew. Another explanation is one of survival and game-script: the Eagles spent much of the second half protecting leads, and conservative zone shells are simply the correct call when you’re playing with a cushion. The Week 8 performance — a season-high 29.63% Cover 3 usage following the bye week — looks like the moment this second-half identity crystallized into a template the staff leaned on for the rest of the year. Situational Aggression on Third Down Even as the defense trended conservative in the aggregate, the splits between early downs and third down reveal a coordinator who understood situational football. Man coverage usage on third down (25.56%) was more than double the early-down rate (12.26%) — a clear signal that Gannon was willing to ask his corners to win one-on-one matchups specifically when the stakes were highest and offenses needed a defined number of yards. This is a fairly conventional approach league-wide, but it’s notable how disciplined the split was: the Eagles weren’t bleeding man coverage into early downs at meaningful rates; they were saving it almost exclusively for third down. That’s evidence of situational discipline rather than randomness — a defense that knew exactly when to take on greater individual risk. Week-to-week trends The risk in any season-long trend analysis is flattening out what was actually a much bumpier ride week to week, and the data here makes that clear. Despite the broader conservative drift, the Eagles swung wildly from game to game. Week 2’s third-down man coverage rate hit a season-high 58.33%, paired with a season-high-tying 33.33% blitz rate — about as aggressive a defensive gameplan as Gannon called all year. The very next week, Week 3, that approach reversed almost entirely: just 11.76% man coverage, 76.47% zone, and a season-low 5.88% blitz rate. That’s not a defense drifting gradually — that’s a coordinator making a deliberate, opponent-specific decision to flip the script entirely from one week to the next. This volatility matters because it complicates the idea of “Gannon’s defense” as a single, fixed identity. The aggregate numbers tell a story of zone-heavy conservatism that deepened as the season went on, but the week-to-week numbers tell a story of a defense being actively game-planned against specific opponents, with the coordinator willing to dial aggression up or down dramatically based on matchup, personnel health, and what that week’s opposing offense was built to exploit. Week 8’s season-high blitz rate (41.67%) and Week 15’s near-equal mark (38.46%) both stand as proof that the second-half “conservative” label wasn’t absolute — Gannon was still capable of calling an aggressive game when the situation demanded it. What does this say about Gannon? Taken together, the data supports a more nuanced read of Gannon than either side of the public debate about him usually allows. He wasn’t simply “too passive,” as some critics argued throughout 2022 — the third-down man-coverage rates and the spikes in blitz aggression in specific weeks show a coordinator capable of asking his defense to take risks when the situation called for it. But he also wasn’t a chess master constantly innovating new wrinkles — the season-long drift toward zone and away from blitzing suggests a defense settling into its most repeatable, lowest-variance version of itself as the year went on, trusting disciplined execution of a smaller menu of calls over an expanding one. That’s consistent with everything else we know about how Gannon talks about his own scheme: that it should adapt to personnel and game state rather than chase complexity for its own sake. The 2022 Eagles had the rare luxury of an elite four-man pass rush, which meant the defense didn’t need to manufacture pressure through blitzing or live-or-die on man-coverage matchups to be effective. The coverage data simply confirms what that personnel advantage allowed Gannon to do: get more conservative, not less, as the season progressed — and still finish 2nd in the league.

summary: There are lots of opportunities for running backs on the Green Bay Packers’ roster this summer. The RB2 job behind Josh Jacobs is effectively up for grabs, and that role could take on even more importance depending on how Jacobs’ legal situation plays out. Yes, Chris Brooks is firmly entrenched as the team’s third down […]
full_text: ASHWAUBENON, WISCONSIN - JUNE 09: Marshawn Lloyd #32 of the Green Bay Packers participates in drills during the Green Bay Packers mandatory minicamp at Don Hutson Center on June 09, 2026 in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images There are lots of opportunities for running backs on the Green Bay Packers’ roster this summer. The RB2 job behind Josh Jacobs is effectively up for grabs, and that role could take on even more importance depending on how Jacobs’ legal situation plays out. Yes, Chris Brooks is firmly entrenched as the team’s third down back. But the Packers need a chance of pace back behind Jacobs, at a minimum, and training camp will surely decide who earns that role. Dows MarShawn Lloyd stay healthy and take control of the job? Will another young player emerge from the pack ahead of him? Is there a chance the Packers keep four running backs on the roster as well? These questions and more will start to get some answers next week when the team begins training camp. Until then, we’ll keep looking ahead at the intriguing position battles to come. 5 Packers players with most at stake during training camp | Packers Wire Jobs will be on the line this summer and a few Packers have huge opportunities to earn more playing time – or to get cut if they fail to impress. Perhaps nobody has a bigger potential swing than third year running back MarShawn Lloyd. title: Texans’ fullback British Brooks unique position heading into training camp
summary: Year two of Nick Caley’s run as offensive coordinator will reveal exactly where this Texans offense is headed. The plan is clear: ease the burden on C.J. Stroud and spread it across a roster built for defined, specialized roles. Every move Houston made this offseason points to that shift. Instead of stacking depth with similar […]
full_text: Jan 4, 2026; Houston, Texas, USA; Houston Texans running back British Brooks (44) carries the ball as Indianapolis Colts linebacker Germaine Pratt (53) defends during the second half at NRG Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Troy Taormina-Imagn Images | Troy Taormina-Imagn Images Year two of Nick Caley’s run as offensive coordinator will reveal exactly where this Texans offense is headed. The plan is clear: ease the burden on C.J. Stroud and spread it across a roster built for defined, specialized roles. Every move Houston made this offseason points to that shift. Instead of stacking depth with similar players, the Texans have doubled down on assembling distinct skillsets at every position. British Brooks fills one of the most specialized roles on Houston’s roster. Part running back, part fullback, part wingback, he gives Caley the backfield versatility that makes the system function. In I‑formation looks last season, Brooks served as the lead blocker, driving downhill on power concepts and clearing out the first defender in his path. While Brooks was the unquestioned starter at fullback, what is interesting is how little he played on offense in 2025. He only accounted for offensive 73 total snaps out of around 1,300 plays on offense. That’s because the Texans leaned on 11 personnel the second-most in the league at 71%. Using the one‑back, one‑tight‑end groupings precluded Brooks from impacting the offense more. Thus, his primary role was on special teams. So why is Brooks such a vital piece of the puzzle in Houston? Brooks’ utility is essential on a competitive 53-man roster. His blocking, special teams ability, and running capabilities allows the offense to be flexible and creative with its formations and skillsets. Last season, he was primarily used in 21 personnel – two running backs and 1 tight end. A rare formation indeed, but one that allowed the Texans woeful offense to incorporate Blake Fisher, get a hat on a hat, and get Brooks matched up against a smaller linebacker. Anytime Fisher took the field in the game against the Baltimore Ravens, Brooks was in the backfield right behind him. Heading into 2026, it’s well known the offense must evolve and improve, and Brooks appears to be making his own physical transformations too. In an interview with Texans Radio earlier this month, British Brooks admitted to losing 17 pounds this offseason to the astonishment of John Harris and Marc Vandermeer. Texans running back British Brooks on Texans All Access told @jharrisfootball & @TexansVoice that he lost 17 lbs this offseason on top of weight lost at the end of last season: “I think coming off the rookie injury I played a lot heavier than what I was the year before & I was… pic.twitter.com/F0AdJ4T5ef — Houston Stressans (@TexansCommenter) July 13, 2026 I’ve never heard John Harris ask a question as blunt as when he looked at Brooks and said, “Did you want to do that?” As if these athletes aren’t fully aware of what their bodies are telling them. Still, a fullback losing weight is genuinely puzzling. Anyone shedding that much mass is remarkable, GLP‑1 or not. And it raises a real possibility: Brooks might be positioning himself to compete outright for the third running back job rather than staying locked into a traditional fullback role. Thanks to NFL Pro, I watched every single offensive snap British Brooks played in 2026. Brooks role truthfully did not have much impact on the outcome of the offensive plays. For the most part, he was neutralizing the linebacker or blocking out on a defensive end. He was included in play action plays as an additional blocker, but rarely went out for a route. Brooks struggled to lock on a linebacker and tended to bounce off after the initial blow. For all this, he did earn multiple carries on short yardage situations and 1st and 10s to gain positive yards. 17 times the Texans handed the ball off to British Brooks. Six of which were either goal line or short yardage situations. The majority of the carries occurred Week 18 when the Texans sat Woody Marks and Nick Chubb. He carried the ball 13 times for 63 yards in a slow but efficient performance. A poor and heavily rotated offensive didn’t help, but he ran hard as you’d expect out of a fullback playing running back in a meaningless game. Interesting enough, Brooks was more effective reading the defense and holes out of shotgun than with Davis Mills under center. Given Nick Caley’s background as a tight end coach, that may be a strategic move. Caley will be more likely to keep a fourth or even fifth tight end over a blocking-specific back who cannot regularly run the ball. And for those wondering if Brooks can move inline to play tight end… keep dreaming. He’s 5’11 and only played two snaps at tight end last year. Brooks is miles better than tight end Cade Stover at blocking at full speed from the fullback position. He has much more reckless abandon and ability to maintain blocks – even if that is something he needs to work on before his third season. If Brooks shifts completely to a running back role, that changes the entire complexion of the Rosterology . The question will be: with the 17 pounds Brooks shed, is he going to convert to running back full time or try to stick at fullback. That will directly impact whether Brooks is seen as a situational blocker who will compete with the tight ends for a roster spot or as the third running back and compete with Jawhar Jordan for a roster spot. Either way, Brooks will be locked in a roster battle this training camp. Such is the life of a position player in a deep in a team’s depth chart. This weight loss and shift to a running back position is savvy. Nick Caley is a former tight end coach on a team with a bevy of tight end options. Odds are, Caley will choose to keep a fourth or fifth tight end on the roster over a fullback. We know Brooks can play fullback, but the odds are better stacked in his favor if he can beat out one Jawhar Jordan over two tight end options. Between running back and tight end, the Texans are likely to keep seven total players on the roster. The average number of each across all NFL teams in 2025 was 3.5 running backs and 3.7 tight ends. Based on the law of averages, the two options appear to be: Option 1: RBs (4) David Montgomery, Woody Marks, Jawhar Jordan, British Brooks and TE (3) Dalton Schultz, Marlin Klein, and Foster Moreau Option 2: RB (3) David Montgomery, Woody Marks, and British Brooks and TE (4) Dalton Schultz, Marlin Klein, Foster Moreau, and Brevin Jordan If you ask me, Option 2 is the superior group. Brevin’s addition improves the offense and provides more speed and versatility. The blocking ability of Moreau and Klein improves the team’s scheme flexibility. However it shapes out for Brooks and the offense, his usage should improve in 2026 while the Texans improve their own offensive approach.

title: What are the Colts’ most valuable trade assets? Ranking Nos. 5-1
summary: After looking at players No. 10 through No. 6 in the Colts’ trade-value rankings, the second part of this exercise turns to the team’s most valuable assets. This does not mean Indianapolis should trade any of these players, and in most cases, the Colts would be creating a major roster hole by even considering it. […]
full_text: After looking at players No. 10 through No. 6 in the Colts’ trade-value rankings , the second part of this exercise turns to the team’s most valuable assets. This does not mean Indianapolis should trade any of these players, and in most cases, the Colts would be creating a major roster hole by even considering it. The goal is simply to estimate each player’s league-wide trade value based on age, production, contract, position and how valuable similar players tend to be around the NFL. 5. Laiatu Latu Projected trade value: Second-round pick, possibly a late first Latu’s value is built on age, contract control and positional importance. Young edge rushers with legitimate pass-rush upside are among the most valuable players in football, and Latu has already shown enough to be viewed as a building block for the Colts’ defense. He is not just a rotational player anymore. He is someone teams would look at and believe there is still another level coming. A second-round pick feels like the safest projected value, but there is a real argument that the number could climb higher. If a team believed Latu was on the verge of becoming a double-digit sack edge rusher, a late first-round pick would not be impossible. Edge is too important, and young pass rushers do not become available often. For the Colts, trading him would make very little sense. They need more pass rush, not less, and moving Latu would create the same type of hole they have been trying to fill for years. Still, in a pure trade-value exercise, he belongs this high because of the position he plays and the trajectory he appears to be on. 4. Quenton Nelson Projected trade value: Second-round pick plus a Day 3 pick Nelson is still one of the best guards in football, and his league-wide reputation remains extremely strong. He is consistent, durable, powerful and respected around the NFL. The reason his value is not higher comes down to age, contract and position. Guards are valuable, but they do not carry the same trade market as quarterbacks, left tackles, edge rushers or corners. Nelson’s salary would also factor into the return, which probably keeps him out of first-round territory. A second-round pick plus a Day 3 selection feels realistic. A contender with offensive line issues could justify that kind of move, especially if it believed Nelson was the difference between a good line and a dominant one. For the Colts, though, Nelson is still worth more than the pick package because of what he means to the offensive identity and the stability he gives the line. 3. Jonathan Taylor Projected trade value: Second-round pick or third-round pick plus another selection Taylor is still one of the best running backs in football, but running back trade value is always complicated. His talent says he should be worth a premium pick. The market for veteran running backs says teams would be more cautious. That is why his projected value probably sits somewhere between a straight second-round pick and a third-round pick plus another selection. A contender with a strong roster and a clear need at running back could talk itself into paying the higher price, especially because Taylor can still change an offense when healthy. He is not just a volume back. He is a game-breaking player who can carry a team through stretches and force defenses to adjust. The issue is that teams are careful with age, mileage and contract cost at the position. Taylor’s value to the Colts is likely higher than his value on the open market because he is still the centerpiece of their offense. Trading him would remove the one player who can consistently tilt the field for Indianapolis, and unless the return was overwhelming, it would be hard to justify. 2. Tyler Warren Projected trade value: Late first-round pick or early second-round pick plus more Warren is the most interesting player on the list because his value is based on youth, upside and cheap contract control. If a young tight end looks like a future difference-maker, the trade value becomes significant quickly. He gives the Colts a rare offensive piece: a player who can win as a receiver, create mismatches, help the run game and become a long-term security blanket for the quarterback. The positional value of tight end keeps this from being a clean top-of-the-first-round type return, but a late first-round pick feels reasonable if another team believes he is on the path to becoming a top-tier player at the position. At minimum, an early second-round pick plus another selection would have to be the conversation. For Indianapolis, Warren is exactly the kind of player a team should want to keep. Young, talented offensive weapons on rookie contracts are extremely valuable, and his role should only grow. This is one of those cases where the trade value may be high, but the practical answer is simple: the Colts should not be interested unless a team badly overpays. 1. Sauce Gardner Projected trade value: Two first-round picks Gardner is the easiest name on the list. The Colts already know his value because they paid a massive price to get him. Elite cornerbacks in their prime do not come cheap, and Gardner checks every major box: age, talent, reputation, position value and proven production. He is one of the rare defensive backs who can change the way a defense is built because he gives a team a true No. 1 corner. Two first-round picks is the right projected value because that is the level of player he is. If anything, the Colts would probably need more than that to seriously consider moving him, especially after already making the aggressive decision to acquire him. Trading him away would defeat the entire purpose of the move. Gardner is the most valuable trade asset on the roster because he combines premium-position value with rare talent and prime years still ahead of him. The Colts have good players, but he is the one whose trade market would be the strongest, cleanest and easiest to define. Final thought The top of the Colts’ trade-value list shows where the roster has legitimate high-end pieces. Gardner is the clear No. 1, Warren is the young offensive asset with the most upside, and Taylor, Nelson, Latu and Raimann all carry strong value for different reasons. That does not mean Indianapolis should move any of them. In most cases, the player is more useful to the Colts than the draft pick would be. This exercise is more about understanding how the league would likely view the roster, and the answer is clear: the Colts have several players with meaningful trade value, but only Gardner sits in the true blockbuster category.

That includes starting quarterback Patrick Mahomes, who was only held out of 11-on-11 team periods during OTA and mini-camp practices. There has […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - JUNE 09: Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs leads the offense in a huddle during mandatory minicamp at The University of Kansas Hospital Arrowhead Training Complex on June 09, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Friday, the Kansas City Chiefs ’ quarterbacks and rookies, along with players rehabilitating pre-existing injuries, will report to Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, Missouri, ahead of the rest of the team. That includes starting quarterback Patrick Mahomes, who was only held out of 11-on-11 team periods during OTA and mini-camp practices. There has been no word on the possibility of Mahomes starting training camp on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list. On Monday, Albert Breer, Sports Illustrated’s senior NFL reporter, shared insight on the biggest storylines heading into training camp with Mahomes’ potential participation listed No. 2 in his rundown. Breer shared the common narrative regarding Mahomes’ maddening desire to be on the field for team drills sooner rather than later, then he pointed out the Chiefs’ return to staggered report dates this camp. This should give Mahomes a few days to practice on the field and go through drills with a partial roster of rookies before he’s tempted to push to full speed when full practices start on the 29th. Breer followed that note with insight from people in the building in Kansas City: There’s an expectation among Chiefs people that Mahomes will be fully cleared this week, and also the knowledge that when they tell him he can go, he will really go . So the plan is to be smart with it, and make sure everyone is doing what’s going to put him in the best position to be at his best from September through February, not just ready for Week 1. It remains to be seen how close to 100% Mahomes will look once he’s allowed in live drills at practice. Regardless, if the expectations of Breer’s sources come to fruition, it would be just another amazing, incredible feat for the legendary quarterback to take the field and work on the same level with his teammates on the first day of this year’s campaign.

title: 10 Biggest Chiefs Questions: How will defensive back roles shake out?
summary: Since defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo took over with the Kansas City Chiefs in 2019, he has gone through multiple iterations of defensive back cores. Initially, the Chiefs were built around safeties Tyrann Mathieu, Juan Thornhill and Daniel Sorensen with Charvarius Ward and Bashaud Breeland as the starting cornerbacks. The defense was at its best when […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - JUNE 09: Mansoor Delane #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs runs through a drill during mandatory minicamp at The University of Kansas Hospital Arrowhead Training Complex on June 09, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images) | Getty Images Since defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo took over with the Kansas City Chiefs in 2019, he has gone through multiple iterations of defensive back cores. Initially, the Chiefs were built around safeties Tyrann Mathieu, Juan Thornhill and Daniel Sorensen with Charvarius Ward and Bashaud Breeland as the starting cornerbacks. The defense was at its best when it could disguise and rotate coverages with the safeties to confuse quarterbacks. As time went on, the Chiefs decided to prioritize bringing in better cornerback talent, which worked tremendously. In 2020, L’Jarius Sneed was drafted in the fourth round. Two years later, Kansas City traded up in the first round to acquire Trent McDuffie before selecting Jaylen Watson in the second round. Sneed and McDuffie would go on to form one of the best NFL cornerback duos in recent years during the 2023 season. Their ability to play man coverage on any boundary or slot receiver was the main reason the Chiefs had an elite defense that carried them to a Super Bowl. Kansas City complemented the two playmaking cornerbacks with a good, smart safety in the wake of letting Mathieu walk in free agency. Justin Reid turned out to be a great addition, and in the same offseason, the team drafted safety Bryan Cook in the second round. From 2022 until last year, the secondary was elite , but all of the pieces making up that secondary are gone. The Chiefs made a flurry of moves to replace their talent in the secondary. Safety Alohi Gilman was signed in free agency as a straightforward fit in Cook’s former role as free safety Cornerback Kadar Kohou is an experienced starter at the Nickel spot, potentially manning the slot this upcoming season. Cornerback L’Jarius Sneed should be back to compete for outside cornerback snaps. Rookie cornerbacks Mansoor Delane, as a starter, and Jadon Canady, likely competing for the Nickel spot, will both be factors in the team immediately one way or another. Including the returning Chiefs, there are two players that should be considered locked-in starters going into the season: Gilman and Delane. Gilman was brought in to replace Cook, and Delane is by far their most talented player. Even if Delane doesn’t play on the boundary, he could play in the slot. Delane should be an instant high-impact starter similar to McDuffie. The questions surround the other spots in the defensive backfield. What is the best role for these players? What will end up being the best combination of defensive backs? When the Chiefs go into nickel or dime, who will come on the field? Let’s start with the other boundary cornerback spot opposite Delane. Boundary Cornerback Going into training camp, there are three options to start opposite Delane: Sneed, Nohl Williams, and Kristian Fulton. Of those three, Williams would figure to be the favorite to start. Williams got the majority of his opportunities at the end of the season when Watson and McDuffie were injured. Williams is an intelligent player who is best playing in underneath zones where he can read the quarterback’s eyes and use his tackling ability. Williams long speed isn’t great, but it’s one of the only negative traits to point out about the second-year cornerback. I believe Williams will win the job, but Fulton and Sneed are veteran players certainly capable of supplanting him. Sneed is back for a second tenure with the Chiefs, but at a much different stage of his career. Sneed hasn’t been able to stay healthy for two years and hasn’t looked close to what he was in 2023. It’s a worthy swing for the Chiefs, but it’s hard to count on him. Fulton feels like the safer bet, but he also has a volatile profile. Fulton did play better by the end of the year, but he struggled for the majority of last season coming off an injury. Slot Defender If Delane plays on the boundary, these are the top four guys that could play in the slot: Canady, Kohou, safety Chamarri Conner and cornerback Christian Roland-Wallace. Conner has played the most in the slot, but it has never been his best position. He can play the run and blitz from the slot, but he struggles to defend slot receivers in man coverage. With the Chiefs needing a starting safety opposite Gilman, it makes sense to move Conner to his more natural position. The Chiefs also have more depth in the slot. Between Kohou, Canady, and Rolland-Wallace, it’s hard to know who will start. Kohou is coming off an injury, so we don’t know how he’ll look athletically. Canady is a rookie I’m excited about for his man coverage ability, but he’s an undersized player who might not hold up in the box. Rolland-Wallace is also an option, but he’s never been a starter and has struggled in spot snaps. If Kohou is healthy and looks like what he did with the Miami Dolphins , he would likely be the starter, but this is a race to watch. Safety Of the three secondary positions, safety might be the easiest to figure out with the lack of safety depth. Gilman will be one of the starters, and the Chiefs’ actions suggest Conner is moving back to safety, who has better tape in that role than third-year safety Jaden Hicks. You could be improving two spots at once with the slot and safety. Unless Hicks has a great training camp, I would expect Conner and Gilman to start. The Bottom Line This isn’t Kansas City’s most talented secondary, but there’s a lot to like about the competition and depth ahead of a 53-man roster cutdown. It gives Spagnuolo plenty of options; it’ll just be about tinkering with what works and how to build the defense around them. It may be a slow process to figuring that out, but by the end of the season, the secondary could peak once the right group of defensive backs is the primary players.
author: Nate Christensen

title: Chiefs training camp preview: How real is competition at right tackle?
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs will return to Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, Missouri, next week, as training camp opens to prepare for the 2026 season. The Chiefs are beginning training camp in an unfamiliar situation: coming off a losing season for the first time in head coach Andy Reid’s tenure. Changes to the […]
full_text: Aug 9, 2025; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Kansas City Chiefs guard Jaylon Moore (77) against the Arizona Cardinals during a preseason NFL game at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images The Kansas City Chiefs will return to Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, Missouri, next week, as training camp opens to prepare for the 2026 season. The Chiefs are beginning training camp in an unfamiliar situation: coming off a losing season for the first time in head coach Andy Reid’s tenure. Changes to the depth chart can be expected following a losing season, and there were plenty of departures after year’s end. One of the most significant was the starting right tackle of three years in Kansas City. Jawaan Taylor was cut in March as a cap-saving measure. Taylor started on the right edge through two AFC titles. While mostly reliable, he was often penalized and a source of frustration amongst fans given his high cap hit and frequent errors or penalties. Taylor eventually signed with the Atlanta Falcons . Right tackle is the only position along the offensive line slated to have a new Week 1 starter this season, and the only real position up for grabs along the starting Chiefs’ offense. During OTAs in June, Andy Reid acknowledged there was a “competition” being held for the starting spot. “Moore has been kind of the mainstay in there, and then we’ve moved guys in there,” Reid said. “We’ll just see, we’ll see what happens. Those other four spots are really pretty solid, and I feel good about whichever one of these guys wins the competition there. I think we got guys that will be okay in that position, it’s just a matter of who ends up being that guy.” It is imperative the Chiefs make the right decision in order to protect quarterback Patrick Mahomes returning from injury; it may be one reason the team isn’t didn’t grant Moore — who has never been a full-time starter — the gig unopposed, despite a $18 million cap hit this year. So let’s take a look at the candidates for who could be the Chiefs’ starting right tackle in September, starting with Moore: Jaylon Moore There are two main contenders to land the starting right tackle job, and Moore is the “mainstay,” as Reid put it. The Chiefs have already shown a lot of faith in the veteran following the release of Taylor, as well as trading away offensive tackle Wanya Morris to the Falcons this offseason. Moore is entering his second season in Kansas City, settling in at right tackle now after playing on both edges as the team’s swing tackle. He started four games at left tackle and two at right tackle, playing 38% of the offense’s snaps over the course of the year; he was credited with three sacks. Moore has 18 career starts after spending the majority of his career as the backup to San Francisco 49ers ’ perennial All-Pro left tackle Trent Williams. He has primarily spent time on the left side, but with Mahomes’ blindside in the hands of Joshua Simmons, Moore has no choice but to focus on the right; it is his first opportunity to enter an NFL season as a starter. In Moore’s two starts at right tackle in 2025, he surrendered nine pressures. In 2025, Pro Football Focus ’ cumulative pass blocking grade was 57.1, ranking 72nd out of 89 eligible tackles. The cumulative run blocking grade assigned to him was 62.9 (ranked 54th). Moore is in the last year of his two-year contract with the Chiefs, and holds a dead-cap number of more than $10 million. Esa Pole Pole enters training camp with an outside shot at winning the right tackle job. He is a previous training camp “darling”, one who was cut by Kansas City last preseason and immediately poached from the practice squad by the New York Jets , before eventually landing back on the Chiefs’ practice squad midseason and filling in at left tackle down the stretch. Pole started the final four games for the Chiefs last season, following a string of offensive-line injuries. The undrafted free agent played admirably and was a bright spot for a depleted roster at the end of the lost season. Pole allowed 15 total pressures and 1 sack in game action, but committed three penalties. The position battle Although Moore is the veteran with more experience, many see Pole as having more upside as a starter — and as a longer-term solution. This would keep Moore as the swing backup tackle. Outside of Moore and Pole, undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson may be a long shot to land the job and make the deep Kansas City roster. However, he impressed coaches in minicamp practices. Benson was a starter at right tackle for the undefeated national champions, the Indiana Hoosiers, in 2025. Reid values continuity and veteran leadership along the offensive line. Having a solid right tackle would significantly bolster an already strong line. He has openly called the right tackle position a competition entering training camp. Is this a serious battle, or just terminology used by Reid to light a fire under Moore to improve training camp and offensive line performance? We’ll find out soon enough when training camp kicks off in St. Joe.
author: Dakota Watson

title: 56 Days until Chiefs football, we are ‘George Karlaftis’ days away
summary: We are 56 days away from the Kansas City Chiefs‘ season-opening game against the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football” in Week 1. The No. 56 is worn by starting defensive end George Karlaftis, who has worn it well enough to be playing on a second contract already in his fifth NFL season. The former […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - DECEMBER 07: George Karlaftis #56 of the Kansas City Chiefs celebrates after making a stop against the Houston Texans during the first quarter at Arrowhead Stadium on December 07, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images We are 56 days away from the Kansas City Chiefs ‘ season-opening game against the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football” in Week 1. The No. 56 is worn by starting defensive end George Karlaftis, who has worn it well enough to be playing on a second contract already in his fifth NFL season. The former first-round pick is signed through 2030. He’s had a stronger start to his career than the franchise’s all-time No. 56 did, but he’ll have to take his game to another level to match how the linebacker finished it. The memorable No. 56s in franchise history Derrick Johnson (2005 – 2017) Dino Hackett (1986 – 1991) Walt Corey (1960 – 1966) The No. 56 who is likely missed the least by Chiefs fans: Ben Niemann (2018 – 2021) Not only is Johnson the franchise’s all-time leading tackler (1,146 total in 13 seasons), no other player in Chiefs history has surpassed the 1,000 mark. He worked hard for the honor, overcoming an early-career benching and a handful of coaching changes to ultimately develop into one of his era’s best off-ball linebackers. He was truly a playmaker at the position before it was as common as we see today, and one particular showcasing of it felt like the turning point of his career. To close the 2009 season, Johnson started just his third game of a dreadful season, the first under head coach Todd Haley. He wound up with two pick-6s (45 and 60 yards on the returns) and caused two other incompletions in a win over the playoff-hopeful Broncos. Johnson was a full-time starter from that point on, earning Pro Bowl honors four times and one first-team All-Pro accolade in 2011. In the last game he wore a Chiefs uniform, Johnson infamously strip-sacked Tennessee Titans quarterback Marcus Mariota for a game-changing turnover — but referee Jeff Triplette waved off the fumble, citing Mariota’s “forward progress.” It stole an all-time career highlight from Johnson, who wound up with the Las Vegas Raiders for one season before retiring after the 2018 campaign. He was inducted into the Chiefs’ Hall of Fame this offseason . 56: The number of punts by Matt Araiza last season The total number of punts by the Chiefs last season, all by Araiza, was the 20th-highest mark in the NFL and below league average (60.4). That’s usually a good sign for an NFL team, but in Kansas City’s case, it highlights issues like red-zone offense and untimely turnovers in place of a punt. Even when quarterback Patrick Mahomes had a rhythm marching down the field, there were countless examples of stalling out as the offense passed the 20-yard line in critical situations. The Chiefs struggled in condensed space, with less ability to spread out coverage and open passing windows as they neared the goal line. The run game worked when Kansas City was able to set up within yards of pay dirt, but farther back in the red area, the lack of acceleration from Chiefs rushers made linebackers and safeties comfortable playing patiently and with depth to respect the pass game, with the end zone right behind them. Overall, the Chiefs’ offense needs to be sharper in situational moments. We don’t want to see more of Araiza, but if Kansas City can establish first-half leads with an effective run game, Araiza’s top-10 rate of punts finishing inside the 20-yard line (45%) indicates he could be an asset in the game of lead management.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

(Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The latest As the career of Kansas City Chiefs center Creed Humphrey has progressed, he has only strengthened the reason to believe he is the NFL’s best center and one of the league’s top offensive linemen. He now has two consecutive first-team All-Pro seasons and hasn’t missed a game in his five-year career. Humphrey has been a Pro Bowler the last four seasons and an All-Pro the past two as the anchor of the line for the Chiefs. Humphrey allowed just eight pressures, one sack and two QB hits last season, according to PFF. 10 Rookie Steals Who Could Embarrass Every Team That Passed in the 2026 NFL Draft | Sports Illustrated Cyrus Allen, WR, Kansas City Chiefs (Round 5, No. 176) Cyrus Allen took advantage of his opportunity at OTAs and minicamp to impress the Kansas City Chiefs during offseason workouts. Inside at guard, Kingsley Suamataia will be coming into a contract year in 2027. It’s possible Lauck gives them a higher ceiling with security at multiple spots to maintain the offensive front. Addressing the “elephant in the room” at another Fanatics Fest appearance Sunday, Skattebo said he is good following the fall and promised to “not hurt myself before the season.” He blamed the botched flip on the “bouncy” floors.
