title: Why Chris Simms thinks Aaron Donald should not return to Rams
summary: On Chris Simms Unbuttoned, Chris Simms revealed that he texted Aaron Donald personally to ask if AD had any plans to come back to the Los Angeles Rams for the 2026 season? Simms reports Donald said that he didn’t know if he’d be coming back (or not) as Donald continues to figure out how he […]
full_text: Inglewood, CA - November 23: Former Los Angeles Rams player Aaron Donald on the field before the Los Angeles Rams and Tampa Bay Buccaneers play an NFL football game at Sofi Stadium on Sunday, Nov. 23, 2025 in Inglewood, CA. (Eric Thayer / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images) On Chris Simms Unbuttoned, Chris Simms revealed that he texted Aaron Donald personally to ask if AD had any plans to come back to the Los Angeles Rams for the 2026 season? Simms reports Donald said that he didn’t know if he’d be coming back (or not) as Donald continues to figure out how he wants to move forward. For Simms, that was all he needed to hear because if AD still isn’t sure whether or not he will be suiting up for the 2026 season, then he more likely than not shouldn’t be suiting up for the Rams. Said Simms on his text exchange with Donald: “We got into it a little bit. I plain out asked, ‘So what do you think? You think you’re gonna give it a shot?‘. And I don’t think he’ll have any problem with me sharing this. He said, ‘Honestly, I don’t know, yet’…I’ll tell you in full transparency as a guy who likes him as a human, as a friend, I told him, ‘If you don’t know yet, then you probably shouldn’t do it‘. That was my advice to him.” Simms goes on to say that he doesn’t doubt Donald, he says multiple times he views Donald as one of the greatest players to ever grace the NFL, but for Simms, it’s July going on August. The season will be here at warp speed, and a player should not be unsure about whether or not they want to play in July. Simms has fair points, BUT there is a flaw in his logic. A flaw I think he would admit to, and that’s that Simms is not Aaron Donald. Whereas it makes total sense for Simms to want to hear Donald say “Yes, I’m in.” Donald doesn’t have to say that in July, he may not have to say he’s ready in August, there is no open timeline that has been presented for when AD needs to make a decision. Donald can seemingly decide at his own pace. Also, if Donald did know his intentions, would he share those details with Simms before anyone else like his family or the Rams? Food for thought. Now, what makes this story a bit more fun than some others is we aren’t speculating about pending legal charges, a major offseason injury or health concerns. We are talking about a future Hall of Famer who MAY decide he wants to unretire to play with another future Hall of Famer in Myles Garrett. It’s fun, it’s exciting and this story isn’t hurting anyone. But if you listen to Simms, it may be more fun for AD to stay on the couch, rather than come back to a situation Donald may not be ready for. Stay tuned, as this story doesn’t have an ending, yet.

title: Rivals put key player on PUP to start training camp
summary: The Seattle Seahawks are putting a lot of weight on the shoulders of defensive back Nick Emmanwori in their attempt to win the NFC West over the L.A. Rams again, but training camp has gotten off to a bad start in that regard. Emmanwori was placed on the Physically Unable to Perform list by the […]
full_text: Feb 8, 2026; Santa Clara, CA, USA; Seattle Seahawks safety Nick Emmanwori (3) against the New England Patriots during Super Bowl LX at Levi's Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images The Seattle Seahawks are putting a lot of weight on the shoulders of defensive back Nick Emmanwori in their attempt to win the NFC West over the L.A. Rams again, but training camp has gotten off to a bad start in that regard. Emmanwori was placed on the Physically Unable to Perform list by the Seahawks on Monday with an undisclosed injury . Emmanwori finished second in Defensive Rookie of the Year voting in 2025 and he was instrumental in Seattle’s NFC Championship victory over the Rams. Emmanwori broke up three passes against Matthew Stafford in the NFC Championship game, including a monumental defense against Puka Nacua. Generally, Seattle’s defense has not fared well against Stafford, Nacua, and the entire Rams offense. But a defense without Emmanwori would be even worse. In OTAs, Emmanwori was participating with no restrictions or a known injury, so this reason to be placed on PUP would be based on something new. Emmanwori missed four games at the start of 2025 with an ankle injury. A player who starts camp on PUP can be activated at any time, but if he is not activated by final cuts, is required to miss at least the first four games of the season. It’s notable information for the Rams-Seahawks rivalry (although the two teams don’t face each other until the end of the season) but also a good reminder that players on the Rams could be going on PUP before the end of this week. Rams camp starts on Saturday.

title: Another DT contract domino for Rams to use with Kobie Turner
summary: As the Los Angeles Rams mull over which players they will be able to extend, and which ones they might not be able to afford, the Green Bay Packers extended defensive tackle Devonte Wyatt to a three-year, $57 million contract on Monday. If that news doesn’t seem that relevant, it should, because Kobie Turner is […]
full_text: Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff is tackled by Green Bay Packers defensive tackle Devonte Wyatt during the second half at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wis., on Sunday, September 7, 2025. | Junfu Han / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images As the Los Angeles Rams mull over which players they will be able to extend, and which ones they might not be able to afford, the Green Bay Packers extended defensive tackle Devonte Wyatt to a three-year, $57 million contract on Monday. If that news doesn’t seem that relevant, it should, because Kobie Turner is up for an extension too and he’s a defensive tackle who the Rams may consider on par with Wyatt. Should Turner cost more, less, or the same as Devonte Wyatt? 𝗕𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗞𝗜𝗡𝗚: Packers are signing star DL Devonte Wyatt to a 3-year $57M extension, per @Schultz_Report pic.twitter.com/8IbD0Ll1kG — JPA (@jasrifootball) July 20, 2026 Who is Devonte Wyatt? A first-round pick out of Georgia in 2022, Wyatt won a national championship and was then added to Green Bay’s defense alongside college teammate Quay Walker. However, Wyatt’s first three seasons were a little bit underwhelming, starting only five games and playing in fewer than 45 percent of the team’s snaps. Wyatt’s season was somewhat better in 2025, playing in 60 percent of the snaps, but also missing seven games with a broken fibula and a torn ankle ligament. That didn’t stop the Packers from extending him to a contract that pays $19 million per season. Clearly the Packers value Wyatt as an integral part of their defensive line and now he’s making almost $20 million AAV. If that’s the case, then how much will Turner want? Kobie Turner’s comparison Wyatt was set to enter the fifth-year option, so his situation was a little bit different than Turner’s. Green Bay already owed him a lot of money going into a contract year, but Turner’s 2026 salary is only $3.9 million . Wyatt’s was set to be $12.9 million, so that gave him more leverage from a contract standpoint. Turner has more leverage when you consider their football accomplishments. Whereas Wyatt has 14.5 sacks and 86 tackles in 41 games since 2023, Turner has 24 sacks and 167 tackles in 51 games over the same period of time. The best ability is availability. Wyatt’s contract places him as the 18th-highest paid defensive tackle by salary. Turner’s next contract is likely to put him in the top-8 Turner may instead be looking at Alim McNeill as a baseline, with $24.5 million per season. The Detroit Lions’ defensive tackle doesn’t get as many sacks as Turner, but should be seen as a comparable player. Can the Rams afford to pay over $25 million for Turner? Is Turner the guy you keep? With so many outstanding contracts on the Rams’ roster, including almost the entire offensive line and Puka Nacua, L.A. has a difficult decision ahead with Kobie Turner. He’s productive, but many fans have argued his production is aided by scheme and teammates. That skepticism won’t be getting any quieter with Myles Garrett on the team…and Aaron Donald possibly joining them next. The Packers valued Wyatt at $19 million per season, so Turner’s next contract will have to be considerably more than that. Is it something the Rams can afford, or is it something that will cost them too much?
author: Kenneth Arthur

title: Is Matthew Stafford the reason for Puka Nacua’s success?
summary: Puka Nacua is one of the most productive and successful receivers in the NFL right now, but would he be among the league’s top weapons if not for Matthew Stafford? If most of his success is credited to Stafford, then the time will come for the Los Angeles Rams to trade or part ways with […]
full_text: Puka Nacua is one of the most productive and successful receivers in the NFL right now, but would he be among the league’s top weapons if not for Matthew Stafford? If most of his success is credited to Stafford, then the time will come for the Los Angeles Rams to trade or part ways with Nacua, which will probably be shortly after the quarterback retires. On the other hand, if Nacua is an elite weapon for any quarterback, then he’d be the perfect player to keep long-term for Ty Simpson. It’s sort of like the chicken and the egg for quarterbacks and receivers: Who deserves more credit? The wrong answer could cost the Rams over $100 million. Rams must keep options open As I wrote last week, the Rams should extend Nacua, but with the caveat that they need to have options to part ways when Stafford calls it quits : Given Nacua’s talent as a receiver and importance to Matthew Stafford, a contract extension is reasonable. Given Nacua’s balls-to-the-wall physical playing style that often gets him hurt and his potential for distractions, a deal that gives the Rams options to part ways would be prudent. That piece was about the correlation between the top-paid wide receivers and the teams making the playoffs. Surprisingly, or not, spending top dollars on a receiver didn’t work out for the majority of those teams. In fact, 12 of the top-15 receivers with the highest cap hits in 2026 were on teams that missed the playoffs. Is that what the Rams will become if they have Puka and not Stafford? I’m assuming for the sake of this article that the Rams will extend Puka Nacua’s contract because they need him right now. As we’ve seen with some recent trades, like the ones involving A.J. Brown and Sauce Gardner, options to make a deal can be open even shortly after an extension is signed. Nacua is important for Stafford, and Stafford is important to Nacua. But given that one of those players is taking his retirement plans on a “year to year” basis, half of the equation could be gone by 2027 or 2028. At which point, the Rams may need to re-evaluate Nacua’s value even after signing an extension. Can Nacua be “Puka” without Stafford? Stafford’s history with top WRs Two years from now there will be a host of variables to consider regarding Nacua staying with the team or not. Has 13 personnel eroded the need for a stud receiver? Is Puka still healthy or has he been injured and missing games? But the most important variable, as far as I’m concerned, is whether Stafford is still the quarterback or not. When he was on the Detroit Lions, Stafford helped Calvin Johnson produce Hall of Fame caliber stats, including three straight first-team All-Pro seasons from 2011 to 2013. We rarely saw Johnson without Stafford, but he was always at his best with Stafford. When Stafford got to the Rams, he immediately helped Cooper Kupp go from a fantastic receiver to being the best receiver in the NFL in 2021. Were it not for Kupp’s injuries, their relationship would have been even more productive. Kupp wasn’t the same last season in Seattle without Stafford, although he was older. He’s also an example of when an extension can go wrong, as Kupp didn’t come close to producing the value needed from a three-year, $80 million deal signed in 2022. When Stafford went down that year, so did the entire team. Stafford has been the constant in three separate record-setting seasons. Most receiving yards in a year: Calvin Johnson with 1,964 in 2012, followed closely by Cooper Kupp’s 1,947 in 2021. In 2023, Stafford helped Nacua set the record for most receiving yards for a rookie with 1,486. Plain and simple, Stafford makes his receivers better. Nacua is best suited for Rams And that’s not necessarily a good thing. ESPN’s Bill Barnwell recently explained why Smith-Njigba was worth more than Nacua in a trade : “ There are teams that would also (correctly) believe that Nacua is a better fit for Sean McVay’s offense than he would be for anyone else .“ If Stafford retires in 1-2 years, the Rams will need to take a long, hard look at Nacua’s value as it applies to the rest of the team in terms of affordability. They’d also have to assume that whoever takes over as QB won’t have the ability to maximize Nacua’s production quite the way Stafford has been able to, even if that quarterback is Ty Simpson and they really like his two years of development behind the scenes. An extension would run from 2027 onward, but a trade could be financially viable by 2028. Preferably 2029, for cap purposes, but teams are more capable of ever than moving players before the time is right. So now is the optimum time to extend Nacua, avoid a franchise tag situation, and keep the most important offensive relationship together for as long as possible. However, if Stafford is more responsible for Puka’s success than Puka himself, the Rams will need to have all options available to them when the quarterback decides he’s had enough success for a career.
author: John Newman

title: One fun fact about every offensive player on the Rams’ 90-man roster
summary: Training camp is finally almost here, which means football is thankfully, mercifully around the corner. In just a few days, 90 players will battle for 53 roster spots and a chance to play for one of the top Super Bowl contenders in the NFL this season. That makes this a great time to meet those […]
full_text: Training camp is finally almost here, which means football is thankfully, mercifully around the corner. In just a few days, 90 players will battle for 53 roster spots and a chance to play for one of the top Super Bowl contenders in the NFL this season. That makes this a great time to meet those players. Below is a list of every offensive player currently listed on the Los Angeles Rams roster with one fun fact about them. Some of the facts are about football, some are about their college careers specifically, some are totally off the board. We also included special teamers on this list. Without further ado, let’s learn something about this year’s offensive Rams: Davante Adams – Wide receiver Adams has 13 more touchdown receptions than anyone else in the NFL since 2020 with 73 (Mike Evans is next with 60). Davis Allen – Tight end In high school, Allen played both ways and was the region and country defensive player of the year at Calhoun High School in Calhoun, Georgia. AJ Arcuri – Offensive lineman He was a five-time Academic All-Big Ten selection at Michigan State. Steve Avila – Offensive lineman With a 79 overall, he was the 79 th -highest rated offensive lineman in last year’s Madden video game. Stetson Bennett – Quarterback His parents met at the University of Georgia School of Pharmacy and were pharmacists at a Publix grocery store when he was born. Austin Blaske – Offensive lineman Won two national championships in college at Georgia (as a teammate of Stetson Bennett) before transferring to North Carolina for his fifth and sixth years. Wyatt Bowles – Offensive lineman Bowles has 180 connections on LinkedIn. Matthew Caldwell – Quarterback He played for four colleges in five years with 30 career games played. Joe Cardona – Long snapper Became the fourth long snapper ever drafted when he went in the fifth round of the 2015 NFL draft to the New England Patriots. Dean Connors – Running back Connors knows how to juggle. Blake Corum – Running back Corum finished second in the NFL in rushing EPA last season (among 49 qualified running backs). CJ Daniels – Wide receiver One of two NFL players from high school’s graduating class, joining long snapper Julian Ashby of the Patriots. Justin Dedich – Offensive lineman Allowed 1.33 goals per game as a high school soccer goalkeeper. Kevin Dotson – Offensive lineman He is the 16th-highest paid guard in the NFL based on total contract value. Tru Edwards – Wide receiver Edwards’s father, Troy, was the Biletnikoff Award winner for the best wide receiver in Division I college football in 1998. Ethan Evans – Punter He is one of three NFL players to ever have come from Division II Wingate University (also including former NFL cornerback David Jones and linebacker Kenwin Cummings). Terrance Ferguson – Tight end Ferguson became the highest-drafted tight end out of Oregon since 1975 when the Rams took him with the 46th-overall selection in 2025. Bryce Henderson – Offensive lineman Before transferring to Vanderbilt, Henderson was a second-team All-Missouri Valley Football Conference selection at South Dakota in 2024. Tyler Higbee – Tight end In 2020, Higbee tallied the only rushing attempt of his 10-year career: A first-quarter one-yard gain against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Jarquez Hunter – Running back Hunter shares a birthday with the late Mary Tyler Moore (December 29). Alaric Jackson – Offensive lineman Jackson was called for four false start penalties in 2024. In the rest of his career, he’s only been called for nine penalties of any kind. Rohan Jones – Tight end He was named team captain at two different high schools. Max Klare – Tight end Klare finished his career at Ohio State, but while at Purdue he once had a strak of 17 consecutive games with multiple receptions. Beaux Limmer – Offensive lineman There are only two players in the NFL with the name “Beaux.” That includes Limmer, as well as New York Giants wide receiver Beaux Collins. Warren McClendon Jr. – Offensive lineman His uncle Willie and cousin Bryan both attended Georgia (like Warren) and also both played for the Chicago Bears (although Bryan never made the 53-man roster). Dylan McMahon – Offensive lineman McMahon was born exactly one year to the day earlier than Caitlin Clark. Harrison Mevis – Kicker Mevis set the SEC record for longest field goal with a 61-yard game winner to beat Kansas State in Sept. 2023. Konata Mumpfield – Wide receiver He recorded his first-career catch in Week 6 last season, a seven-yard gain in a win over the Baltimore Ravens. Puka Nacua – Wide receiver His given first name is actually “Makea,” while Puka is a nickname that means “ fat and chubby ” in Samoan (it was given to him as a baby). Colby Parkinson – Tight end Between three years at Stanford and six years in the NFL, Parkinson has only fumbled once (Week 1 of last season versus the Houston Texans; he lost the fumble, but the Rams won the game). Brennan Presley – Wide receiver At Oklahoma State, Presley caught 315 passes in his five seasons, the 14th-most in FBS history. David Quessenberry – Offensive lineman He is one of the 50 oldest players currently on an NFL roster. Mark Redman – Tight end There is no relation between him and 2006 MLB All-Star pitcher Mark Redman . Ronnie Rivers – Running back Rivers once won $514,000 playing poker in Las Vegas . Tyler Scott – Wide receiver Three Cincinnati Bearcats were named to Bruce Feldman’s College Football Freaks list in 2022, all of whom, including Scott, are now in the NFL (also including wide receiver Tre Tucker of the Las Vegas Raiders and tight end Josh Whyle of the Green Bay Packers). Coleman Shelton – Offensive lineman Shelton only started two games in his first three years in the NFL (all in Year 3), but has started every game he’s played in the last four seasons (including all 17 games the last three years). Ty Simpson – Quarterback His father, Jason, is the head coach for the University of Tennessee at Martin football team. Xavier Smith – Wide receiver Smith spent a year after high school working at Amazon before his mother and coworkers encouraged him to continue pursuing football at Florida A&M. Matthew Stafford – Quarterback Did you know Matthew Stafford played high school football with Clayton Kershaw? All right, fine. Stafford owns the NFL single-season record for the most fourth-quarter comebacks by a quarterback with eight (accomplished with the Detroit Lions in 2016). Keagen Trost – Offensive lineman Trost is a 25-year-old rookie who spent seven years in college football between four schools. Dan Villari – Tight end Villari started his college career as a quarterback, throwing three passes across four appearances for Michigan in 2021. Jordan Waters – Running back The St. Louis Battlehawks selected Waters on Day 2 of this past winter’s UFL draft before eventually signing a futures deal with the Rams in February. Jordan Whittington – Wide receiver He has nine brothers and sisters, seven of which are older than him. Kyren Williams – Running back Williams attended the same high school as James Gladstone, currently the general manager for the Jacksonville Jaguars and the former director of scouting for the Rams, a position he held when Williams was drafted. Mario Williams – Wide receiver A member of the 2022 USC team that lost the Cotton Bowl to Tulane, Williams left USC two seasons later and transferred to Tulane. Now, when your friends ask you “Who’s this guy?” when they read a report from training camp, you can share a fun fact and look like the smartest fan around. Stay tuned for defensive list.
author: Brendan Dzwierzynski

title: L.A. Rams News: What will the Aaron Donald talk be this week?
summary: Is Aaron Donald coming back to the Los Angeles Rams? Is Aaron Donald not coming back to the Los Angeles Rams? Does anyone know what’s going to happen? I don’t, and I expect another week of speculation, but who knows? Maybe AD makes a decision this week. It’s big new for the Rams who would […]
full_text: Is Aaron Donald coming back to the Los Angeles Rams? Is Aaron Donald not coming back to the Los Angeles Rams? Does anyone know what’s going to happen? I don’t, and I expect another week of speculation, but who knows? Maybe AD makes a decision this week. It’s big new for the Rams who would seemingly love to have Donald back. Would Donald love to be back? Great question. We’ll see. In the meantime, enjoy the speculation, enjoy the possibilities. We should have an answer soon enough. Training camp for the Rams starts Saturday so maybe we’ll know by then? Stay tuned. Thank you for checking out Turf Show Times and have a great Monday! Why Aaron Donald may make surprising decision amid Rams rumors (yardbarker) “On Monday, NFL insider Albert Breer of Sports Illustrated explained why fans shouldn’t yet assume that Donald will be on the Rams’ active roster in September. Aaron Donald has been “very happy in retirement” “Donald was very happy in retirement, and never ruminated to those in the organization that he wanted to come back,” Breer wrote. “In other words, this isn’t a guy who has had some enormous struggle adjusting to civilian life. The 10-time Pro Bowler is a happy retiree, by all accounts, which is to say the idea of going back to that life isn’t something he’ll view as a failure.” Los Angeles Rams’ trade for Myles Garrett looks even better after NFL evaluators reveal their true feelings about Jared Verse (atozsports) “Verse is a quality run defender. Nobody disputes that. But it becomes difficult to classify any edge rusher as truly elite when he finishes a healthy season with 4.5 sacks. The analytics community will point to pressures, hurries, and how Verse affects the pocket. Those metrics have value. But the NFL is a results-based business, and the most valuable result a pass rusher can deliver is putting the quarterback on the ground. A sack is an immediate loss of yards. It moves the chains backward. It helps the defense get off the field, which gives the offense more opportunities to score. A pressure or a forced throw can influence an outcome, but a sack guarantees one.“ Puka Nacua on whether he wants to stay with Rams: ‘That’s the plan’ (ramswire) “However, despite not having a deal in hand, Nacua remains committed to the goals of this season and he hopes to secure a long-term deal for the future. According to NFL reporter Arye Pulli, when questioned about whether he wants to remain in Los Angeles, Nacua recently stated that staying with the Rams is his intent. “That’s the plan,” Nacua said at Fanatics Fest.“ Training camp will answer nagging Rams draft question still awaiting verdict (ramblinfan) “While sixth-rounder CJ Daniels will have every chance to claim the WR3 mantle for himself, he is not the default frontrunner that a first-rounder or a Day 2 pick could have been. As a result, the team will stage a wide-open melee during training camp and into the preseason to determine who, if anyone, is ready to step up as a third option. The outcome will also provide a verdict as to whether selecting quarterback Ty Simpson with the 13th pick, rather than a win-now contributor, was a mistake that will materially hurt LA’s Super Bowl hopes this season.“

title: Rookies with best chance to be Week 1 starters on Las Vegas Raiders’ roster
summary: While the 2026 NFL draft class is considered a foundational piece of the Las Vegas Raiders’ roster/rebuild, none of the 10 players drafted are currently slated to be a starter heading into training camp, according to Ourlads’ depth chart. Of course, the pecking order that the coaches have is what’s really important, and players can […]
full_text: May 20, 2026; Henderson, NV, USA; Las Vegas Raiders safety Treydan Stukes (31) practices during organized team activities at Intermountain Health Performance Center. Mandatory Credit: Candice Ward-Imagn Images | Candice Ward-Imagn Images While the 2026 NFL draft class is considered a foundational piece of the Las Vegas Raiders’ roster/rebuild, none of the 10 players drafted are currently slated to be a starter heading into training camp, according to Ourlads’ depth chart . Of course, the pecking order that the coaches have is what’s really important, and players can earn their spots during training camp. But the former isn’t public information yet; camp is still about a week away from getting going, and there isn’t an obvious rookie starter right now. Even the No. 1 pick of the draft is expected to begin the summer and regular season as a backup. So, which rookies have the best chance to be a Week 1 starter when the Raiders host the Miami Dolphins on Sept. 13? QB Fernando Mendoza As referenced above, Mendoza is entering training camp behind Kirk Cousins as the starting quarterback in Las Vegas. But let’s be honest, this “competition” is more about the rookie being ready for NFL action than anything else. The coaches, and even Cousins, have said that the best quarterback needs to be on the field, regardless of experience. If the Indiana product can hit the ground running and prove that he’s ready to go, then the plan to have Cousins be the bridge-gap starter goes out the window. S Treydan Stukes Part of the uncertainty surrounding Stukes being a starter is centered around what position Rob Leonard and Co. want to play him at. The second-rounder was primarily a nickelback at Arizona, but the Raiders also traded for Taron Johnson to cover the slot. It seems like the former Wildcat’s best chance at being a Week 1 starter is by beating out Isaiah Pola-Mao for the free safety role. Pola-Mao struggled at that spot last year, and Stukes has the traits to be a quality backend defender in the NFL. It’s just a matter of how quickly he can pick up the position. CB Jermod McCoy The health of McCoy’s knee has been one of the biggest looming questions in Vegas since the organization drafted him roughly three months ago. But it’s a situation where if he’s healthy and can get back to his 2024 form, the fourth-round pick is the most talented cornerback on the roster. Obviously, there are a few major variables in that equation, but there is a situation where the Tennessee product beats out Darien Porter for a starting spot. DT Brandon Cleveland Outside of McCoy, the pickings start to get slim after the second round when it comes to immediate starters. Third-rounders Keyron Crawford and Trey Zuhn III both have several players ahead of them on the depth chart, while Mike Washington Jr. was drafted to complement Ashton Jeanty. Then, Dalton Johnson is a long shot to beat out Jeremy Chinn at free safety, and Malik Benson has a murky path to the starting lineup since he’s a similar type of receiver as Tre Tucker and Jalen Nailor. Ironically, the last player drafted by the Raiders this offseason has a somewhat direct route to be a first-stringer. The defensive tackle group as a whole is pretty weak, and the unit could use a quality run-stuffer. That’s where Cleveland, whose calling card is stopping the run from multiple alignments, has a decent chance to be a Week 1 starter despite the round he was selected in. It might be a long shot since there are plenty of competitors at defensive tackle. But with no one at the position locked into a starting job heading into camp, the NC State product has a fighter’s chance. Wildcard: CB Hezekiah Masses Masses is a “wildcard” since McCoy has more talent and thus the better chance to start, and it’d be pretty unlikely that Eric Stokes loses his spot after getting paid in the offseason. However, the Cal product reportedly had a good showing during OTAs and minicamp to turn some heads, getting some run with the first-team defense while McCoy was on a pitch count. The fifth-round corner had really good ball production at Cal last season, recording five interceptions and 13 PDs . That could show up and standout during training camp.

title: Las Vegas Raiders Summer Scouting: WR Rankings
summary: I broke down the 2027 scouting classes in my early summer scouting series, and the room has a ton of potential with a long list of potential standout players. I broke down the offense and defense in articles and I suggest reading those for a broad aspect of the room. These rankings are extremely early, […]
full_text: Indiana's Charlie Becker (80) heads toward the endzone as Miami's Jakobe Thomas (8) pursues and Romanas O.J. Frederique Jr. (29) looks to tackle during the College Football Playoff National Championship college football game at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens on Monday, Jan. 19, 2026. | Rich Janzaruk/Herald-Times / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images I broke down the 2027 scouting classes in my early summer scouting series, and the room has a ton of potential with a long list of potential standout players. I broke down the offense and defense in articles and I suggest reading those for a broad aspect of the room. These rankings are extremely early, and they will evolve over not only the summer but the next 8-10 months throughout the season, and into draft season. Some lists will feature 10, 15, 20, or more ranked prospects but I’ll include others on the list below to note. Jeremiah Smith, Ohio State – 6’3, 225, Jr Smith has broken into the notion for 2027 since his freshman season, and he’s not only arguably the top player in the 2027 class but also the best Ohio State WR in the last 5-6 years. Smith has an elite frame, has a career 163 receptions, 2558 yards, and 27 touchdowns. He has an electric release package, explosive release out of cuts, shows an elite ability to go out of his frame, work the boundary, and come down with a ton of high contested catches. Smith’s route running is smooth, fluid, and he has elite hip flexibility to dip and run in his routes. He’ll convert to YAC situations well, and has the elite blue chip WR mentality. Cam Coleman, Texas – 6’3, 205, Jr Coleman doesn’t get enough credit largely because of Smith. He’s headed to his first year with the Longhorns, and is coming off a 708 yard, 56 reception season for Ole Miss. Coleman is an exceptional athlete, likely better than Smith, his route running is much improved, and he has a tremendous amount of lower body agility. Coleman works well in a ton of concepts, is an electric YAC threat with his start stop ability. Coleman has exceptional deceleration, sinks his hips, and drives on the ball or route concept to make a play on the ball. He pairs that with twitch, physical profile, and a mentality to get the ball through contact. He’ll need to improve the drops, but he’s not far off Jeremiah Smith. Charlie Becker, Indiana – 6’4, 208, R-So A breakout end to 2025 put Becker on the map, and he’s among the best pure athletes at the position. Becker was arguably the best, or second best receiver on the Hoosiers last year, and he shows an elite ability to explode off the line of scrimmage, runs fluid routes, and he controls his body well. Becker is by far the best contested catch receiver in the class, he’s shown a tremendous ability to go up and get the ball, tracks it well though the air, and his concentration through traffic is exceptional. Becker has smooth feet, quick hips, and he’s an advanced route runner. YAC is a strong point, as is his ability to transition throughout concepts, drive on the ball, and he’s also shown a diverse route tree. Becker has a chance to cement himself as the third receiver in the class with a full season of 2026. Omarion Miller, Arizona State – 6’2, 210, Jr The top of the 2027 WR class is big, and Miller’s the smallest but he’s absolutely rocked up and shows a ton of physical traits. A breakout 2025 saw him log 808 yards, 8 touchdowns, and 45 receptions for Colorado, and the Arizona State offense should feature him similar to Jordyn Tyson. Miller is an elite short yardage receiver, has an explosive step off the LOS, works his cuts well, and is juiced up at the position with a ton of athletic traits. miller sinks his hips well, he flys downfield, and as a YAC threat he’s among the best in the class with his lower body athletic ability. His hands are adequate, with a 8% drop rate in 2025, and he’s not one to take away the ball in contested catch situations. I’d also like to see him do better driving back on the ball, and his deceleration looks a bit clunky but he’s effective. Mario Craver, Texas A&M – 5’9, 175, Jr The smallest of the top five receivers, he’s a true short yardage receiver. Craver will step into the role that KC Concepcion left, he has a ton of raw traits and his overall immediate acceleration is electric. Craver has an ability to separate from receivers, track the ball over his shoulder, and he has tremendous short area burst out of cuts. Craver does well working from the slot, he can beat press coverage, and he’s a smart receiver showing a ton of IQ against man and zone coverage with an ability to find open spots in coverage, use leverage against DBs, and also stem his route into a concept. I’d like to see him add more muscle to stay dynamic, and I’d also like to see Craver work more on the sideline. Wyatt Young, Oklahoma State – 6’0, 200, R-So Young is a prototypical “big slot” he has quick acceleration, is extremely efficient, and a great YAC threat. Young cuts well, has fluid lower body mechanics, and he can work through contact well. He’s able to work a variety of route concepts, has a deep understanding of leverage, coverage schemes, and knows when the flip back to the quarterback. Young had a tendency over the middle to let the ball come to him, and I’d like to see him attack the ball out of his frame more often but the pure raw strength, lower body flexibility, and YAC makes him intriguing. He’ll get the first chance to continue on his 2025 season (70 rec, 1264 yards, 10 TD) at the next level going from North Texas to Oklahoma State. Eric Singleton, Florida – 5’10, 190, Sr Nick Marsh, Indiana – 6’3, 205, Jr Marsh is big, he’s physical, and he’s got good athleticism. He can work at Z, X, and in the slot with good explosiveness, initial acceleration, and he shows a ton of twitch and explosion throughout the route concept start to end. Marsh has good footwork, he’s a sharp route runner, and does best with the ball in his hands using his explosiveness, lower body flexibility, and IQ to his advantage. He’ll need to refine his ability in contested catch situations, with average physicality, and his ability to work back to the ball is an issue as well. Marsh is the 2nd option in the Indiana offense, but he’s excelled the last two seasons with Michigan State focused heavily on the intermediate and short yardage. Ryan Coleman-Williams, Alabama – 6’0, 185, Jr I’ll talk quick here, but Williams can easily be at the top of this board, as many thought he’d be after the 2024 season with 860+ yards in his first season. His drop rate spiked in 2025 to 14%, he’s got tremendous athleticism, ball skills, and YAC traits but he struggled to find the ball in space last year, suffered concentration drops, and his route tree was limited. This isn’t a “make or break” year but with a good year Coleman-Williams can easily become a round one name. Junior Sherrill, Vanderbilt – 5’11, 190, R-Jr Evan Stewart, Oregon – 6’0, 175, R-So TJ Moore, Clemson – 6’3, 200, R-So Ian Strong, California – 6’3, 215, R-Jr Strong has a tremendous frame, but consistency has flagged him. He’s explosive downfield, has fluid hips, and he does show the ability to be an excellent Z option or 4th receiver. Strong is in a new offense at Cal, which should allow him to be more versatile, and establishing a diverse route tree is big for his draft stock. The frame, lower body athleticism, and strength is crucial and it showed last year in a junior season with 52 receptions, 762 yards, and 5 touchdowns. Ryan Wingo, Texas – 6’2, 217, R-Jr Jordan Faison, Notre Dame – 6’0, 210, R-Jr Faison was a lacrosse player who converted to football, and he’s established a good career with a ton of upside. He was the focal point of the Notre Dame passing game in 2025 with 49 receptions, 640 yards, and 4 touchdowns. Faison has a ways to go technique wise, but his lower body athleticism is exceptional. He has elite start/stop ability, is an exceptional YAC receiver, and understands the game well. Faison…

title: Raiders 2026 season: Who could go worst to first?
summary: In the NFL, turnarounds can be fast and dramatic. Teams go from being one of the dregs of the league one season to a Super Bowl contender the next nearly every year. Let’s take a look at the eight teams that finished in last place in 2025 to see which teams have the best chance […]
full_text: In the NFL, turnarounds can be fast and dramatic. Teams go from being one of the dregs of the league one season to a Super Bowl contender the next nearly every year. Let’s take a look at the eight teams that finished in last place in 2025 to see which teams have the best chance of going from worst to first: Detroit Lions: We’re not going to overthink this and take it simple. The Lions were tied for last place in the NFC North with the Minnesota Vikings with a 9-8 record. They’re a winning team. They’re still dangerous. Yes, the NFC North is talented, but so are the Lions. With a little luck they didn’t get last season, they can win the division. New Orleans Saints: The Saints won four of their final five games last season and finished 6-11. Thus, they have momentum heading into this season. If Tyler Slough continues to show he can be a solid starter, the Saints can easily win a very winnable NFC South. Tennessee Titans: We’re dropping a tier here. But keep an eye on Tennessee. I’m a believer in Robert Saleh. If Cam Ward can take a big leap and the Jacksonville Jaguars and Houston Texans regress some, this is a possible worst-to-first squad. New York Giants: I know the Giants a flavor of the moment and a favorite worst-to-first candidate. The reasons are clear: They have a talented young staff and a top head coach in John Harbaugh. Still, I’m not sure its going to result in instance success. One of those reasons is the NFC East is fairly strong. New York Jets: We’re dropping another tier. I think any of the four remaining teams are longshots to win their division. I’m not a big believer in the Jets and the AFC East is tough. Las Vegas Raiders: If Klint Kubiak and Fernando Mendoza are the real deals in their new roles, anything is possible. But, man, the AFC West is ridiculously strong. So, it won’t be easy. Cleveland Browns: The Browns are bad. More power to them. I just don’t see it. Arizona Cardinals: I don’t think the Cardinals are the worst team on this list and they can show improvement. But come on; the rest of the NFC West teams are all serious playoff contenders and among the best teams in the league. Good luck, Arizona. Join the conversation! title: What will Brock Bowers be worth when he’s extension eligible?
summary: Recently, the tight end market began to move and it’s something Brock Bowers and the Las Vegas Raiders will be monitoring in the next year or so. Bowers, the Raiders’ brilliant first-round draft pick in 2024, will be eligible for a contract extension next offseason, after his third NFL season. I would expect the Raiders […]
full_text: HENDERSON, NEVADA - MAY 28: Brock Bowers #89 of the Las Vegas Raiders attends a news conference after an OTA offseason workout at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center on May 28, 2026 in Henderson, Nevada. (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Recently, the tight end market began to move and it’s something Brock Bowers and the Las Vegas Raiders will be monitoring in the next year or so. Bowers, the Raiders’ brilliant first-round draft pick in 2024, will be eligible for a contract extension next offseason, after his third NFL season. I would expect the Raiders to try to extend Bowers as soon as they are allowed to rather than hand his a fifth-year option. Bowers is a franchise player who the Raiders will want to retain for his entire career. There is no need to play games or delay extending him. The only question is just how much Bowers will make. The Atlanta Falcons just gave Kyle Pitts a three-year, $54 million extension and The Jacksonville Jaguars gave Brendan Strange a three-year, $48 million deal. Bowers will likely dwarf those contracts. Tight ends such as Tucker Kraft of the Green Bay Packers, Sam LaPorta of the Detroit Lions and Dalton Kincaid of the Buffalo Bills could all soon get extension as well. So, Bowers and the Raiders will be watching those deals. Right now, the top tight end contracts per year average belong to George Kuttle of the San Frnisico 49ers at $19.1 million a season and Trey McBride of the Arizona Cardinals at $19 millon a season. I would think Bowers can hit the $20-22 million a season range within the next calander year. And he’ll be worth every penny of the deal.

title: Von Miller comments about having his eye on the Raiders
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders franchise has a history of dealing with Pass Rusher Von Miller. The former defensive player of the year and Super Bowl MVP has haunted the Raiders’ tackle for most of the last decade. Miller is past his prime at 37, but he is still producing in the NFL on the back […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - JULY 11: Von Miller of the Washington Commanders looks on during UFC 329 at T-Mobile Arena on July 11, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders franchise has a history of dealing with Pass Rusher Von Miller. The former defensive player of the year and Super Bowl MVP has haunted the Raiders’ tackle for most of the last decade. Miller is past his prime at 37, but he is still producing in the NFL on the back end of his career. With the Washington Commanders’ last season, Miller had 36 pressures according to PFF, with nine sacks on the year. Even with losing a step, Miller can help any team’s pass rush as a mentor and player. While hosting the Sack Summit in Las Vegas, he was joined by Raiders pass rusher Maxx Crosby. He then became a guest on Crosby’s Rush podcast and discussed where he wants to play next season. When describing the type of team he wants to play for, he attempted to capture Crosby’s attention. “I would love to be on a team that has a great quarterback, a great pass rush, a system in place … (pauses to look at Crosby) Raiders!” The Raiders did add Kwity Paye and re-sign Malcolm Koonce. Miller would be a welcome addition. He can help out Sack Summit attendee Keyron Crawford develop into a better edge rusher, as well as other young players. John Spytek might not make the move, but Miller is open to the opportunity. title: Two Miami Dolphins make ESPN’s ‘All-Backup Team’
summary: After a major gutting — and restocking — of the Miami Dolphins’ depth-chart this offseason by new general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan, the team’s roster is lacking stars in the eyes of many personalities around the league. If you put stock into what the so-called experts are saying, it could be a very tough year for […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDNES, FL - JUNE 09: Miami Dolphins kicker Zane Gonzalez (45) practices field goal kicking during the Miami Dolphins OTA on Tuesday, June 9, 2026 at Baptist Health Training Complexr in Miami Gardens, FL (Photo by Peter Joneleit/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After a major gutting — and restocking — of the Miami Dolphins’ depth-chart this offseason by new general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan, the team’s roster is lacking stars in the eyes of many personalities around the league. If you put stock into what the so-called experts are saying, it could be a very tough year for the team from sunny South Florida. While players like running back De’Von Achane, center Aaron Brewer and linebacker Jordyn Brooks have received praise recently, it was two under-the-radar names that made Bill Barnwell’s fantasy “All-Backup Team” in an article released by ESPN on Monday morning. Offensive lineman Jamaree Salyer and kicker Zane Gonzalez were named by Barnwell as two rotational players who could play an important role for the Dolphins during the 2026 season. Here’s what the ESPN writer had to say about both: “Let’s get the kicker off the board! The Dolphins are one of the few teams with two veteran kickers on their roster, so Gonzalez is an easy pick for us after hitting 86.4% of his attempts last season in Atlanta. Salyer is a swing tackle who did a solid job at left tackle as a rookie in 2022 with the Chargers; having a sixth or seventh lineman with real experience on the blind side is a relative luxury.” Kickers are… well, kickers, but Barnwell’s point about Salyer could be a salient one if anyone on Miami’s offensive line is forced to miss time due to injury or insufficient play. Right tackle Austin Jackson has a long injury history, so him missing a game or two (or more) wouldn’t surprise anyone, but there’s also Jonah Savaiinaea at the right guard spot — a player who was rated as the worst guard in the league by Pro Football Focus for his dismal play during the 2025 NFL season. If Miami is forced to play a backup along the offensive line at any point during the upcoming year, they could do a whole lot worse than Salyer as a fill-in.

title: Vikings Training Camp Preview
summary: The Minnesota Vikings will begin training camp next week, beginning with rookies reporting on July 26th and veterans on July 28th. There will be a total of 13 practices open to fans, beginning with the August 1st practice and ending with the joint practices with the Ravens on August 19th and 20th. The first padded […]
full_text: EAGAN, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 11: Justin Jefferson #18 of the Minnesota Vikings looks on during training camp at Twin Cities Orthopedics Performance Center on August 11, 2025 in Eagan, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings will begin training camp next week, beginning with rookies reporting on July 26th and veterans on July 28th. There will be a total of 13 practices open to fans, beginning with the August 1st practice and ending with the joint practices with the Ravens on August 19th and 20th. The first padded practice is August 3rd. So what are some things to look for and camp battles that could play out? I’ve broken it down by position group. Managing Training Camp One thing that I felt happened last year in training camp was that it was too much about just getting through it healthy and not so much about preparing as much as possible for the regular season. Kevin O’Connell was pretty casual walking around and making jokes during training camp last year, coming off a 14-3 season, Coach of the Year award, and contract extension. Justin Jefferson was given training camp off after a minor hamstring injury, and other veterans missed a lot of time. He didn’t play starters much in preseason games either. I didn’t write much about it at the time- I thought I may be making too much out of the more casual approach- and there were legitimate reasons to hold players out and not play them much, but it’s something I’m paying more attention to this year. That more casual approach showed up in the first joint practice against the Patriots, who were a lot more physical and competitive as Mike Vrabel was looking to establish a culture as a new coach with a lot of young players who weren’t really expected to compete last season at that point. The Vikings did better the second day of joint practices, but the exercise did more to buoy the previously 4-13 Patriots than provide any momentum for the Vikings. Looking back, we can appreciate how valuable setting a tone can be early on. The Patriots went to the Super Bowl and Mike Vrabel won Coach of the Year. The previous year, Kevin O’Connell took advantage of everyone writing off the Vikings as a six-win team to give them a chip on their shoulder and set a tone that helped propel them to the 14-win season. So, given all that, it will be interesting to see what approach Kevin O’Connell takes toward training camp this year. Quarterback Of course all eyes will be on the competition between Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy for the starting quarterback job. Who gets first-team reps and how many? Who is more accurate? Who makes more mistakes? Who shows more flashes? How improved does McCarthy look compared to last year? Is Murray mastering the scheme or struggling to do so? How does the team react to each quarterback? Beyond those elements, is the competition really close or not? Is there enough visual evidence to determine who’s winning? What if things get tense during practices and it becomes a distraction? Will the loser handle it gracefully? Ultimately each quarterback will be measured on being able to call the play and lineup on time, make the right adjustments at the line, play with proper timing and mechanics, process and make progressions, and throw with timing and accuracy. Watching training camp doesn’t provide insight into all of those things, but sometimes we can judge a bit about some of the hidden elements by the quarterback’s comfort level. And making it uncomfortable for both will be Brian Flores’ defense. There are no actual sacks in training camp, but there are would-be sacks. Who is able to handle pressure better? Lastly, when does Kevin O’Connell declare a winner? Is there a gradual slide in reps toward the winner before it is declared or is it even until the end? How the competition is managed may be as important as the competition itself. Offensive Line The first thing to look for is the health of Christian Darrisaw. Is he still taking some practices off? If so, is it precautionary or because he still can’t handle a full load? All signs point to a fully healthy Darrisaw but sometimes later that doesn’t prove to be the case. A fully healthy Darrisaw would be a big improvement in the offensive line over last year when he missed half the season. The second thing about the offensive line is how they practice. Beat reporters commented several times during the offseason program that the offensive line was pushing the limits in terms of how hard they were practicing. What does it look like in training camp? Is new offensive line coach Keith Carter looking to establish more of an offensive line identity? How the interior offensive line fares against the interior defensive line in padded practices will be interesting as well. I would expect the offensive line to win against the rookies most of the time. If that’s not the case, there potentially are some positive and negative adjustments in expectations that would need to be made. The battles for the backup positions will be interesting to watch as well. Where the backups are playing may be as interesting as judging the competition. Who is competing for the backup center position? Does third-round pick Caleb Tiernan play tackle or guard- or some of both? Does Walter Rouse take snaps at guard? There are a lot of moving parts there and it will likely take some time to understand what the coaching staff vision is with the backups in this group. Running Backs Among the veterans, I’m curious how the reps will be divided. Does Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason split them evenly or what? Is there evidence of any changing role or workload? For the rookies Demond Claiborne and Max Bredeson, how many reps are they given and are they worked in with the starters at all? I’m particularly interested in how much Bredeson works with the starters as a sign of how big his role will be this season. Frank Smith used a fullback more in Miami than Kevin O’Connell has with the Vikings, so it will be interesting to see how big a role the Vikings are envisioning for Bredeson. Whether Demond Claiborne gets any significant first-team reps will also be interesting. Wide Receivers It will be interesting to see how involved Justin Jefferson is in training camp. I don’t think you could say his rapport with any of the Vikings quarterbacks is good at this point. What’s the plan there? And apart from better quarterback play, is there anything else on tap to get Jefferson back into prime form? Or doesn’t he need to practice? I expect Jordan Addison to be involved extensively. And I’m curious how Jauan Jennings will be used. For the backups, is there notable improvement from Tai Felton? Does Myles Price get many reps? What about Dillon Bell? Does he continue to stand out? I’m also curious which of the backups are given reps on special teams and how they look with them. Is Myles Price still the returner? Any significant competition? Tight Ends The main thing I’m looking for in this group is any signs of changing roles or usage that might signal an evolution in scheme. This is likely T.J. Hockenson’s last season with the Vikings after he was asked to restructure his contract- is there any sign of a changing role for him this season or is it business as usual? Edge Rushers I’m mainly interested in who the primary backups will be here and if Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins is in the mix as a true edge rusher. Are there any standouts among the backups? I’m also curious to see Dallas Turner battle Christian Darrisaw. Interior Defensive Line This group is likely to be a big focus in padded practices. How are the two top draft picks doing? Is there improvement among last year’s backups? Any standouts? Any surprises? Is Caleb Banks full-go? There is a bigger range of outcomes for this group this season with so many young players that any clues about their development will be newsworthy. Linebackers All eyes will be on second-round pick Jake Golday here. Does he get any reps with…

title: Big Citrus, Brad Childress & Jettas’ Bounce-Back: Vikings Camp Preview
summary: In this episode of the Two Old Bloggers podcast, hosts Darren Campbell and Dave Stefano deliver a must-listen deep dive for every Vikings fan starving for real football talk. The duo kicks off with a major announcement — Two Old Bloggers has officially joined the Bleav Network under their Vikings 1st & SKOL banner — […]
full_text: EAGAN, MINNESOTA - JUNE 10: Justin Jefferson #18 of the Minnesota Vikings participates in a drill during minicamp at Twin Cities Orthopedics Performance Center on June 10, 2026 in Eagan, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images In this episode of the Two Old Bloggers podcast, hosts Darren Campbell and Dave Stefano deliver a must-listen deep dive for every Vikings fan starving for real football talk. The duo kicks off with a major announcement — Two Old Bloggers has officially joined the Bleav Network under their Vikings 1st & SKOL banner — then pivots into the positions, players, and storylines that will define Minnesota’s 2026 season before a single live rep is taken in Eagan. With the Murray-McCarthy quarterback debate intentionally set aside, Darren and Dave zero in on what they’ll actually be watching when the pads come on. Darren is locked in on rookie defensive tackle Domonique “Big Citrus” Orange, calling him the best chance the Vikings have had to replace Linval Joseph’s run-stuffing dominance since his peak years. “The Vikings have not had a big dominant run-stuffing defensive tackle since Linval Joseph’s peak years in 2015 to 2018,” Darren noted. Linebacker Jake Golday also earns serious attention — Darren wants to see whether the 6’4″ Cincinnati product can leapfrog veteran Ivan Pace Jr. on the depth chart. Safety prospect Jakobe Thomas rounds out the rookie watch list, with Darren believing Brian Flores will find every possible way to use his do-it-all skill set if he translates his Miami production to the NFL level. On offense, the interior offensive line depth is flagged as a genuine vulnerability — with Blake Brandel’s elevation to center leaving the guard and center backups dangerously thin beyond Michael Jurgens (309 career snaps) and Joe Huber (89 snaps). The punter competition between veteran Johnny Hekker and Australian prospect Brett Thorson adds some late-July intrigue. In the episode’s “This Week in Vikings Land” segment, the guys discuss ESPN’s NFL positional rankings, where Justin Jefferson checked in at No. 2 at receiver — still elite, even after a down statistical year driven largely by poor quarterback play. Darren makes the case that Jefferson’s age (just turned 27), elite route running, and a healthier 2026 quarterback situation should produce a vintage Justin Jefferson season. “I think we will see him return to the kind of numbers we’re used to seeing from him,” Darren said. The guys also analyze Kyler Murray’s fit in the KOC offense, arguing his mobility and RPO ability can unlock dimensions of the Vikings’ passing attack that Kirk Cousins and Sam Darnold simply couldn’t provide. Finally, a detour into Brad Childress history — sparked by a local interview — gives Darren a chance to break down the three reasons Zygi Wilf pulled the plug in 2010: locker room dysfunction, unilateral roster moves (cutting Randy Moss without telling ownership), and a fan base that never embraced him. Key Points Two Old Bloggers officially joins the Bleav Network (Vikings 1st & SKOL) Rookie DT Domonique Orange is the top training camp watch — can he be a day-one starter? title: Who could be some potential Saints Training Camp surprises this year?
summary: Every year, teams go into training camp with predictions and expectations for certain position battles. This is a normal occurrence when coaches are trying to figure out their roster during the offseason, but sometimes, things change. An undrafted free agent who nobody expected to stand out has a great preseason/training camp, a veteran ends up […]
full_text: Sep 14, 2025; Miami Gardens, Florida, USA; Miami Dolphins quarterback Zach Wilson (0) looks on before a game against the New England Patriots at Hard Rock Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Nathan Ray Seebeck-Imagn Images | Nathan Ray Seebeck-Imagn Images Every year, teams go into training camp with predictions and expectations for certain position battles. This is a normal occurrence when coaches are trying to figure out their roster during the offseason, but sometimes, things change. An undrafted free agent who nobody expected to stand out has a great preseason/training camp, a veteran ends up regressing to the point of not being able to start, or a position battle goes the opposite way from what was predicted. When looking at the New Orleans Saints’ roster, it’s hard to say with full confidence that at least one of the outcomes above will happen. The Saints were able to improve the entire team this offseason, including the depth. This will trigger some heated position battles during training camp and preseason, and here are some outcomes that could surprise many. Zach Wilson wins QB2 When the Saints signed Zach Wilson this offseason, it was a shocking move many did not expect. Spencer Rattler was the likely QB2 for 2026, but it was clear the Saints still wanted to bring in competition. As of now, Rattler is the likely candidate to win the backup spot, but Wilson still has a path to that spot. Do not forget that Wilson was a former #2 overall selection. Yes, Wilson is considered to be a draft bust due to the beginning of his career, but the same title was put on Super Bowl-winning QB Sam Darnold, Tampa Bay Buccaneers starter Baker Mayfield, Indianapolis Colts starter Daniel Jones, and San Francisco 49ers QB Mac Jones, who is probably a year away from becoming a starter somewhere. QB development takes time, especially for a QB like Wilson, who was not ready to start in the NFL. If he finally feels comfortable in an offense and can develop under a staff that is built for that purpose, Wilson could have a really good training camp and preseason, which may lead to him winning the job. Brock Rechsteiner fills the last WR spot The area New Orleans made significant investment in this offseason was at WR, and it’s truly incredible to see how much can change in an offseason. Chris Olave, Jordyn Tyson, Devaughn Vele, Bryce Lance, and Barion Brown form an exciting group with versatility, talent, potential, and athleticism that the Saints have not seen in a long time. But with those 5 spots taken, that leaves 1 more spot to fill before the 53-man roster deadline. It’s going to be interesting to see what happens in this battle because of how many other WRs will be fighting for this last spot. Former New England Patriots WR Ja’lynn Polk is the favorite due to the chemistry he has built with the team and his potential, but one UDFA may put up a good fight. Brock Rechsteiner was a rookie mini-camp invitee who had already surprised many on the staff, leading the team to sign him right away. Rechsteiner is a more explosive player than Polk is, but Polk brings the contested catch ability that could really help this WR room. Drops have also been an issue in Polk’s young career, and if that continues and Rechsteiner becomes a consistent impact player, it would be hard for the Saints to go with Polk. Jeremiah Wright becomes the Saints’ starting RG Okay, here’s my long shot. When the Saints were going through their draft process, one prospect was probably the most likely selection I have seen since my time covering the Saints: Jeremiah Wright. He was projected to go on day 3, but the Saints kept getting linked with him and had many meetings with the player. It was clear early on that the Saints loved this player, even if he is more of a developmental prospect than others. They see the potential, and it’s likely that Wright is the long-term option at RG. So, if he still needs development, how can he become the starter? Well, that’s why this is a long shot. For this to happen, Cesar Ruiz would either have to be injured or really regress this offseason, which would be very unexpected. Then, Wright needs to show development and consistency throughout training camp and the pre-season. This is not an impossible outcome, just extremely unlikely.

Slayton is still here, though, and as the longest tenured player on the roster with Dexter Lawrence gone, there will be an opportunity for him to defy all those odds stacked against him yet again. Of course, his absence this spring after undergoing surgery to repair a sports hernia leaves open the chance that others will pass him by on the depth chart. Veterans Odell Beckham Jr., Juju Smith-Schuster and Braxton Berrios were all signed to fight for spots, while rookie Malachi Fields showed enough flash to earn more reps in camp. Seemingly every time critics say to not expect production from Slayton, he delivers. I could see that again in 2026. NFL players with the most on the line in 2026: One from every team | The Athletic New York Giants: Kayvon Thibodeaux, OLB. The Giants listened to trade calls on Thibodeaux this offseason, but elected to keep the No. 5 pick from the 2022 draft when the offers were underwhelming. Thibodeaux was available because the Giants traded for Brian Burns in 2024 and drafted Abdul Carter in 2025. Thibodeaux is set to earn $14.75 million on his fifth-year option as a backup. With a less talented roster, we need a quarterback who can get white-hot for stretches of time. Thibodeaux is likely to be the odd man out in a stacked group of edge rushers in New York. Brian Burns and Abdul Carter are the two primary starters, while first-round rookie Arvell Reese will also see snaps off the edge as a pass rusher. title: Ex-scout: 2 2nd-year Giants  set for a breakout year
summary: The New York Giants 2026 training camp is just a week away. With it we’ll get our first real look at how the next era of Giants’ football will take shape under John Harbaugh. The Giants’ recent history has alternated between disappointing seasons and nightmare seasons, with little to show for the constant losing. The […]
full_text: ﻿New York Giants edge defender Abdul Carter celebrates a play | Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images The New York Giants 2026 training camp is just a week away. With it we’ll get our first real look at how the next era of Giants’ football will take shape under John Harbaugh. The Giants’ recent history has alternated between disappointing seasons and nightmare seasons, with little to show for the constant losing. The team has had plenty of high draft picks, but they haven’t developed to lift the team out of the doldrums. Former NFL scout Bucky Brooks believes that could be at an end, and cites two Giants defenders on his 2026 All-Breakout defense . He believes that both edge defender Abdul Carter and defensive tackle Darius Alexander have the tools and opportunities to take dramatic leaps this year. Brooks notes that NFL pro personnel evaluators look at second and third year players who end the seasons strongly when evaluating which young players might be primed for breakout performances. Both Carter and Alexander played significantly better for Mike Kafka and Charlie Bullen than they did under Brian Daboll and Shane Bowen. This is what Brooks had to say about each: Abdul Carter – Edge defender The third overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft was expected to take the league by storm as a freakishly athletic pass rusher with disruptive skills. While Next Gen Stats credited Carter with 72 QB pressures — including a league-best 48 quick pressures (occurring in under 2.5 seconds) — his sack production was underwhelming, with just four on the season. I expect him to get home more often in 2026. Under new defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson, the Giants are preparing to unleash “organized chaos” via a quintet of rare athletes in the front seven: Carter, Brian Burns , Kayvon Thibodeaux , Arvell Reese and Tremaine Edmunds . Carter should see his numbers explode in Year 2 with plenty of one-on-one opportunities. Darius Alexander – Defensive tackle New York’s trade of decorated defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence to Cincinnati creates a huge opportunity for Alexander to flex his muscles as a disruptive force between the tackles. The 2025 third-round pick not only has a clear path to a starting role, but Roy Robertson-Harris ‘ season-ending injury will lead to more playmaking opportunities for the youngster on a sack-obsessed front line. After notching three sacks and three tackles for loss over his final six games in 2025, the 6-4, 310-pounder is primed for a breakout season as a key piece of the Giants’ rejiggered defensive puzzle. Chris’ thoughts First and foremost, the Giants absolutely need both of these players to live up to their pre-draft evaluations. Both have the potential to be impact players in the NFL, with rare athletic traits and the upside to be real problems for opposing players. I do agree with Brooks that their play down the stretch suggests a significant improvement in year two for both Carter and Alexander. The fact that both Brian Daboll and Shane Bowen were fired mid-season last year gives us a rare chance to do a relatively controlled A-B comparison for the defense, and the improved play is encouraging. Abdul Carter’ rate stats suggest that he can be a devastating pass rusher when he sets his mind to it, which he did after Kafka raised the levels of accountability. Carter’ explosiveness and lower-body fluidity are simply rare, and he moves like a young Von Miller. His ability to create quick pressure backs up the comparison, but the failures to finish speak to a young and inexperienced player who needs to pay closer attention to details in the biggest moments. John Harbaugh should keep the levels of accountability high, and Bullen remains to keep working with Carter on the finer points of his position. That bit of continuity, as well as a (hopefully) improved scheme under Wilson should create the kind of environment Carter needs to realize his potential. Likewise, Alexander improved steadily in the second half of the season. Part of Alexander’s slow start could have been missing much of his rookie off-season to an undisclosed injury. However, an improved attention to detail during the week under Bullen may have helped the Toledo product raise his game. Alexander became a regular presence in opponents’ backfields down the stretch last year. The absence of Dexter Lawrence, Rakeem Nunez-Roches, and Roy Robertson-Harris will give him the opportunity to build on the momentum Alexander established at the end of the year. The most frustrating aspect of the Giants’ defensive play the last couple years hasn’t exactly been the results. Rather, it’s the fact that they have a number of players at every level who should be better than they’ve been. The conversation around the Giants in general, and defense in particular, would be entirely different if young players like Carter, Alexander, Deonte Banks , and Tyler Nubin can all take a step forward. If they can play up to their potential and maintain the flashes we’ve seen, the Giants’ defense could be legitimately scary.
author: Chris Pflum

title: NY Giants training camp: Who will replace Gunner Olszewski?
summary: Spring practices did not really give us any hints on how the New York Giants will replace kick returner/punt returner/reserve wide receiver Gunner Olszewski, lost for the season to a torn Achilles tendon. We did review some of the options back in May, immediately after Olszewski’s injury. Let’s take an updated look at the situation […]
full_text: Gunner Olszewski watching the Giants practice this spring after tearing his Acghilles tendon. | Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images Spring practices did not really give us any hints on how the New York Giants will replace kick returner/punt returner/reserve wide receiver Gunner Olszewski, lost for the season to a torn Achilles tendon. We did review some of the options back in May , immediately after Olszewski’s injury. Let’s take an updated look at the situation with training camp almost here. Braxton Berrios Berrios was signed by the Giants on June 1, one of three wide receivers the Giants added after the Olszewski injury. In both skillset and experience, Berrios is the closest 1:1 potential replacement for Olszewski on the 90-man roster. A seven-year veteran, Berrios has handled similar responsibilities to Olszewski. Berrios has handled 100 punt returns in his career, for an impressive 11.3 yards per return average. On kickoffs, he has a 24.9-yard average on 91 returns. As a receiver, he has 140 catches, with a career-best of 46 with the New York Jets in 2021. He was a First-Team All-Pro that year, averaging 13.1 yards on punt returns and 30.4 on kickoff returns. The question for Berrios will be whether back-to-back injury-plagued seasons have taken some quickness and explosion away from him. Berrios suffered a torn ACL with the Miami Dolphins in 2024 and dealt with hamstring injuries while playing for the Houston Texans last season. He played in only 10 games over those two years. Where he could fit : Punt return, kickoff return, wide receiver depth Deonte Banks I almost didn’t put Banks on the list. If he is on the roster, which seems a safe bet provided he is healthy, Banks has to be part of the kickoff return tandem after what he did a season ago. After never having returned kickoffs before, Banks averaged 32.7 yards on 19 returns, second in the NFL in yards per return. No matter how good he ends up being at cornerback, Banks’ newfound success returning kickoffs could significantly extend his career. Where he could fit : Kickoff return Calvin Austin Before the signing of Berrios, Austin looked like the first option to replace Olszewski as the punt returner. He could still emerge with that role. Austin had an 8.9-yard average on 73 punt returns in three seasons with the Pittsburgh Steelers. Whether the Giants want to use him on punt return might be impacted by how much they rely on him as a slot receiver. Austin has no experience returning kickoffs. Where he could fit : Punt return Tyrone Tracy Tracy is one of the Giants’ playmakers. Rightly or not, he is probably going to get the short end of a running back time share with Cam Skattebo. The Giants have dabbled with using him as a kickoff returner the past seasons (eight returns, 24.1 yards per return). Using him in that role would be a way to put the ball in his hands on a few additional occasions. Tracy has practiced as a punt returner, but hasn’t done that in an NFL game. Where he could fit : Kickoff return Eric Gray Gray cannot be Option A as a returner. It is, in fact, difficult to see Gray finding a spot on the 53-man roster. Still, Gray has done both kickoff and punt return jobs for the Giants in his first three seasons. Not well — 4.0 yards averaged on seven punt returns, 24.2 yards averaged on 27 kickoff returns, and six fumbles over three seasons. Still, he has done both jobs and has to be considered. Where he could fit : Punt return, kickoff return Devin Singletary Singletary, 29, had only returned four kickoffs before the 2025 season. He returned 12 kickoffs for the Giants last season, averaging a solid 26.1 yards per return. Using Singletary in that role is probably not going to be Plan A, but he has shown he can do the job adequately if needed. Where he could fit : Kickoff return Damon Bankston An undrafted free agent running back, Bankston probably has to make an impression on kickoff return to have a chance to make the 53-man roster. He averaged 36.2 yards on 12 kickoff returns with two touchdowns for New Mexico State in 2025. A spot on the practice squad seems more likely. Where he could fit : Kickoff return Xavier Gipson The Giants have 14 wide receivers on their 90-man roster entering training camp. I would rank Gipson 14th, so Gipson would seem unlikely to make the 53-man roster. If he somehow does, the return game will have a lot to do with it. Over three seasons with the New York Jets and Philadelphia Eagles, Gipson averaged 9.1 yards on 74 punt returns and 25.9 yards on 51 kickoff returns. Unfortunately, Gipson has a habit of fumbling the football — 12 in 157 career touches as a returner, receiver, and rusher — and that cost him jobs with both the Jets and Eagles. Where he could fit : Punt return, kickoff return Dante Miller In three seasons with the Giants, “Turbo” has been on the active roster for two games and has never touched the ball. He figures as an extreme long shot to make the 53-man roster. Yet, his speed still has fans curious and still has him on an NFL roster with a chance. Even at age 27. Miller averaged 21.0 yards on two preseason kickoff returns last season, his only opportunities in that role in three preseasons.

title: NY Giants’ RB Cam Skattebo reacts to furor over failed backflip
summary: New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo went viral over the weekend for a backflip flop at Fanatics Fest in New York City. He reacted to the five-alarm fire that set off in some corners of the fanbase by promising not to get hurt before training camp. “I’m gonna address the elephant. I will not […]
full_text: Cam Skattebo | Getty Images for Fanatics New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo went viral over the weekend for a backflip flop at Fanatics Fest in New York City. He reacted to the five-alarm fire that set off in some corners of the fanbase by promising not to get hurt before training camp. “I’m gonna address the elephant. I will not hurt myself before the season,” Skattebo said Sunday during a Q and A on Sirius XM. Skattebo did admit to realizing during the flip that he wasn’t going to stick the landing. “Yeah, so what happened was, I don’t know if you guys know WWE or not, those floors are bouncy,” Skattebo said. “So when I took off, I was mid-air, like, holy cow, I’m not gonna land this, I’m way too high. Landed, but it had too much cushion. It wasn’t a stiff, firm ground. So that’s why I kinda like went back, safely landed, got back up, was good to go. So nothing came out from that. I’m perfectly fine. Nothing happened. We’re good.” Skattebo said he enjoys the wild man persona. “I totally enjoy that part. I think I less enjoy the brain dead kind of guy. But it is what it is,” Skattebo said. “I mean, the New York people love it, so I’m just gonna keep being me. And if they wanna say I’m brain dead and I don’t have no brain, then who cares? F— it, you know?” Most importantly, Skattebo, coming back from a severe right ankle dislocation, said he is “ready to go.” I mean, we did our throwing trip. Obviously I have to keep working and conditioning it and stuff, but we did our throwing trip and I mean, he (Jaxson Dart) can kind of tell you how I look,’“ Skattebo said. Dart agreed that the running back “looks great.” “I feel great. I would say the last two weeks of my training has felt the most normal, and it’s been excellent,” Skattebo said. “I feel great and I’m ready to go.” Giants fans just want him to stay that way.
